perOption.C: Gives the magnitude of the centripetal force in newtons.
perOption.D: Multiplies the centripetal force by the radius as if there were displacement along the radius.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q12.body: Each star’s gravitational pull supplies the other star’s centripetal force. For the star of mass $2M$, the separation is $3x$ and the orbital radius is $x$, so $GM(2M)/(3x)^2=(2M)x\omega^2$. This gives $\omega^2=GM/(9x^3)$ and $\omega=\tfrac13\sqrt{GM/x^3}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses $2M$ as the attracting mass for the star on the inner orbit.
perOption.C: Uses $2x$ as the separation in Newton’s law of gravitation.
perOption.D: Uses the orbital radius $x$ as the separation in Newton’s law of gravitation.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.body: For the fixed mass of gas, $T=pV/(nR)$. The products $pV$ at X, Y and Z are $(1.5\times10^6)(0.001)=1.5\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}$, $(0.4\times10^6)(0.003)=1.2\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}$ and $(0.4\times10^6)(0.005)=2.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}$, respectively. Therefore $T_Z>T_X>T_Y$, which is the ordering shown by A.

perOption.A: Correct. It gives the required temperature ordering.
perOption.B: Shows equal temperatures at X and Y despite their different $pV$ products.
perOption.C: Shows equal temperatures at X and Y and a fall to Z, though $pV$ is lowest at Y and highest at Z.
perOption.D: Treats Y to Z as isothermal even though volume increases at constant pressure.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.issues: A is the only option with the correct endpoint ordering, but its Y–Z segment curves upward. At constant pressure, T is proportional to V, so Y–Z must be a straight rising line. No option is fully correct.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q14.body: Mean translational kinetic energy is proportional to thermodynamic temperature. Argon and helium are at the same temperature, so their mean translational kinetic energies are equal and their ratio is $1$.

perOption.A: Uses the square of the inverse mass ratio as the energy ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the inverse mass ratio as the energy ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes that the heavier atom has the same mean-square speed as the lighter atom.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The key says hydrogen in its explanation where the question says helium.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.body:
The normal force $N$ is smallest at the highest point, where the downward acceleration is greatest. Weight acts downwards and the normal force acts upwards, so $mg-N=ma_{\max}$.

For SHM, $a_{\max}=\omega^2x_0$, giving $N=(60)(9.81)-(60)[2\pi(0.50)]^2(0.20)=470.1647\ \mathrm{N}\approx470\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Assumes contact is lost, which would require the platform’s downward acceleration to reach $g$.
perOption.B: Gives the downward resultant force at the highest point.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the normal force at zero acceleration.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The stem leaves vertical simple harmonic motion implicit. Frequency and amplitude alone do not determine the acceleration of a general oscillation.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.body:
At $t=1.0\ \mathrm{s}$ the pulse is between P and O and begins reflecting at the fixed end. At $t=1.5\ \mathrm{s}$ the inverted pulse has fully reflected and lies between P and O.

As it passes P from $1.5$ to $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$, P moves slightly downwards first, then farther upwards before returning to equilibrium.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses the order of the two lobes in the reflected trace.
perOption.C: Keeps the incident pulse’s signs, omitting inversion at the fixed end.
perOption.D: Swaps the relative sizes of the small downward and large upward lobes.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q17.body: The light at P is polarised along the first transmission axis, which makes an angle $180^\circ-(60^\circ+45^\circ)=75^\circ$ with the second transmission axis. Projecting the amplitude onto the second axis gives $A\cos75^\circ$ at Q.

perOption.A: Treats the two axes as sloping in the same direction and uses $15^\circ$.
perOption.B: Uses the second axis’s angle to the horizontal.
perOption.C: Uses the first axis’s angle to the vertical.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.body: Use the vertical fringe pattern to find the spacing of the horizontal threads. The measured span is between the two second-order spots, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}[(0.0548/2)/2.00]=0.7849^\circ$. From $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, with $n=2$ and $\lambda=685\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$, the spacing is $1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Treats the full 54.8 mm vertical span as the centre-to-first-order displacement.
perOption.B: Using the horizontal spot spacing gives the spacing of the vertical threads.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a diffraction angle much smaller than the angle fixed by the vertical spots and screen distance.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q19.body: The Rayleigh criterion gives $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b=(550\times10^{-9})/(1.8\times10^{-3})=3.05556\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad}$. Using the small-angle arc relation, $0.77\approx L_{\max}\theta_{\min}$, so $L_{\max}\approx2519.996\ \mathrm{m}$, giving $2500\ \mathrm{m}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses a distance at which the angular separation is about 110 times the limiting angle.
perOption.B: Uses a distance at which the angular separation is about 61 times the limiting angle.
perOption.C: Uses a distance at which the angular separation is about 9 times the limiting angle.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key uses the syllabus approximation θ ≈ λ/b. The circular-aperture Airy criterion gives about 2.1 km, which is absent from the options.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q20.body: At the empty corner, the two $+Q$ charges produce equal fields pointing left and up. The $-Q$ charge produces a weaker field towards the bottom right because it is farther away. Adding the three vectors gives a resultant pointing diagonally up and left.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Gives a rightward component even though the field from the right-hand $+Q$ dominates horizontally.
perOption.C: Uses the direction of the weaker field from $-Q$ as the resultant.
perOption.D: Gives a downward component even though the field from the lower $+Q$ dominates vertically.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q21.body: Ion B has charge $-2e$, so the rightward uniform electric field exerts a leftward force on it. Ion A has charge $+2e$ and attracts B, so the electrostatic force due to A points along BA, diagonally upwards and left.

perOption.A: Treats B as positive in the uniform field and treats the two ions as repelling.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Tilts the uniform-field force away from the horizontal and treats the two ions as repelling.
perOption.D: Tilts the uniform-field force downwards even though the field lines are horizontal.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q22.body: In B and D the ideal diodes are reverse-biased, so no current flows and X is at $0\ \mathrm{V}$ in both lighting conditions. In A and C the diodes conduct, and the higher LDR resistance in the dark increases the potential difference across the LDR. In A the LDR is between X and $0\ \mathrm{V}$, so X rises. In C the LDR is above X, so X falls.

perOption.A: Correct. X rises as the LDR takes a larger share of the supply voltage.
perOption.B: The reverse-biased diode opens the circuit and X stays at $0\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.C: The LDR takes more of the supply voltage, leaving less across the fixed resistor below X.
perOption.D: The reverse-biased diode opens the circuit and X stays at $0\ \mathrm{V}$.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q23.body: The full circumference is $2\pi(1.0)=6.2832\ \mathrm{cm}$. The resistance wire therefore subtends $(5.9/6.2832)\times360^\circ=338.04^\circ$. Resistance is proportional to arc length, so the potential divider gives $V_{\mathrm{out}}=(94^\circ/338.04^\circ)(9.0\ \mathrm{V})=2.50\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Uses $360^\circ$ as the angle subtended by the resistance wire.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses too large a fraction of the track for the $94^\circ$ segment.
perOption.D: Treats the segment’s length fraction of about $0.278$ as though the supply were $10\ \mathrm{V}$.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q23.issues: The key’s alternate method prints 2.2716 V as an intermediate value. Its own arc-length ratio gives 2.50 V.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q24.body: The electric force on the electrons points upwards in the plane of the paper and has speed-independent magnitude $eE$. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a downward magnetic force of magnitude $Bev$. Halving the speed halves the downward force, leaving an upward resultant in the plane of the paper.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Assumes the downward magnetic force dominates after the speed is halved.
perOption.C: Assigns an out-of-plane force even though both forces act in the plane of the paper.
perOption.D: Uses the direction of the magnetic field as the direction of the force.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q25.body: The maximum induced e.m.f. is $E_0=NBA\omega=NBA(2\pi f)$. Substituting the coil area and frequency gives $(20)(0.010)(8.0\times10^{-3})^2[2\pi(25)]=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Gives the numerical value of the peak flux linkage before multiplying by angular speed.
perOption.B: Uses the frequency $f$ in place of $2\pi f$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the coil’s effective area or flux-change rate by hundreds of times.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q26.body: A radius sweeps area $A$ in one rotation of period $T$. Faraday’s law gives $E=|\mathrm{d}\Phi/\mathrm{d}t|=BA/T=BAf$. Thus $3.7\times10^{-7}=(3.6\times10^{-5})A(1500/60)$, giving $A=4.1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

perOption.A: Gives far too little swept area to produce the measured e.m.f. at the stated rate.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives a swept area that would produce about 85 times the measured e.m.f.
perOption.D: Gives an area incompatible with the very small measured e.m.f. at 25 revolutions per second.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.body: The mean power in the resistor is $\langle P\rangle=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R$. The sine wave has $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=V_p/\sqrt{2}$, giving mean power $V_p^2/(2R)$. The square wave has magnitude $V_p$ throughout, so its rms voltage is $V_p$ and its mean power is $V_p^2/R$. The ratio is $2$.

perOption.A: Gives the reciprocal ratio and squares it again.
perOption.B: Inverts the requested ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the sine wave’s rms voltage as half its peak voltage.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.body: From the de Broglie relation, $p=h/\lambda$. Conservation of energy gives $eV=\tfrac12 mv^2=p^2/(2m)$ for an electron starting from rest. Substituting gives $V=h^2/(2em\lambda^2)=(6.63\times10^{-34})^2/[2(1.60\times10^{-19})(9.11\times10^{-31})(1.0\times10^{-10})^2]\approx150\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the kinetic energy associated with the momentum fixed by the wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the kinetic energy by using too large a value for $p^2/(2m)$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the accelerating voltage by about a factor of two, consistent with dropping the factor of one-half in the kinetic energy.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q29.body: The energy released is the difference between the reactant and product masses multiplied by $c^2$. Substituting gives $[(7.018+1.008)-2(4.004)](1.66\times10^{-27})(3.00\times10^8)^2=2.6892\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$, which rounds to $2.7\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Uses $c$ instead of $c^2$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Counts only one helium nucleus in the products.
perOption.D: Uses the numerical mass difference in atomic mass units as though it were in kilograms.

cjc-2024-prelim-p1-q30.body: The $\beta$ decay from Pb to $^{214}\mathrm{Bi}$ leaves the mass number unchanged, so X must account for the drop from 218 to 214. An $\alpha$ particle is a $^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus and carries away four nucleons, ruling out A and C. If Y were $\alpha$ decay, its daughter would be Pb, ruling out D.

perOption.A: A $\gamma$ decay at X cannot account for the decrease of four in mass number.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: A $\beta$ decay at X leaves the mass number unchanged.
perOption.D: An $\alpha$ decay at Y would produce Pb in place of At.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q1.body: One decimetre is $1\times10^{-1}\ \mathrm{m}$. This equals $1\times10^2\ \mathrm{mm}$ or $1\times10^1\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: One millimetre is a hundredth of a decimetre.
perOption.B: Ten millimetres are a tenth of a decimetre.
perOption.C: One centimetre is a tenth of a decimetre.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q2.body: The velocity–time graph has a positive, constant gradient, so the acceleration is constant. Velocity increases at this fixed positive value of $a$, giving a vertical line on the velocity–acceleration graph.

perOption.A: Shows acceleration increasing as velocity rises, with acceleration initially zero.
perOption.B: Shows both quantities increasing from zero, even though the initial velocity–time gradient is positive.
perOption.C: Holds velocity constant while varying acceleration.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q3.body: Take upwards and rightwards as positive. Vertically, $v_y=u_y+a_yt=8.00+(-1.62)(9.00)=-6.58\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Horizontally, $v_x=u_x+a_xt=4.00+(0)(9.00)=4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed is $\sqrt{(-6.58)^2+(4.00)^2}=7.70\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses approximately the magnitude of the vertical component alone.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the magnitudes of the perpendicular velocity components.
perOption.D: Uses the change in vertical velocity as the speed.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q4.body: Let one square weigh $W$, so the two squares on the right weigh $2W$ and the whole sheet weighs $3W$. If the centre of gravity lies a horizontal distance $\bar{x}$ from B, the moment of the combined weight about B equals the sum of the individual moments: $3W\bar{x}=W(0.5x)+2W(1.5x)$. Thus $3\bar{x}=3.5x$, giving $\bar{x}=1.2x$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Gives equal weight to the single square and the pair when averaging their positions.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the centre of the right-hand pair alone.
perOption.D: Places the centre of gravity beyond $1.5x$, the position of the right-hand pair’s centre.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q4.issues: The stem describes the original square sheet as having length x, but the diagram labels each small square with side x and the solution follows the diagram.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q5.body: Let $k$ be the spring constant of one spring. For each arrangement, $F_{\mathrm{net}}=k_{\mathrm{eff}}e$, where $F_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the load and $e$ is the extension. In A, $e=2/(0.5k)=4/k$, and in B, $e=1/(k/3)=3/k$. In C, $e=6/(2k)=3/k$, and in D, $e=8/(3k)\approx2.7/k$. A has the largest extension.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The smaller load on the three springs in series gives only $3/k$.
perOption.C: The two parallel springs share the load, giving only $3/k$.
perOption.D: The three parallel springs give the smallest extension, about $2.7/k$.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q6.body: Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power. Over the same time $t$, the useful electrical output power is $Y/t$ and the chemical input power is $W/t$, giving $(Y/t)/(W/t)=Y/W$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adds the intermediate thermal energy to the original chemical input.
perOption.C: Measures the efficiency of converting thermal energy to electrical energy alone.
perOption.D: Adds the intermediate and final energies to the original input.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q7.body: Force is proportional to extension in the initial straight part of the elastic region shown. The work done is the area under the force–extension curve all the way to its endpoint, where the wire breaks. D labels the elastic and plastic regions correctly and shades this full area.

perOption.A: Omits the area under the later part of the curve.
perOption.B: Interchanges the labels for the elastic and plastic regions.
perOption.C: Omits the area under the initial part of the curve.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The key calls the elastic region proportional. Proportionality describes the initial straight segment, and elastic deformation can also occur beyond the limit of proportionality.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q8.body: One rotation is $2\pi$ radians. The angular velocity is $\omega=2\pi/T=2\pi/(24\times60\times60)=7.27\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses 3600 seconds as the period, omitting the factor of 24.
perOption.B: Uses approximately the period of Earth’s orbit around the Sun.
perOption.C: Divides by the period in minutes and reports the result in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.body:
The centripetal force has constant magnitude, and the acceleration always points towards the centre. The kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2$ is constant because the speed is constant.

At the lowest point, $T-mg=F_{\mathrm c}$, so $T=F_{\mathrm c}+mg$. At the highest point, $T+mg=F_{\mathrm c}$, so $T=F_{\mathrm c}-mg$. The tension is therefore lower at the highest point.

perOption.A: This statement is true because $mv^2/r$ has constant magnitude.
perOption.B: This statement is true because the acceleration is centripetal.
perOption.C: This statement is true because $\tfrac12 mv^2$ is constant.
perOption.D: Correct. The stated tension comparison is reversed.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.issues: Constant speed in a vertical circle is stipulated and would require a tangential force away from the top and bottom, beyond weight and purely radial tension.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Gravitational potential is $\phi=-GM/r$. Moving P and Q closer to the mass makes both potentials more negative, so both magnitudes increase.

The field strength $g=GM/r^2$ increases at both points as $r$ decreases. Its gradient is steeper closer to the mass, so the field-strength difference across the same separation also increases.

perOption.A: Both potential magnitudes increase and the field-strength difference increases.
perOption.B: Treats increasingly negative potentials as decreasing magnitudes.
perOption.C: Assumes the fixed separation gives a fixed difference even as the field-strength gradient steepens.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q10.issues: The question stem says ‘gravitational field strength between the two points’ while the table and worked solution specify the difference in field strength.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.body: Taking motion towards the wall as positive, each elastic collision changes the molecule’s momentum by $\Delta p=-mv-(+mv)=-2mv$. By Newton’s third law, the force on the wall is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on the molecule. With $N$ collisions per second, the average force on the wall has magnitude $N|\Delta p|=2mvN$.

perOption.A: Counts only the incoming momentum and omits the momentum of the rebound.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the molecule’s kinetic energy, which has units of joules.
perOption.D: Divides by the collision rate and omits the factor of two from the reversal.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.issues: The key computes a signed momentum change of −2mv, then uses 2mv in its force calculation. The explanation makes the use of the magnitude explicit.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q12.body: Using $Q=mc\Delta\theta$, equate the heat gained by the metal to the heat lost by the liquid. The final temperature $\theta_f$ satisfies $mc(\theta_f-20)=(3m)(2.5c)(100-\theta_f)$. Cancelling $mc$ gives $\theta_f-20=750-7.5\theta_f$, so $\theta_f\approx91\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Places equilibrium closer to the metal’s starting temperature even though the liquid has the greater total heat capacity.
perOption.B: Averages the two temperatures as though their total heat capacities were equal.
perOption.C: Underestimates the liquid’s heat capacity advantage, so the temperature drop of the liquid is too large.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q13.body: The flat part of the graph from 4 to 7 minutes is the melting interval, so the substance receives $2000\times3\ \mathrm{J}$ during fusion. Using $Q=mL$ gives $2000\times3=1\times L$, so $L=6000\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: At fixed power and mass the steeper liquid segment implies a smaller specific heat capacity, since $P=mc\,\Delta\theta/\Delta t$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The $3\ \mathrm{K}$ on the graph is the rise from room temperature to the melting point.
perOption.D: The graph has no second plateau showing when vaporisation begins.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.body: At $t=0$, the gravitational potential energy is maximum because the bob is at an extreme of its swing. Its gravitational potential energy is zero at equilibrium, which it passes twice per cycle, so there are two minima per period.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows one minimum per period $T$.
perOption.C: Starts at zero although the bob is released at its highest point.
perOption.D: Starts at zero and shows one minimum per period $T$.

cjc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The question PNG includes six subsequent questions. The transcription covers Q14.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: For $x=ab^2/c$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta x/x=\Delta a/a+2\Delta b/b+\Delta c/c$. In percentage terms, option A gives $(4+2(2)+4)\%=12\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $20\%$.
perOption.C: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $9\%$.
perOption.D: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $14\%$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: The velocity of P relative to Q is $\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_Q=\mathbf v_P+(-\mathbf v_Q)$. Add the $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ westward vector to the tip of the $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ northward vector to obtain the steep northwest arrow.

perOption.A: Points southeast and understates the north–south component.
perOption.B: Points northwest but understates the northward component relative to the westward component.
perOption.C: Reverses the relative velocity and shows Q moving relative to P.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The complete sheet and the cut-out have centres $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M, respectively. Subtract the cut-out's first moment from the complete sheet's, giving $\rho tg[(4.0)(4.0)(2.0)-(1.0)(2.0)(3.0)]=26\rho tg$, using centimetres throughout. The remaining weight times its distance $y$ below M is $14\rho tg\,y$, so $y=26/14=1.857\ \mathrm{cm}\approx1.9\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Shifts the centre too far upward for a cut-out of area $2.0\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shifts the centre toward the cut-out, as if the removed metal added weight.
perOption.D: Shifts the centre downward despite the removal of metal below the original centre.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The key labels the calculation as torques about M. The weights act along the vertical symmetry line through M, so the calculation uses first moments of weight with respect to depth below M.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: The magnetic force $NBIL$ on the lowest side acts horizontally to the right. Balancing moments about the pivot gives $Mg(L/2)\sin 30^\circ=NBIL(L\cos 30^\circ)$. Substituting $0.30(0.025)\sin 30^\circ=100B(0.40)(0.050)(0.050)\cos 30^\circ$ gives $B=0.043\ \mathrm T$.

perOption.A: Omits the $\cos 30^\circ$ factor from the magnetic force's moment arm.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor from the weight's moment arm.
perOption.D: Uses the full side length in the weight's moment arm.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: By $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, the constant positive force produces constant acceleration, so velocity increases along a straight line. When the net force is zero, acceleration is zero and the velocity–time graph is horizontal.

perOption.A: Copies the force pulse and shows instantaneous changes in velocity.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows deceleration after the force has dropped to zero.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration during a constant force.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The cart has a forward tension $T$ and a backward resistive force of $40\ \mathrm N$. Newton's second law gives $T-40=600(0.15)$, so $T=130\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: A tension of $65\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $25\ \mathrm N$ to accelerate the cart.
perOption.B: A tension of $100\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $60\ \mathrm N$ of net force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A tension of $195\ \mathrm N$ gives $155\ \mathrm N$ of net force, exceeding the required $90\ \mathrm N$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The useful output power is $Fv=1600(11)=17\,600\ \mathrm W$, all of which goes into overcoming resistance at constant speed on level ground. The fuel supplies $1.8\times10^6/60=30\,000\ \mathrm W$. The efficiency is $(17\,600/30\,000)\times100\%\approx59\%$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the ratio of the $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful power to the $30.0\ \mathrm{kW}$ fuel input.
perOption.B: At the stated fuel input, this percentage accounts for only about $10\ \mathrm{kW}$ of useful power.
perOption.C: This percentage treats the roughly $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful output as only a little over a third of the $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ input.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The total energy is the initial kinetic energy $E=\tfrac12mu^2$. At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, but the constant horizontal velocity is $u\cos60^\circ=u/2$, so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12m(u/2)^2=E/4$. By energy conservation, the gravitational potential energy there is $3E/4$, so the two curves cross.

perOption.A: Shows zero kinetic energy at the top, as for a vertical launch.
perOption.B: Shows equal energies at the top, as for a $45^\circ$ launch.
perOption.C: Keeps kinetic energy above half the total, as for a launch below $45^\circ$.

dhs-2024-prelim-p1-q1.body: By dimensional analysis, $\sqrt{g\lambda}$ has units $\sqrt{\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}}=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. These are the units of velocity.

dhs-2024-prelim-p1-q2.body: The second displacement is $\mathbf{s}_2=\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{s}_1$. The resultant and $-\mathbf{s}_1$ are perpendicular, so $s_2=\sqrt{140^2+150^2}=205\ \mathrm{cm}$. dhs-2024-prelim-p1-q3.body: The acceleration during braking is $a=(0-15)/1.2=-12.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Using $v^2=u^2+2as$ gives $0=15^2+2(-12.5)s$, so the braking distance is $9.0\ \mathrm m$. Add the distance travelled during the reaction time to get $9.0+15(0.10)=10.5\ \mathrm m$.

dhs-2024-prelim-p1-q4.body: In a perfectly elastic collision, the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach. The approach speed is $1.30-(-0.50)=1.80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Only D has the same separation speed, $1.30-(-0.50)=1.80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

dhs-2024-prelim-p1-q5.body: By Newton’s third law, the contact forces the blocks exert on each other are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. One acts on $m_1$ and the other acts on $m_2$.

dhs-2024-prelim-p1-q7.body: For a constant force, work is the force multiplied by the displacement in its direction. For the work against gravity, the relevant displacement is the vertical rise $q$, so the work is $Wq$.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q2.issues: Page 6 incorrectly invokes cancellation in its distance discussion. The unsigned areas are 5vt₂/16 for Y and vt₂/2 for X, so the keyed comparison still holds.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The elastic potential energy is the area under the force–extension graph. The triangular area grows from $\tfrac12F_1x_1$ to $\tfrac12F_2x_2$. The increase is therefore $\tfrac12(F_2x_2-F_1x_1)$.

perOption.A: Uses rectangular areas and misses the factor of one-half.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Squares the extensions and omits the triangular-area factor.
perOption.D: Squares the extensions even though the base of each triangle is the extension itself.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Applying Newton’s second law to the lift gives $T-W_2-D=m_{\mathrm{lift}}a$. If $T=D+W_2$, the resultant is zero, so $a=0$ and the lift has constant velocity, including the possibility of rest.

perOption.A: The cable tension equals the combined weight only when the lift system has zero acceleration.
perOption.B: Equal forces on the man imply zero acceleration, which also allows motion at constant nonzero velocity.
perOption.C: Both forces act on the man, and their magnitudes can differ when he accelerates.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: The downhill component of weight is $F=mg\sin\theta$, so $a=F/m=g\sin\theta$. With double the mass, the downhill force doubles to $F'=2mg\sin\theta$. Dividing by the new mass gives $a'=F'/(2m)=g\sin\theta=a$.

perOption.A: The downhill component of weight doubles when the mass doubles.
perOption.B: Assumes the downhill force stays fixed as the mass doubles.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the force but overlooks the doubling of the mass.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: For the two blocks together, the net force is $54-6.0=48\ \mathrm{N}$, so their common acceleration is $48/8.0=6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Applying Newton’s second law to the $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block gives a resultant horizontal force of $2.0(6.0)=12\ \mathrm{N}$. This is also the contact force if the friction shown acts entirely on the larger block, as assumed in the key.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the resultant force on the smaller block.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of the larger block with the common acceleration.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong system or force balance for the smaller block, whose resultant is 12 N.
perOption.D: Uses the resultant force on both blocks combined.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The wording gives only total friction and does not explicitly distinguish resultant force from contact force. A gives the resultant, and it gives the contact force if the 2.0 kg block has no friction, as the key assumes from the diagram.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: At the top, tension and weight both act downwards towards the centre, so $T+W=mv^2/r$. The required resultant is $0.10(6.0)^2/0.50=7.2\ \mathrm{N}$ and the weight is $0.10(9.81)=0.98\ \mathrm{N}$. Hence $T=7.2-0.98=6.22\ \mathrm{N}\approx6.2\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Gives the ball’s weight alone.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the entire centripetal force and ignores the contribution of weight.
perOption.D: Adds the weight even though it already acts towards the centre.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The key takes $g_X=g_Y=GM/r^2$ and $g_Z=2GM/r^2$. It resolves the fields of X and Y along the line through O and Z, using $30^\circ$ for each angle, so their components perpendicular to that line cancel and their components away from Z sum to $2(GM/r^2)\cos30^\circ=\sqrt{3}GM/r^2$. Subtracting this from Z’s field gives the key’s result, $G(2M-\sqrt{3}M)/r^2$ towards Z.

perOption.A: Treats the three fields as cancelling despite Z having twice the mass of X or Y.
perOption.B: Points the resultant towards X even though the additional mass is at Z.
perOption.C: This is the physical result at the centre, where the three equal-mass contributions cancel and the extra mass at Z supplies the net field.
perOption.D: Correct according to the key’s component calculation.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The key uses 30° instead of 60° between each of the X and Y field vectors and the direction directly away from Z. With O at the centre as drawn, three equal-mass contributions cancel and Z’s extra mass gives GM/r² towards Z, option C.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Gravitational potential is a scalar, so add the three contributions at O directly. This gives $\phi=-GM/r-GM/r-G(2M)/r=-4GM/r$. The potential has no direction.

perOption.A: Treats the three negative potentials as if they could cancel by symmetry.
perOption.B: Uses a single mass-M contribution and assigns a direction to a scalar.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong sign and assigns a direction to a scalar.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: Option D explicitly prints the minus sign, although the key’s closing comment describes it as implied.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The total energy is $E=\tfrac12mv_0^2=\tfrac12m(\omega x_0)^2$, so $E\propto(x_0/T)^2$. Doubling $x_0$ and tripling $T$ gives $E_{\mathrm{new}}/E_{\mathrm{old}}=(2/3)^2=4/9$. The new energy is $(4/9)(18\ \mathrm{mJ})=8\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies the factor of $2/3$ without squaring it.
perOption.C: Doubles the energy directly and ignores the change in period.
perOption.D: Squares the amplitude factor but ignores the longer period.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The angles between successive polariser axes are $40^\circ-30^\circ=10^\circ$ and $60^\circ-40^\circ=20^\circ$. W transmits half the incident unpolarised intensity, so $I_W=0.5I_0$. By Malus's law, $I_X=0.5I_0\cos^2 10^\circ=0.4849I_0$, then $I_Y=I_X\cos^2 20^\circ\approx 0.428I_0\approx 0.43I_0$.

perOption.A: Uses the absolute $60^\circ$ angle at Y instead of its $20^\circ$ angle relative to X.
perOption.B: Uses the absolute axis angles instead of the angles between successive axes.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds the $0.5I_0$ already transmitted by W.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: At the original area, intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling the amplitude gives $k(2A)^2=4I$. Focusing the same power onto one-third of the original area then gives $(4IS)/(S/3)=12I$.

perOption.A: Treats intensity as proportional to amplitude instead of amplitude squared.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the gain from doubling the amplitude, which is a factor of four.
perOption.D: Doubles the result again even though squaring the amplitude ratio already accounts for the doubling.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Using the key's resolution approximation, $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the dish diameter. This gives $\theta_{\min}=(0.40\times10^{-6})/5.1=7.843\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{rad}$. For a small angle, the minimum separation is $x=\theta_{\min}D=(7.843\times10^{-8})(2.8\times10^{25})\approx2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Halves the separation, as would happen if the stated diameter were doubled.
perOption.B: Correct. This follows from the key's resolution approximation.
perOption.C: Inverts the angular ratio to $b/\lambda$ and halves the resulting separation.
perOption.D: Uses $b/\lambda$ instead of $\lambda/b$, giving a vastly larger separation.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key uses the syllabus approximation $\lambda/b$. The circular-aperture Rayleigh factor of 1.22 gives about $2.7\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$, which is unlisted. B is still the closest listed value.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The mean translational kinetic energy satisfies $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, so $c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\propto T$. Hence $T/(2T)=c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}^2$, which gives $c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}=\sqrt{2}\,c_{\mathrm{rms}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the rms speed itself as directly proportional to temperature.
perOption.C: Applies an extra factor of two after taking the square root of the temperature ratio.
perOption.D: Squares the temperature ratio instead of taking its square root.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: The connected containers have the same pressure $p$ at equilibrium. Using $n=pV/(RT)$ gives $n_X=p(2V)/[R(2T)]=pV/(RT)$ and $n_Y=pV/(RT)$. The school's working therefore gives $n_X/n_Y=1.00$, even though its answer label is A.

perOption.A: Inverts the volume ratio while keeping the temperature ratio in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct. The volume and temperature factors cancel.
perOption.C: Accounts for the doubled volume but ignores the doubled temperature.
perOption.D: Treats the amount of gas as directly proportional to temperature at fixed pressure and volume.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The summary table and worked-solution label show A, matching keyAnswer, but the worked calculation gives 1.00, which is B. A is incorrect.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The water releases $0.150(4180)(20.0)=12540\ \mathrm{J}$ as it cools to $0^\circ\mathrm C$. Warming the ice to $0^\circ\mathrm C$ takes $0.100(2100)(10.0)=2100\ \mathrm{J}$, leaving $10440\ \mathrm{J}$ for melting. This melts $10440/334000=0.03126\ \mathrm{kg}$, or $31.3\ \mathrm g$. The remaining $68.7\ \mathrm g$ of ice coexists with water at $0^\circ\mathrm C$.

perOption.A: Confuses absolute zero with the melting point and reports the mass melted as the mass remaining.
perOption.B: Finds the correct ice mass but confuses absolute zero with the melting point.
perOption.C: Reports the mass that melts as the mass that remains.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: In $I=nAvq$, the number density is $n=N/V$ and the wire volume is $V=AL$, giving $I=Nvq/L$. Hence $N=IL/(vq)=(12)(0.35)/[(5.0\times10^{-4})(1.60\times10^{-19})]=5.3\times10^{22}$.

perOption.A: Treats the drift speed as a multiplier, effectively using a short transit time for slow electrons.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the wire length when converting the carrier count per unit length to the total count.
perOption.D: Divides by the wire length instead of multiplying by it.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The ideal diode conducts only during the positive half-cycle, and the peak load voltage is $V_0=12.0\ \mathrm V$. The full-cycle average power is half that for an unrectified sine wave of the same peak voltage, so $\langle P\rangle=\tfrac12(V_0^2/2R)=12.0^2/(4\times50)=0.72\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Assumes the diode blocks both half-cycles.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the average power for an unrectified sine wave.
perOption.D: Uses the peak power as the cycle average.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Closing all three switches puts the external resistors in parallel, so $1/R_{\mathrm p}=1/4+1/8+1/12=11/24$ in inverse ohms. Adding the internal resistance gives $R_{\mathrm{tot}}=(24/11+1.00)\ \Omega=(35/11)\ \Omega$. The cell current is $I=2.00/(35/11)=0.629\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Adds all four resistances as though they were in series.
perOption.B: Uses only the $4.00\ \Omega$ branch and neglects the internal resistance.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the parallel resistance alone and omits the internal resistance.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: Let $k$ be the fraction of the way the slider has moved from the top of the upper resistor, with $0\le k\le1$. The equal resistors each drop $3.0\ \mathrm V$, so $V_X=6.0-3.0k$ in volts. The potential difference $V_Y-V_X=3.0k$ therefore ranges from $0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Measures from the bottom rail, giving a range of $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Connects X and Y across the supply, fixing the output at $6.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.D: Measures across the fixed lower resistor, so the output ranges from $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm V$ as the effective upper resistance varies.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key's distractor note says D is fixed at 3.0 V. The diagram shows the slider bypassing part of the upper resistor, so D actually varies from 3.0 V to 6.0 V.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The capacitor on AB is in parallel with the AC–CB series branch, so the branch has $5.0\ \mathrm V$ across it. Its equivalent capacitance is $(1/2+1/3)^{-1}\ \mathrm{\mu F}=1.2\ \mathrm{\mu F}$, giving each series capacitor a charge of $Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=6.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$. Thus $V_{BC}=Q/C_{BC}=6.0/3=2.0\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the charge required on the series capacitors for a total drop of $5.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Splits the voltage equally across two unequal capacitances.
perOption.D: Gives the voltage across AC instead of BC.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: By Newton's third law, the forces on the two wires have equal magnitudes. Currents in the same direction attract, while currents in opposite directions repel. In A, both currents flow downwards, so each force points towards the other wire.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows unequal forces and repulsion between currents flowing in the same direction.
perOption.C: Shows attraction even though the currents flow in opposite directions and should repel.
perOption.D: Shows unequal forces even though the two forces are a Newton's third-law pair.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The field points downwards from the $5.00\ \mathrm{kV}$ plate to the $0\ \mathrm V$ plate, so the positive proton experiences a downward force. Its magnitude is $F=qE=(1.60\times10^{-19})(5000/0.100)=8.00\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm N$. This gives $a=F/m=4.790\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and the transit time is $t=L/v_x=0.150/(2.52\times10^6)=5.952\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm s$. Thus $y=\tfrac12at^2=8.49\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$, or $8.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$ downwards.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the force on the positive proton.
perOption.C: Overestimates the displacement from the downward acceleration and horizontal transit time.
perOption.D: Overestimates the displacement and reverses the force direction.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The original force is $F=kQ^2/r^2$. Each charge becomes $Q+3Q=4Q$ and the separation becomes $2r$, so $F_{\mathrm{new}}=k(4Q)(4Q)/(2r)^2=4kQ^2/r^2$. Hence $F_{\mathrm{new}}/F=4$.

perOption.A: Applies the charge increase to only one charge, making it cancel the factor of four from the distance.
perOption.B: Treats each new charge as $3Q$ instead of $4Q$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses an inverse-distance law instead of the inverse-square law.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The magnetic flux density $B$ stays constant because the external field is unaffected by the rotation. The initial flux is maximal, and the tilt reduces the area projected perpendicular to the field, so the flux decreases.

perOption.A: Confuses the decreasing component normal to the coil with a decrease in the field magnitude.
perOption.B: Assumes rotation strengthens the external field and increases the flux.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes the flux increases as the coil tilts away from its maximum-flux orientation.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: By Faraday's law, the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is $|\mathcal E|=N|\Delta\Phi|/\Delta t$. With $1500$ turns and a flux change of $0.85\ \mathrm{Wb}$ in $0.19\ \mathrm s$, this gives $1500(0.85/0.19)\approx6711\ \mathrm V\approx6710\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero final flux in place of the nonzero change in flux.
perOption.B: Calculates the induced e.m.f. for one turn only.
perOption.C: Underestimates the rate of change of flux linkage across all 1500 turns.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Photon energy is $E=hf=hc/\lambda$, so $E$ is directly proportional to $1/\lambda$. The graph of $E$ against $1/\lambda$ is therefore a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Shows a nonlinear dependence on reciprocal wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes energy directly proportional to wavelength.
perOption.D: Shows energy increasing with wavelength even though it decreases.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The energy levels are $E_n=h^2n^2/(8mL^2)$, and the ground state has $n=1$, giving $E=h^2/(8mL^2)$. For the second particle, $E'=h^2/[8(2m)(2L)^2]=E/8$.

perOption.A: Accounts only for the doubling of mass.
perOption.B: Accounts only for the width doubling, or treats both effects as linear.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Squares the mass ratio as well as the width ratio.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Starting with $N$ nuclei, $3N/4$ decay in two half-lives. Approximating nuclear masses by their nucleon numbers in atomic mass units, the change is $\Delta m=[-(3N/4)(210)+(3N/4)(206)]\,\mathrm u=-3N\,\mathrm u$. Relative to the initial mass $210N\,\mathrm u$, this is a decrease of $1/70\approx1.43\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the surviving quarter of the parent nuclei to count the emitted alpha particles.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Confuses the fraction of parent nuclei remaining with the fraction of mass lost.
perOption.D: Assumes the full mass of each decayed nucleus leaves the sample.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Beta particles can penetrate several millimetres into tissue and deposit ionising energy in surface and near-surface tumours. Their limited range helps spare deeper healthy tissue.

perOption.A: Alpha particles are stopped by the outer layer of skin before reaching a deep tumour.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gamma rays can reach deep tissues, so their use is not limited to surface conditions.
perOption.D: Alpha particles emitted inside the body have too short a range to reach external detectors.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q1.body: Estimate Singapore’s population at 5 million and the average mass per person at $60\ \mathrm{kg}$. Multiplying gives $(5\times10^6)(60)=3\times10^8\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It matches the population times the estimated mass per person.
perOption.B: Implies 600 kg per person at a population of 5 million.
perOption.C: Implies 6,000 kg per person at a population of 5 million.
perOption.D: Implies 60,000 kg per person at a population of 5 million.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q2.body: The key treats sets 1 and 2 as similarly accurate, with set 1 less precise. Set 3 is precise but inaccurate because its readings are tightly grouped away from the actual value. Its narrower spread makes it more precise than set 1.

perOption.A: Correct. Set 1 has the wider spread.
perOption.B: Set 2 is centred on the actual value.
perOption.C: Set 3 is centred farther from the actual value than set 1.
perOption.D: Set 3 has a narrower spread, indicating less random error.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q2.issues: The key calls sets 1 and 2 equally accurate. The drawn mean of set 2 is closer to the actual value, which still rules out B.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q3.body: For $P=mv^2/(2t)$, the fractional uncertainties add as $\Delta P/P=\Delta m/m+2\Delta v/v+\Delta t/t$. In percentage terms this is $0.5\%+2(3.0\%)+2.0\%=8.5\%$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the combined uncertainty, including the doubled speed term.
perOption.B: Counts the speed uncertainty only once.
perOption.C: Correct. The speed term contributes 6.0%.
perOption.D: Counts the speed uncertainty three times.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q4.body: The gradient of the displacement–time graph is the velocity. The velocity tends to zero at $t_2$, so the displacement graph must flatten there.

perOption.A: Shows constant displacement while the car is still moving forward.
perOption.B: Keeps a positive constant gradient throughout braking.
perOption.C: Shows an increasing gradient, indicating that the car speeds up.
perOption.D: Correct. The gradient falls to zero at the stopping time.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q5.body: The target is $4.50\ \mathrm{m}$ horizontally from the launcher and $1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ below it. Substitute $t=4.50/(10\cos\theta)$ into $-1.50=10t\sin\theta-\tfrac12gt^2$. The roots are about $-6.3^\circ$ and $77.8^\circ$, so only the latter is above the horizontal. No listed option gives that angle alone.

perOption.A: A horizontal launch passes above the target at its horizontal position.
perOption.B: A 45° launch passes above the target at its horizontal position.
perOption.C: Both angles send the balloon above the target at its horizontal position.
perOption.D: 78° works to the stated precision, but 12° misses.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q5.issues: The school marks Q5 void. The input keyAnswer A is a placeholder. No listed option is physically correct.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q6.body: The sand arrives with zero horizontal speed and accelerates to the belt’s speed. Its rate of horizontal momentum gain is $(m/\Delta t)\Delta v=4.0(1.5-0)=6.0\ \mathrm{N}$. The total driving force is $17+6.0=23\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Gives only the extra force needed to accelerate the sand.
perOption.B: Subtracts the extra force from the empty-belt driving force.
perOption.C: Ignores the sand’s change in momentum.
perOption.D: Correct. The driving force increases by 6.0 N.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q7.body: Initially the speed is steady, so $mg\sin\theta=k(1.38)$, where $kv$ is the air resistance. At the higher steady speed, $mg\sin\theta+F=k(5.55)$. Thus $F=80(9.81)\sin5^\circ[5.55/1.38-1]=207\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the extra force needed to balance the increased drag.
perOption.B: Correct. The extra force makes up the increase in air resistance.
perOption.C: Gives the full drag at the higher speed and ignores the downhill component of weight.
perOption.D: Scales the full weight with speed instead of using the downhill component and subtracting its contribution.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q7.issues: The key prints 138 in the final substitution. The preceding working and the result use 1.38.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q8.body: The man and barrel each move $9\ \mathrm{m}$ before they are level. By conservation of energy, $m_{\rm barrel}g\Delta h=m_{\rm man}g\Delta h+\tfrac12(m_{\rm man}+m_{\rm barrel})v^2$. Therefore $v=\sqrt{2(120-80)(9.81)(9)/(80+120)}=5.94\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The net loss of gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy of both masses.
perOption.B: Assigns too much of the barrel’s energy loss to the man’s motion.
perOption.C: Treats the motion as free fall through 9 m and ignores the effect of the other mass.
perOption.D: Requires far more kinetic energy than the system’s net loss of gravitational potential energy.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q9.body: Water pressure increases with depth, so it is greater at the bottom of the submarine than at the top. The resulting net upward pressure force is the upthrust.

perOption.A: The air density affects the submarine’s average density, while the upthrust comes from the surrounding water pressure.
perOption.B: Displaced volume determines the upthrust’s magnitude, while the pressure difference produces it.
perOption.C: In equilibrium the net upward force from the water equals the submarine’s weight.
perOption.D: Correct. Pressure is greater at the bottom than at the top.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q10.body: Vertical equilibrium gives $T\sin\phi=H\sin\theta+W$, with both angles measured from horizontal. The horizontal components balance, so the larger vertical component gives $T>H$, and the vertical equation also gives $T>W$. Taking moments about the cable attachment gives $(L/4)H\sin\theta=(L/4)W$. Thus $H>W$, giving $W<H<T$.

perOption.A: The hinge’s downward component equals the weight, so the full hinge force is greater than the weight.
perOption.B: The tension’s vertical component alone exceeds the weight.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight is smallest and the tension is largest.
perOption.D: The horizontal components balance and the tension has the greater vertical component.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q11.body: Each half of the drawn cord has length $L=\sqrt{0.5^2+x^2}$, so the total extension is $2(L-0.5)$. Equating elastic potential energy to the balloon’s kinetic energy gives $\tfrac12(80)[2(\sqrt{0.5^2+x^2}-0.5)]^2=\tfrac12(0.2)(10)^2$. Solving gives $x=0.56\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Gives the total cord extension instead of the transverse draw length.
perOption.B: Correct. The cord geometry gives a draw length of 0.56 m.
perOption.C: Gives the length of one stretched half of the cord.
perOption.D: Gives the total stretched length of the cord.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q12.body: Viewed from above the North Pole, Earth turns through $\theta_{\mathrm{Earth}}=(2\pi/24)(18)=1.5\pi$ rad. At the first repeat pass the plane has gone one extra revolution, so $\theta_{\mathrm{plane}}=1.5\pi+2\pi=3.5\pi$ rad. Setting $3.5\pi=(2\pi/T)(18)$ gives $T=10.3\ \mathrm{h}$.

perOption.A: Allows two extra revolutions, which would put an earlier overhead pass at 9 hours.
perOption.B: Correct. It gives the first repeat pass.
perOption.C: Treats the observer as stationary and takes the elapsed time as the plane's period.
perOption.D: Gives the plane Earth's angular speed, so there is no relative lap.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q12.issues: The school notes that the answer is not unique. B assumes the next overhead pass, while A (6.5 h rounded) also fits if an intervening pass at 9 h is allowed.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q13.body: From $a=r\omega^2$, the disc's angular speed is $\omega=\sqrt{120/0.030}=\sqrt{4000}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. At the second point, $v=r\omega=(0.050)\sqrt{4000}=3.16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Gives the linear speed at the original radius.
perOption.B: Underestimates the speed increase, which is proportional to radius at fixed angular speed.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the required speed by using the diameter in place of the radius.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q14.body: At the instant the engine is fired, its thrust cancels gravity, so the net force is zero. By Newton's first law, the spacecraft continues with its existing velocity, which is tangent to the orbit.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A circular path with a longer period still requires a net inward force.
perOption.C: A circular path with a shorter period still requires a net inward force.
perOption.D: An inward spiral assumes a change in motion despite the zero net force.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q15.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GM_{\mathrm{Earth}}m/r^2=mv^2/r$. This gives $v=\sqrt{GM_{\mathrm{Earth}}/r}\propto 1/\sqrt r$. Hence $v_{\mathrm{new}}=7780\sqrt{6610/6890}=7620\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses an inverse-radius dependence for speed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the radius ratio inside the square root.
perOption.D: Treats speed as directly proportional to the orbital radius.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q16.body: The displacement follows a sine curve, so the velocity follows a cosine curve. The kinetic energy $E_K=\tfrac12mv^2$ follows a squared cosine curve, peaking at $t=0$ and repeating every $T/2$, as in C.

perOption.A: Copies the displacement curve, giving negative kinetic energy for part of the cycle.
perOption.B: Squares the displacement, putting the energy peaks at the turning points.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Shows one peak per cycle and starts at zero despite the maximum initial speed.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q16.issues: The question stem prints ‘as a time period T’, evidently intended as ‘has a time period T’.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q17.body: Damping is a resistive force. It acts opposite to the velocity of the vibrating object relative to its surroundings.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The acceleration depends on the resultant force and can point with or against the damping force.
perOption.C: At a given displacement the object can move in either direction, so displacement alone cannot determine the direction of damping.
perOption.D: A force proportional to displacement in simple harmonic motion is the restoring force.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q18.body: The wavelength is $\lambda=v/f=340/1000=0.340\ \mathrm{m}$. Since $\Delta s/\lambda=\Delta\phi/(2\pi)$, the phase difference is $\Delta\phi=(0.17/0.340)(2\pi)=\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Treats the separation as one eighth of a wavelength.
perOption.B: Treats the separation as one quarter of a wavelength.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assigns a full cycle to a separation of half a wavelength.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q19.body: By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta\approx\lambda/b$ for slit width $b$. Thus $\theta_{\mathrm{new}}/\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=b_{\mathrm{old}}/b_{\mathrm{new}}=2$, giving $1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Treats the angle as directly proportional to slit width.
perOption.B: Ignores the effect of the slit width on the angle.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Applies an inverse-square dependence to the slit width.

ejc-2017-promo-p1-q20.body: The grating equation is $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$. With $d=1/N$ and $n=2$, $\sin\theta_2=2\lambda/(1/N)=2N\lambda$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio of the second-order path difference to the line spacing.
perOption.B: Substitutes the line density for the line spacing.
perOption.C: Divides by the order number instead of multiplying by it.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q1.body: Pressure has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ and density has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Dividing pressure by density gives $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, so $\sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$ has the required units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Inverting the product of pressure and density gives $\mathrm{kg^{-1}\,m^2\,s}$ after taking the square root.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Dividing density by pressure gives $\mathrm{m^{-1}\,s}$ after taking the square root.
perOption.D: Multiplying pressure by density leaves units of $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ after taking the square root.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q2.body: Let $Q=\rho_s-\rho_f=1800\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, so $\Delta Q=\Delta\rho_s+\Delta\rho_f=20+10=30\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. From $\mu=5Qd^2/(9v_T)$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta\mu/\mu=\Delta Q/Q+\Delta v_T/v_T+2\Delta d/d$. Substituting gives $30/1800+0.04/1.60+2(0.4/20.0)$, or $8.2\%$.

perOption.A: Counts the fractional uncertainty in diameter only once.
perOption.B: Omits the sphere density uncertainty from the uncertainty in the density difference.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds fractional uncertainties for the two densities separately, although the formula uses their difference.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q3.body: The resultant force is forward from the start to C, so the car's velocity increases over that interval. From C to D the resultant force acts backwards, so the velocity decreases. The greatest velocity occurs at C.

perOption.A: Acceleration at A is still positive, so the car continues to gain velocity.
perOption.B: B marks the greatest acceleration while the velocity is still increasing.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Zero acceleration at D follows a period of decreasing velocity.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q3.issues: The key repeats D at both ends of the braking interval. The graph shows that the interval runs from C to D.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q4.body: At the peak, the initial vertical kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy, so $\frac{\tfrac12mu_1^2}{\tfrac12mu_2^2}=\frac{mg(4y)}{mgy}=4$. Hence the ratio of initial vertical speeds is $u_1/u_2=2$. Each ball returns to its launch height, so its final vertical speed equals its initial vertical speed, giving the same ratio of 2.

perOption.A: Mechanical energy is conserved without air resistance, so the initial and final speeds match at ground level.
perOption.B: Ball 1 takes longer to travel the same horizontal distance, so its horizontal speed is smaller.
perOption.C: Using $0=u_yt-\tfrac12gt^2$ gives $t=2u_y/g$ for the nonzero root, so Ball 1 flies for twice as long.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q5.body: The car and trailer have the same acceleration. The net force on the trailer is $600-200=400\ \mathrm{N}$, so their acceleration is $400/400=1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The net force on the car is $F_{\mathrm{car}}=m_{\mathrm{car}}a=(1200)(1.0)=1200\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Gives the net force on the trailer.
perOption.B: Gives the tow force rather than the resultant force on the car.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the full tow force as the trailer's resultant force, giving an acceleration of 1.5 instead of 1.0.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q5.issues: The worked key prints 600 − 400 = 400 N and gives the acceleration in m s⁻¹. The question diagram labels the opposing force as 200 N, and the acceleration unit is m s⁻². Both slips are corrected in the explanation.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q6.body: Horizontal momentum is conserved, and initially only the trolley has horizontal momentum. Thus $m_{\mathrm{trolley}}v_{\mathrm{trolley}}=m_{\mathrm{total}}v_{\mathrm{final}}$, giving $(5.00)(1.25)=(5.35)v_{\mathrm{final}}$ and $v_{\mathrm{final}}=1.17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $(0.350/5.00)(1.25)$, an estimate of the speed lost, as the final speed.
perOption.B: Uses an excessive effective final mass for the conserved horizontal momentum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Ignores the block's contribution to the final moving mass.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q7.body: Both springs carry the same tension of $3.0\ \mathrm{N}$. Their extensions are $x_P=3/30=0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ and $x_Q=3/10=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. The total is $x_P+x_Q=0.40\ \mathrm{m}=400\ \mathrm{mm}$. The key also uses the series spring constant, $k_\mathrm{eff}=k_Pk_Q/(k_P+k_Q)=300/40\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, which gives $x_\mathrm{total}=3/(300/40)=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Gives an extension ten times too small, as with a misplaced decimal in the unit conversion.
perOption.B: Splitting the load equally and considering only spring Q gives $150\ \mathrm{mm}$.
perOption.C: Correct. Both extensions add to $400\ \mathrm{mm}$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the sum of the two extensions.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q8.body: The two equal weights combine into a downward force $2W$ acting midway between their lines of action. In equilibrium the three nonparallel forces must have a common point of intersection. The line of action of $2W$ meets the wire at D, so the hinge force acts along AD.

perOption.A: AB misses the common point at D.
perOption.B: AC uses the line of action of the load’s weight alone.
perOption.C: Correct. AD passes through the common point at D.
perOption.D: AE uses the line of action of the beam’s weight alone.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q9.body: Conservation of energy gives $\tfrac12 mv^2=mgh$, so $h=v^2/(2g)$. The ratio of the new height to the original height is $((0.50v)/v)^2=0.25$.

perOption.A: Correct. Halving the speed quarters the height.
perOption.B: Treats the height as proportional to speed.
perOption.C: Taking the square root of the speed ratio gives about $0.71$, but height scales with speed squared.
perOption.D: Assumes the height stays the same even though the speed is halved.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q10.body: Using $s=ut+\tfrac12 at^2$ gives $1.0=\tfrac12 gt^2$, so $t=\sqrt{2/g}$. The average power is the gravitational potential energy lost per unit time, giving $\bar P=5g/\sqrt{2/g}=5g^{3/2}/\sqrt2\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Loses the factor of $\sqrt2$ when rationalising the denominator.
perOption.B: Uses too high a power of $g$ because dividing by the fall time contributes only $g^{1/2}$.
perOption.C: Correct. Dividing the energy lost by the fall time gives this expression.
perOption.D: Uses a full factor of $g$ from dividing by the fall time, which contributes $g^{1/2}$.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q11.body: A partial vacuum reduces air damping. The amplitude is generally higher, with a sharper and higher resonance peak.

perOption.A: Shows a lower peak, as expected with stronger damping.
perOption.B: Shows a lower peak and shifts it to a lower frequency, as stronger damping can do.
perOption.C: Correct. The peak rises above the original amplitude.
perOption.D: Leaves the peak amplitude at its original value.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q12.body: Friction acts towards the axis and supplies the centripetal force. The platform’s upward support force balances the child’s downward weight.

perOption.A: Correct. Inward friction supplies the centripetal force.
perOption.B: Points friction outwards and adds a separate inward centripetal force.
perOption.C: Adds an outward centrifugal force to the forces seen from the ground.
perOption.D: Draws an extra force and labels it centripetal even though its arrow points outwards.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q13.body: The lift is at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal, so $F_{\mathrm{lift}}\sin60^\circ=mg$ and $F_{\mathrm{lift}}\cos60^\circ=mv^2/r$. Dividing gives $\tan60^\circ=gr/v^2=(9.81)(5000)/v^2$. This gives $v=168\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses a speed that would supply too little inward acceleration at the given turn radius.
perOption.B: Using a radius ten times too small would give a speed close to this value.
perOption.C: Correct. The horizontal lift component supplies the centripetal force.
perOption.D: Inverts the tangent relation by swapping the vertical and horizontal components.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q14.body: Geostationary satellites share a fixed orbital height and complete one orbit every 24 hours. Their centripetal acceleration $r\omega^2$ is therefore the same. Their gravitational potential energy $m\phi$ and kinetic energy can differ if the masses differ.

perOption.A: At the same gravitational potential, $m\phi$ can differ because the masses can differ.
perOption.B: At the same orbital speed, $\tfrac12 mv^2$ can differ because the masses can differ.
perOption.C: Correct. Both satellites have the same centripetal acceleration.
perOption.D: Both satellites complete one revolution in 24 hours, so their angular speeds are equal.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q15.body: Gravitational potential is $\phi=-GM/r$. Doubling the distance from Earth’s centre halves the potential to $-400\ \mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}}$. The external work against gravity is the increase in potential energy, $m(\phi_Q-\phi_P)=0.50[-400-(-800)]=+200\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

perOption.A: Gives the work done by gravity, which is negative during the outward move.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong sign and halves the potential change again.
perOption.C: Correct. The gravitational potential energy increases by $200\ \mathrm{kJ}$.
perOption.D: Uses the numerical change in potential without multiplying by the mass.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q15.issues: The question leaves the agent doing the work implicit. The key gives external work against gravity for zero change in kinetic energy. Gravity itself does −200 kJ.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q16.body: The phase difference satisfies $\Delta\phi/(2\pi)=\Delta s/\lambda=3/2$, so $\Delta\phi=3\pi$. P and Q are in antiphase, so Q is displaced downwards and moves downwards when P is displaced upwards and moves upwards.

perOption.A: Reverses the direction of motion but keeps the same displacement direction.
perOption.B: Treats points separated by $3\lambda/2$ as in phase.
perOption.C: Reverses the displacement but keeps the same direction of motion.
perOption.D: Correct. Antiphase reverses both directions.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q17.body: The receiver stays in the same position, so there is no distance correction. The power intercepted equals intensity times area, and intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude. The intercepted power therefore changes by a factor of $3^2(0.5)=9/2$, giving $9E/2$.

perOption.A: Accounts for the halved area alone.
perOption.B: Treats intensity as proportional to amplitude rather than amplitude squared.
perOption.C: Correct. The intensity increases ninefold while the area halves.
perOption.D: Squares the area factor as well as the amplitude factor.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q17.issues: The worked key prints the new area in both numerator and denominator. Its numerical substitution correctly uses the new-to-original area ratio of 0.5.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q18.body: When waves overlap, each contributes the displacement it would produce on its own at that point and instant. The resultant displacement is the vector sum of those individual displacements.

perOption.A: Correct. The individual displacements add as vectors.
perOption.B: The sum of two stationary waves can itself be stationary, so progressive waves are not a general result.
perOption.C: Diffraction is an application of adding wave contributions, and this statement gives no rule for adding displacements.
perOption.D: A stationary wave is a special result of superposing suitable counter-propagating waves.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q19.body: For a double slit the spacing between successive dark fringes is $x=\lambda D/a$, where $D$ is the screen distance and $a$ is the slit separation. Increasing the wavelength $\lambda$ increases $x$.

perOption.A: Decreasing the screen distance decreases the spacing.
perOption.B: Increasing the slit separation decreases the spacing.
perOption.C: Higher frequency means a shorter wavelength and hence smaller spacing.
perOption.D: Correct. A longer wavelength increases the spacing.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q20.body: The stars subtend an angle $\theta\approx s/r$ and the Rayleigh criterion gives $\theta\approx\lambda/b$ for aperture diameter $b$. Taking $\lambda=400\ \mathrm{nm}$, $b\approx r\lambda/s=(5.5\times10^{16})(400\times10^{-9})/(3.0\times10^{11})\ \mathrm{m}$, of order $0.1\ \mathrm m$.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the closest listed minimum for a visible wavelength.
perOption.B: Greatly overestimates the aperture needed to resolve the pair.
perOption.C: Implies a much finer angular resolution than the separation requires.
perOption.D: Overestimates the required aperture by about six orders of magnitude.

ejc-2018-promo-p1-q20.issues: The question omits the wavelength. The key assumes 400 nm and uses the syllabus approximation to the Rayleigh criterion, giving about 0.073 m and making 0.1 m the closest option.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q1.body: Earth’s radius is about four times the Moon’s radius. With a football of radius $0.12\ \mathrm{m}$ representing Earth, the model Moon should have a radius of about $0.03\ \mathrm{m}$, matching a tennis ball.

perOption.A: A basketball is much too large for a radius of about $3\ \mathrm{cm}$.
perOption.B: Correct. A tennis ball has a radius of about $3\ \mathrm{cm}$.
perOption.C: A golf ball is smaller than the required model Moon.
perOption.D: A cherry has a radius well below the target.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q2.body: The mean reading is $3.06\ \mathrm{A}$. Applying $1\%$ to each extreme gives corrections of about $0.03\ \mathrm{A}$, so the lower and upper bounds are $3.04-0.03=3.01\ \mathrm{A}$ and $3.08+0.03=3.11\ \mathrm{A}$. Half the adjusted range is $0.05\ \mathrm{A}$, giving $(3.06\pm0.05)\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Uses half the observed range alone.
perOption.B: Uses the full observed range as the uncertainty.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds the meter uncertainty to the full observed range.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q3.body: Apply $v^2=u^2+2as$ at both heights with upward positive, giving $v_A^2=u^2-2gy_A$ and $(v_A/4)^2=u^2-2gy_B$. Eliminate $u^2$ to get $15v_A^2=32g(y_B-y_A)$. Thus $v_A=\sqrt{32(9.81)(3.06)/15}=8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Gives only about $0.19\ \mathrm{m}$ of rise before the speed falls to a quarter.
perOption.B: Gives only about $0.76\ \mathrm{m}$ of rise before the speed falls to a quarter.
perOption.C: Gives only about $1.72\ \mathrm{m}$ of rise before the speed falls to a quarter.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q3.issues: The key uses plus signs in its height equations despite upward height being positive, then uses the positive height difference in its numerical calculation. The rewrite corrects the signs.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q4.body: The cart accelerates from rest at X, so the gaps between successive dots initially grow. On the nearly level section the cart moves at roughly constant speed, so the gaps are approximately equal there. In A the gaps widen again on the final downhill stretch.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The gaps keep growing through the nearly level section, where the speed should be roughly constant.
perOption.C: The initial equal gaps indicate constant speed from X.
perOption.D: The initial equal gaps indicate constant speed from X.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q4.issues: The key’s explanation omits the final downhill stretch. A shows renewed acceleration there and is the best match.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q5.body: The horizontal speed is constant, so horizontal displacement increases linearly with time as in Graph 3. The loss of kinetic energy equals the gain in gravitational potential energy, so kinetic energy decreases linearly with vertical displacement. The projectile still has horizontal speed at the highest point, so its kinetic energy remains positive as in Graph 4.

perOption.A: Graph 1 implies increasing horizontal speed and Graph 2 implies zero kinetic energy at the highest point.
perOption.B: Graph 1 implies increasing horizontal speed.
perOption.C: Graph 2 implies zero kinetic energy at the highest point.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q6.body: Treat the $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ blocks as one system. The tension in the string joining the $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ blocks supplies the system’s horizontal resultant force, so $T=(2+3)(2)=10\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Finds the tension in the string between the two lighter blocks.
perOption.B: Finds the resultant force on the middle block alone.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the combined mass of the two blocks on the right.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q7.body: Let $\theta$ be the angle of the tension to the horizontal. Vertical equilibrium gives $T\sin\theta=mg$, and forward acceleration gives $T\cos\theta=ma$. Thus $\tan\theta=g/a\approx2$, so $\theta=63.4^\circ$ and the angle to the vertical is $26.6^\circ$. The bob hangs backward so that the horizontal component of tension points forward.

perOption.A: A forward displacement would make the horizontal component of tension point backward.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the angle to the horizontal and puts the bob on the wrong side.
perOption.D: Uses the angle to the horizontal.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q8.body: The initial and final momenta both have magnitude $p=mv$ and make angles of $30^\circ$ above and below the horizontal respectively. Their horizontal components cancel when the vectors are subtracted, while the vertical components give a downward change of magnitude $p\sin 30^\circ+p\sin 30^\circ=p=mv$.

perOption.A: Treats equal momentum magnitudes as equal momentum vectors.
perOption.B: Counts only one vertical momentum component.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes the entire momentum vector reverses.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q9.body: The aeroplane, glider and ship can each move with constant velocity in the situations described, allowing their forces to balance. The speedboat changes velocity as it changes direction at constant speed. Its acceleration requires a resultant force, so it cannot be in equilibrium.

perOption.A: The aeroplane can climb with constant velocity and balanced forces.
perOption.B: The glider can travel at constant altitude with constant horizontal velocity.
perOption.C: The ship can be towed at constant velocity with balanced forces.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q10.body: The water pushes upwards on the bottom with force $\rho_B A$ and downwards on the top with force $\rho_T A$. The pressure forces on the vertical curved surface have no vertical component, so the upthrust is $(\rho_B-\rho_T)A$.

perOption.A: Gives a pressure difference and omits the area needed to obtain a force.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Subtracts the weight and gives the net vertical force due to water and gravity.
perOption.D: Adds the weight even though upthrust comes from the water’s pressure forces.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q10.issues: The key gives only a recall cue about the origin of upthrust. The question uses rho for pressure.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q11.body: Vertical force balance gives the weight $W=16+9=25\ \mathrm{kN}$. Taking moments about the front wheels gives $Wx=9(1.50)$, so the centre of gravity is $x=0.540\ \mathrm{m}$ behind the front wheels. Adding the front overhang gives $0.540+0.600=1.14\ \mathrm{m}$ from the front of the van.

perOption.A: Measures from the front wheels.
perOption.B: Measures from the rear wheels.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Measures from the rear end of the van.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q12.body: The initial elastic potential energy equals the kinetic energy at P plus the work done against friction, since there is no net change in gravitational potential energy. Thus $E_k=\frac12 kx^2-fd$.

perOption.A: Subtracts a gravitational energy term even though the start and end heights are equal.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the energy dissipated by friction to the kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Adds the frictional loss and treats P as lower than the starting point.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q13.body: At the maximum speed the net force is zero, so $P/v_{\max}=kv_{\max}^2$ and $k=P/v_{\max}^3=110\times10^3/21^3$. At $15.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ the engine force is $P/15$. Subtract the drag to get $F_{\rm net}=\frac{110\times10^3}{15}-\frac{110\times10^3}{21^3}(15)^2\approx4660\ \mathrm{N}$, or $4.7\ \mathrm{kN}$ forwards.

perOption.A: Gives the resistive force alone.
perOption.B: Results from scaling the resistance linearly with speed.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the engine force alone.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q14.body: The surfaces have the same linear speed at the point of contact because there is no slipping, so $v_1=v_2$. Using $v=r\omega$ for each rim gives $R\Omega=r\omega$, hence $\Omega=(r/R)\omega$.

perOption.A: Equates angular speeds despite the different radii.
perOption.B: Assigns different linear speeds to the surfaces at the contact point.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assigns different linear speeds at the contact point and inverts the angular-speed ratio.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q15.body: At Y the string is just taut, so the tension is zero and $mg=mv_Y^2/l$. The kinetic energy at Y is therefore $\frac12 mgl$. By energy conservation, $\frac12 mv^2=\frac12 mgl+mg(2l)=\frac52 mgl$, giving $v=\sqrt{5gl}$.

perOption.A: Gives the speed at Y and omits the energy needed to rise from X.
perOption.B: Allows a rise of only one string length if all the initial kinetic energy is converted to gravitational potential energy.
perOption.C: Accounts for the rise but assumes zero speed at Y.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q16.body: Gravity supplies Europa’s centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mr(2\pi/T)^2$. Cancelling Europa’s mass gives $M=(2\pi/T)^2r^3/G$. With $r=6.7\times10^5\times10^3\ \mathrm{m}$ and $T=85\times60^2\ \mathrm{s}$, this gives $M=1.90\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Understates the mass required for the given radius and period by many orders of magnitude.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overstates the mass, so it predicts a much shorter orbital period at the given radius.
perOption.D: Overstates the mass, so it predicts a much shorter orbital period at the given radius.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q17.body: The equal-mass stars pull in opposite directions with equal force at the midpoint of PQ. The resultant force there is zero, so the graph must reach the horizontal axis.

perOption.A: Shows a peak where the forces cancel.
perOption.B: Places the maximum at the midpoint despite cancellation.
perOption.C: Leaves a nonzero force at the midpoint.
perOption.D: Correct. The force magnitude reaches zero.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q17.issues: D is the best available graph. Its rounded minimum is schematic, since the exact force magnitude has a cusp.

ejc-2019-promo-p1-q18.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GM_{\mathrm E}m/r^2=mv^2/r=mr\omega^2$. This gives $K=GM_{\mathrm E}m/(2r)$ and $GM_{\mathrm E}=r^3\omega^2$. Adding $U=-GM_{\mathrm E}m/r$ gives $E=-GM_{\mathrm E}m/(2r)=-K=U/2$. Equal total energies imply equal gravitational potential energies.

perOption.A: This is true because equal total energies fix $m/r$, so the smaller radius gives the smaller mass.
perOption.B: Correct. The two gravitational potential energies are equal.
perOption.C: This is true because the larger radius gives a smaller $\omega$.
