ejc-2023-promo-p1-q14.issues: The key reverses the sign of the tension difference in its final equation. Its radial equations give bottom tension minus top tension equal to 2mg, so B is correct. Constant speed assumes a tangential influence that offsets gravity during the revolution.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q15.body: The gravitational field strength is $g=GM/r^2$, so $g\propto1/r^2$. With $r$ the Earth’s radius, the field-strength ratio is $\frac{10}{5}=\left(\frac{x}{r}\right)^2$. Hence $r=\frac{x}{\sqrt2}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the field-strength ratio and gives a radius larger than the exterior distance.
perOption.B: Introduces an extra factor of two after taking the square root of the field-strength ratio.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-linear dependence on distance.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q16.body: For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force, so $\frac{GMm}{R^2}=\frac{mv^2}{R}$. Rearranging gives $E_K=\frac12 mv^2=\frac{GMm}{2R}$. At the same satellite mass, increasing $R$ decreases $E_K$.

perOption.A: An equatorial satellite has a period of about $24\ \mathrm{h}$ only at the appropriate circular orbital radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The period satisfies $T^2=\frac{4\pi^2R^3}{GM}$, so it is independent of the satellite mass.
perOption.D: At fixed radius, $E_P+E_K=-\frac{GMm}{2R}$ becomes more negative as the satellite mass increases.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q16.issues: The worked comment on D says M increases, but the varying mass is the satellite mass m.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q17.body: A uniform gravitational field has the same magnitude and direction at every point. A test mass released from rest moves along the field lines, and gravitational potential can vary from point to point.

perOption.A: Gravitational potential changes along the field direction.
perOption.B: A test mass released from rest moves in the direction of the field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The field points in one fixed direction throughout the region.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q18.body: Kinetic energy is maximum at $t=0$, so the mass starts at equilibrium and its velocity has cosine form. Kinetic energy peaks twice per oscillation, so the graph gives $T=0.800\ \mathrm{s}$ and $\omega=2\pi/T=7.85\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. From $2.0=\tfrac12(0.50)v_0^2$, the speed amplitude is $v_0=2.83\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Hence the matching velocity is $v=2.83\cos(7.85t)$.

perOption.A: Uses twice the motion’s angular frequency and starts at zero speed, although kinetic energy is initially maximum.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses twice the motion’s angular frequency and starts at maximum displacement, although the mass is initially at equilibrium.
perOption.D: Uses the displacement amplitude as the acceleration amplitude, whose magnitude is $\omega v_0=22.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q18.issues: The key’s intermediate acceleration expression uses v₀x₀ where ωv₀ is required. Its numerical acceleration amplitude and answer B are correct. The energy graph alone leaves the sign of the initial velocity undetermined.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q19.body: The angular speed is $\omega=v/r=2.0/0.40=5.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, so $T=2\pi/\omega=1.26\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $T/4<0.40\ \mathrm{s}<T/2$, the shadow has crossed the centre and is still moving in the same direction. Its final position is $x=x_0\cos(\omega t)=0.40\cos(5.0\times0.40)=-0.17\ \mathrm{m}$. The distance travelled is $0.40+0.17=0.57\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the final distance from the centre and omits the initial 0.40 m.
perOption.B: Correct. The shadow travels 0.40 m to the centre and another 0.17 m beyond it.
perOption.C: Overestimates the distance beyond the centre, which is 0.17 m.
perOption.D: Counts an extra 0.40 m of travel by using the full diameter before adding 0.17 m.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q19.issues: The key prints T/4 as both bounds on the elapsed time. The upper bound is T/2.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q20.body: The school treats damping in air as small and damping in a vacuum as negligible. The maximum amplitude therefore increases at the pendulum’s natural frequency $f_o$.

perOption.A: Correct. The curve peaks higher at $f_o$.
perOption.B: Places the peak below $f_o$.
perOption.C: Places the peak above the indicated natural frequency $f_o$.
perOption.D: Shows a lower, broader peak characteristic of increased damping.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q20.issues: A is the intended qualitative sketch. With exactly zero damping, the ideal driven oscillator has no finite steady-state amplitude at resonance.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q21.body: The path difference along the direction of travel is $\Delta s=0.22\sin 25^\circ$. The phase difference is $\Delta\phi=\frac{\Delta s}{\lambda}\,2\pi=\frac{0.22\sin25^\circ}{1.7}\,2\pi=0.34\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Uses half the full-cycle phase factor, giving half the phase difference.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos25^\circ$ for the projection along the direction of travel.
perOption.D: Uses the entire ear separation as the path difference.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q22.body: The graphs give a wavelength of $0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ and a period of $2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$. The wave speed is $v=f\lambda=\lambda/T=0.6/(2.0\times10^{-3})=300\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the amplitude as the wavelength and treats milliseconds as seconds.
perOption.B: Treats the period of 2.0 ms as 2.0 s.
perOption.C: Uses the 0.4 m amplitude as the wavelength.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q23.body: The marked $\theta$ is measured from the dashed reference perpendicular to A’s transmission axis. At $\theta=0,\pi,2\pi$, the transmission axes are perpendicular and the transmitted intensity is zero. At $\theta=\pi/2,3\pi/2$, the axes are parallel and the transmitted intensity reaches $I_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows full transmission at $\theta=0$, where the axes are perpendicular.
perOption.C: Repeats every $\pi/2$ and shows full transmission where the axes are perpendicular.
perOption.D: Shows zero transmission at $\pi/2$ and $3\pi/2$, where the axes are parallel.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q24.body: The initial path difference is zero, so constructive interference gives a large signal. The next constructive maximum occurs at a path difference of one wavelength, $8.4\ \mathrm{cm}$. A slide of $4.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ adds $4.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ to each of the upper and lower arms, giving the required total.

perOption.A: Produces a half-wavelength path difference and destructive interference.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the second recurrence because the path difference increases by two wavelengths.
perOption.D: Gives the fourth recurrence because the path difference increases by four wavelengths.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q25.body: The open tube at its fundamental produces sound with wavelength $\lambda=2L$. The air column in the burette resonates at the same frequency at lengths $x$ and $y$. Successive resonant lengths differ by half a wavelength, so $y-x=\lambda/2=L$.

perOption.A: Assigns the open tube’s half-wavelength length to the first resonance of the closed air column.
perOption.B: Uses one third of the second resonant length as the open tube length, missing the factor of two between a quarter and a half wavelength.
perOption.C: Halves the separation even though that separation is already half a wavelength.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q26.body: The two waves have equal amplitudes, frequencies and speeds and travel in opposite directions, so they form a stationary wave where they overlap. At X the two displacements can add to $2A$, where $A$ is the amplitude of either wave, making X an antinode. Y has an amplitude between zero and $2A$, and Z always has zero displacement.

perOption.A: Destructive interference at the nodes still leaves a stationary wave elsewhere.
perOption.B: Correct. X is an antinode.
perOption.C: Y has a nonzero amplitude below the antinode amplitude.
perOption.D: Z has zero amplitude and is a node.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q27.body: A stationary wave forms along PQ, with adjacent maxima separated by $\lambda/2$. The ship takes $1/f$ seconds to go between maxima, and its speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is $v\times10^3/(60\times60)=5v/18$. Using distance travelled equals speed times time gives $\lambda/2=(5v/18)(1/f)$, so $\lambda=5v/(9f)$.

perOption.A: Equates the distance between maxima to a full wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the speed in kilometres per hour directly and takes the spacing as a full wavelength.
perOption.D: Uses the correct half-wavelength spacing but skips the speed conversion.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q27.issues: The stationary-wave interpretation assumes the transmitters remain coherent.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q28.body: For line density $N$, the slit spacing is $d=1/N$ and the grating equation is $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At the limiting angle $90^\circ$, $\frac{1.0\times10^{-3}}{300}\sin90^\circ=n(450\times10^{-9})$, giving $n=7.4$. The highest integer order is 7, so the total is $7+7+1=15$, including the central maximum.

perOption.A: Counts the seven orders on just one side and omits the centre.
perOption.B: Counts one side and the central maximum only.
perOption.C: Counts both sides but omits the central maximum.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q29.body: The coincident maxima have the same diffraction angle $\theta$. The grating equation gives $d\sin\theta=2\lambda_X=3\lambda_Y$, so $\lambda_X/\lambda_Y=3/2$.

perOption.A: Treats the maximum for Y as first order and uses 1 in place of 3.
perOption.B: Takes the ratio of the orders directly and reverses the wavelength ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the stated third order for Y and uses a factor of two alone.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q30.body: Visible wavelengths range from about $400$ to $700\ \mathrm{nm}$, so use $550\ \mathrm{nm}$ as an estimate. At the resolution limit the small-angle approximation and Rayleigh criterion give $s/r\approx\theta\approx\lambda/b$. Substituting $\frac{1.4}{r}=\frac{550\times10^{-9}}{5.0\times10^{-3}}$ gives $r\approx13\ \mathrm{km}$.

perOption.A: Is too small by a factor of 1000, as when the millimetre-to-metre conversion is applied twice.
perOption.B: Is too small by a factor of 100, as when the estimated wavelength is converted to metres two powers of ten too large.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Is too large by a factor of ten, as when the estimated wavelength is converted to metres one power of ten too small.

ejc-2023-promo-p1-q30.issues: The question supplies no wavelength. The key estimates 550 nm and uses the syllabus approximation for Rayleigh resolution.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q1.body: Write electrical power as $P=IV$. In $k=(IV/I^2)(\lambda/L)^2$, the units of the two lengths cancel. The unit of $k$ is therefore $\mathrm{V/A}=\Omega$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Keeps the unit of power without dividing by the unit of current squared.
perOption.C: Divides the power unit by one factor of current and misses the second factor.
perOption.D: Cancels the length units correctly but overlooks the remaining electrical units.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q2.body: The velocity changes sign at the top because the ball reverses direction. The shorter ascent and longer descent on the height–time graph indicate air resistance. Work done against air resistance reduces the ball’s kinetic energy, so the landing speed is smaller than the launch speed. The areas before and after $t_1$ on the velocity–time graph must be equal in magnitude because the ball returns to its starting height.

perOption.A: Keeps velocity positive on the way down.
perOption.B: Keeps velocity positive on the way down.
perOption.C: Shows a landing speed comparable to the launch speed despite the energy lost to air resistance.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q2.issues: D is the best qualitative choice. Its increasing downward slope magnitude near landing is inconsistent with ordinary speed-dependent drag, and the plotted curves are schematic.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q3.body: Taking down and right as positive, $s_y=\tfrac12gt^2$ because the initial vertical velocity is zero, and $s_x=u_xt$. Combining them gives $s_y=\tfrac12g(s_x/u_x)^2$, so $s_x\propto u_x\sqrt{s_y}$. Thus $\frac{x_A}{x_B}=\frac{2}{1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}=\sqrt2=1.41$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio of the horizontal speeds, giving $\tfrac12\sqrt{\tfrac12}$.
perOption.B: Treats the time of fall as directly proportional to the drop height.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Inverts the height ratio under the square root, giving ball A the longer fall time.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q4.body: Let $F_{AB}$ be the magnitude of the force exerted by A on B, and let $a$ be the common acceleration. For Z, $F_{YZ}=4ma$; for Y, $F_{XY}-F_{ZY}=3ma$. Newton’s third law gives $F_{ZY}=F_{YZ}=4ma$ and $F_{YX}=F_{XY}=7ma$. The ratio is therefore $7ma/(4ma)=7/4$.

perOption.A: Uses the mass of X alone in the numerator.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of Y alone and compares it with the total mass.
perOption.C: Divides the contact force at X–Y by the applied force on all three blocks.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q5.body: Taking upwards as positive, Newton’s second law gives $U-m_{\mathrm{wood}}g-T=m_{\mathrm{wood}}a$. When the string breaks, $T=0$, so $(1000)(1.0)(9.81)-(800)(1.0)(9.81)=(800)(1.0)a$. This gives $a=2.45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ upwards, or $2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses the density ratio difference of 0.25 as an acceleration without multiplying by gravity.
perOption.B: Uses the displaced-water to wood density ratio as the acceleration without subtracting weight or multiplying by gravity.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the full upthrust without subtracting the block’s weight.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q5.issues: Q5’s worked solution prints the acceleration unit as m s⁻¹. The explanation uses m s⁻².

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q6.body: At the bottom, $N_B-mg=mv_B^2/r$. At the top, assume $N_T$ points downwards, so $N_T+mg=mv_T^2/r$. Conservation of energy gives $mg(2r)=\tfrac12m(v_B^2-v_T^2)$. Subtracting the top force equation from the bottom one and substituting the energy relation gives $N_B-N_T=6mg$. Since $N_B=5.5mg$, $N_T=-0.5mg$ under the downward convention, so the normal force is $0.5mg$ upwards.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the negative result in the downward convention as a downward force.
perOption.C: Adds the required inward resultant to the weight when calculating the upward force.
perOption.D: Adds the weight to the required inward resultant and assigns the sum to a downward normal force.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The key omits mg after 5.5 in one line of working.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q7.body: The net work done is the change in kinetic energy, so with zero initial kinetic energy, the kinetic energy at $s$ equals the area under the $F$–$s$ graph up to $s$. Its gradient is therefore $F$. From $s_1$ to $s_2$ the gradient increases from zero, and from $s_2$ to $s_3$ it decreases back to zero. The kinetic energy rises throughout that interval and stays constant after $s_3$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows kinetic energy falling after $s_2$, although the force is still positive and does positive work.
perOption.C: Shows negative kinetic energy between $s_2$ and $s_3$.
perOption.D: Shows negative kinetic energy immediately after $s_2$.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The initial-rest condition and zero net force before s₁ leave no mechanism for the object to reach s₁. A is the intended work–energy graph.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q8.body: At altitude $80\,000\ \mathrm{m}$, the potential is $\phi=-GM/(6.371\times10^6+80\,000)$. Using the magnitude of the surface field, $9.81=GM/(6.371\times10^6)^2$, gives $GM=3.98\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3\,s^{-2}}$. Substitution gives $\phi=-6.2\times10^7\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}=-62\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Gives a potential magnitude far too small for a point still close to Earth’s surface.
perOption.B: Underestimates the magnitude obtained by dividing $GM$ by the full distance from Earth’s centre.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses giga instead of mega for the calculated magnitude of 62.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The worked solution has inconsistent signs for the surface field and omits the negative sign and per-kilogram unit in its final result. The printed option C has the correct sign and unit.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q9.body: For a circular orbit, $T^2$ is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius. The heights $r$ and $3r$ correspond to orbital radii $2r$ and $4r$. Hence $(T'/T)^2=(4r/2r)^3=8$, giving $T'=2\sqrt{2}\,T$.

perOption.A: Takes the square root of the radius ratio without first cubing it.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the altitude ratio and takes its square root without first cubing it.
perOption.D: Uses the altitude ratio of 3 in place of the orbital-radius ratio of 2.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q10.body: The acceleration magnitude is greatest at the amplitude $x_0$, where $a_{\max}=\omega^2x_0$. With $\omega=2\pi f$, this gives $a_{\max}=4\pi^2(10\,000)^2(0.32\times10^{-3})=1.26\times10^6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $omega x_0$, the maximum speed.
perOption.B: Uses $omega x_0$ and leaves the amplitude in millimetres.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the amplitude in millimetres as though it were in metres.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q10.issues: The key labels the acceleration result Hz. The explanation uses m s⁻².

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q11.body: The displacement–time graphs show that Q’s amplitude decays faster than P’s, so Q is more heavily damped. Greater damping lowers the peak amplitude and shifts the peak to a lower driving frequency. Graph A shows both effects.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Gives the more heavily damped Q a higher resonance peak.
perOption.C: Shows amplitude minima where resonance should produce peaks.
perOption.D: Places Q’s peak at a higher driving frequency than P’s.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q12.body: Let $h$ be the heat-loss rate and $L_v$ the specific latent heat of vaporisation, so $P_1=m_1L_v+h$ and $P_2=m_2L_v+h$. In $P_1m_2-P_2m_1$, the latent-heat terms cancel, leaving $(m_2-m_1)h$. Thus $h=(P_1m_2-P_2m_1)/(m_2-m_1)$.

perOption.A: Dividing a power difference by a mass-loss-rate difference gives $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$ instead of a heat-loss rate.
perOption.B: Subtracting the heater powers cancels the common heat-loss term.
perOption.C: Power divided by mass-loss rate has units $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q12.issues: The key’s proof for D omits the denominator on the left side of its displayed equation.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.body: Over the full cycle the change in internal energy is zero, so $\Delta U=Q+W=0$, with $W$ the work done on the gas. The compression contributes $W_{AB}=(1.0\times10^5)(20.0-5.0)\times10^{-6}=1.5\ \mathrm{J}$, the constant-volume leg contributes zero, and the expansion contributes $W_{CA}=-4.2\ \mathrm{J}$. Hence $0=Q+(-4.2+1.5)\ \mathrm{J}$ and the overall heat gain is $2.7\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Adds the magnitudes of compression and expansion work and reports a heat loss.
perOption.B: Reports the net work done on the gas as the heat gain.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of compression and expansion work as though both transfer energy out by work.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q14.body: Let $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$ be the intensities emerging from the three polarisers. Since $\theta$ is measured from the axis of $\mathrm{P}_1$, Malus’ law gives $I_3=I_2\cos^2(\theta-30^\circ)=I_1\cos^2 30^\circ\cos^2(\theta-30^\circ)$. Substituting the given intensities gives $14=30\cos^2 30^\circ\cos^2(\theta-30^\circ)$, so one possible setting is $\theta=68^\circ$.

perOption.A: Reports the angle between the axes of the second and third polarisers.
perOption.B: Uses the complement of the angle between the last two axes.
perOption.C: Uses an axis difference of $27^\circ$, which transmits too much light at the third polariser.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.body: The key uses the syllabus form of the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the lens diameter. For small angles, $s/r\approx\theta$, so $s\approx r\lambda/b=(100)(550\times10^{-9})/(10\times10^{-2})$. This gives $5.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}=0.55\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Gives a separation below the limit obtained from the stated distance and aperture.
perOption.B: Gives a separation below the limit obtained from the stated distance and aperture.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the result under the syllabus approximation.
perOption.D: This exceeds the syllabus estimate and is the closest option to the circular-aperture result.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The syllabus approximation gives keyed C. For a circular aperture, the Airy-pattern Rayleigh criterion uses 1.22λ/b, giving 0.671 mm, with D (0.65 mm) closest. The diagram also mislabels the 10 cm diameter as 10⁻² m, though the calculation uses 0.10 m.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.body: At an overlapping maximum, $d\sin\theta=n_1\lambda_1=n_2\lambda_2$. Thus $n_2/n_1=480/640=3/4$, and the smallest nonzero orders are $n_1=4$ and $n_2=3$. Using $d=0.01/5000\ \mathrm{m}$ gives $(0.01/5000)\sin\theta=4(480\times10^{-9})$, so $\theta=74^\circ$.

perOption.A: Gives too small a path difference to reach even the first nonzero order of either wavelength.
perOption.B: Treats a first-order-scale angle as an overlap, although the first orders occur at different angles.
perOption.C: Uses an angle whose path difference is not an integer multiple of both wavelengths.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.issues: The question implicitly excludes the shared zero-order maximum at 0°, which is absent from the options.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q17.body: Point X is measured relative to the $0\ \mathrm V$ end of the variable resistor, so its potential equals the drop across that resistor. At $100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ the potential divider gives $V_X=30[100/(100+500)]=5\ \mathrm V$. At $500\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ it gives $V_X=30[500/(500+500)]=15\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Uses the maximum total resistance at the minimum-resistance setting.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes the 25 V drop across the fixed resistor at the minimum variable resistance.
perOption.D: Gives the range across the fixed resistor.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.body: In A and B the diode is reverse-biased, so the heater branch cannot conduct. At low temperature, the NTC thermistor has higher resistance and a larger share of the supply voltage appears across it. The heater branch should therefore be connected across the thermistor with the diode oriented to conduct, as in D.

perOption.A: The diode is reverse-biased.
perOption.B: The diode is reverse-biased.
perOption.C: The heater branch is across the fixed resistor, whose voltage falls as the thermistor cools.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The printed stem leaves out the diode shown in each diagram. The batch marks the question as text even though the circuit diagrams are essential. No heater threshold is specified, so the circuit establishes the intended direction of change in heater power.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q5.body:
The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity. As the two velocities are perpendicular, $|\Delta\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{0.40^2+0.30^2}=0.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The magnitude of the change in momentum is $m|\Delta\mathbf{v}|=(0.20)(0.50)=0.10\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the momentum magnitudes as if the velocities were parallel.
perOption.B: Correct. The perpendicular components give a momentum change of $0.10$ in the stated units.
perOption.C: Adds the momentum magnitudes as if the velocities were opposite.
perOption.D: Uses the change in velocity without multiplying by the ball’s mass.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q6.body:
The drone hovers, so its thrust equals its weight. The four propellers give the initially stationary air downward momentum at a rate of $4(0.400/1.00)(v-0)$.

Equating this to the drone’s weight gives $4(0.400/1.00)(v-0)=1.20(9.81)$, so $v=7.36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the drone’s mass in place of its weight when balancing thrust.
perOption.B: Omits both the factor of four for the propellers and the factor of $g$ in the weight.
perOption.C: Correct. The four propellers together supply enough thrust to balance the weight.
perOption.D: Assigns the entire thrust to the airflow from one propeller.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q7.body:
The initial momentum is zero, so fragment C must balance the momentum of A and B along their respective directions. The component equations are $(3m)(4.0)=mv\sin\theta$ and $(2m)(6.0)=mv\cos\theta$.

Dividing gives $\tan\theta=1$, so $\theta=45^\circ$.

perOption.A: A $30^\circ$ angle would make C’s horizontal momentum component smaller than its vertical component.
perOption.B: Correct. C’s horizontal and vertical momentum components have equal magnitudes.
perOption.C: A $60^\circ$ angle would make C’s horizontal momentum component larger than its vertical component.
perOption.D: A $70^\circ$ angle would give a horizontal-to-vertical momentum ratio far above one.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.body:
At constant velocity, $F_{\mathrm{drive}}=F_{\mathrm{resistive}}+mg\sin\theta$. The driving force is the useful power divided by speed, so $\frac{60}{100}\frac{80\,000}{6.5}=F_{\mathrm{resistive}}+(1000)(9.81)\sin45^\circ$.

This gives $F_{\mathrm{resistive}}\approx450\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The downslope weight component accounts for most of the driving force.
perOption.B: Uses the full input power to calculate the driving force.
perOption.C: Uses the driving force as the resistive force and omits the downslope weight component.
perOption.D: Adds the downslope weight component to the driving force when solving for resistance.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q10.body:
The vertical component of the spring tension balances the weight, so $kx\cos\theta=mg$. Its horizontal component provides the centripetal force, so $kx\sin\theta=mr(2\pi/T)^2$.

Dividing the equations and using $r=0.108\sin27^\circ$ gives $\tan27^\circ=\frac{4\pi^2(0.108\sin27^\circ)}{T^2(9.81)}$, so $T=0.62\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The two components of spring tension determine the period.
perOption.B: This period gives a centripetal force too small for the horizontal component of tension.
perOption.C: Treats $10.8\ \mathrm{cm}$ as $10.8\ \mathrm{m}$, making the period ten times too large.
perOption.D: This period would require a much larger orbital radius at the stated angle.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.body:
For a circular orbit, the total energy is $E=-K$, so equal kinetic energies give equal total energies. Since $K=GMm/(2r)$, the more massive satellite A must have a larger orbital radius.

The relation $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$ gives A a longer period, and $\omega=2\pi/T$ then gives it a smaller angular velocity.

perOption.A: Correct. In a circular orbit, total energy is the negative of kinetic energy.
perOption.B: At fixed $K$, the relation $K=GMm/(2r)$ gives A a larger radius.
perOption.C: The larger radius of A gives it a longer period because $T^2\propto r^3$.
perOption.D: A’s longer period gives it a smaller angular velocity because $\omega=2\pi/T$.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.issues: Both the key and the intended answer assume circular orbits, which the question leaves implicit.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q12.body: A thermometer uses a property that changes with temperature, so the property can be calibrated. Linearity is an assumption used in constructing empirical centigrade scales, while a thermometer can also be calibrated using a nonlinear response.

perOption.A: A solid or gas can also supply a thermometric property.
perOption.B: Linearity is a calibration assumption in an empirical centigrade scale, and a nonlinear property can also be calibrated.
perOption.C: Correct. A temperature-dependent property supplies the thermometer reading.
perOption.D: An ideal-gas equation of state applies to a particular model, while thermometers can use a range of substances and properties.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q13.body:
The period is $T=1/f=1/1.50\approx0.67\ \mathrm{s}$. Starting at the crest gives $x=x_0\cos\omega t$, so at $0.75\ \mathrm{s}$ the displacement is $0.120\cos[(2\pi)(1.50)(0.75)]\approx0.08485\ \mathrm{m}$, or about $85\ \mathrm{mm}$.

P travels four amplitudes in the first cycle and then moves down from $120$ to $85\ \mathrm{mm}$, giving $4(120)+(120-85)=515\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the distance after the first complete cycle.
perOption.B: Gives the final displacement from equilibrium instead of the accumulated distance.
perOption.C: Undercounts the completed cycle, which alone contributes $480\ \mathrm{mm}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The full cycle and the final partial cycle give $515\ \mathrm{mm}$.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key truncates the intermediate displacement to 0.0848 m. The calculated value is about 0.08485 m and gives the same answer.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.body:
Particles on either side of a compression are displaced towards its centre. Taking right as positive, the particles between P and the central compression are displaced to the right and those between the compression and Q are displaced to the left.

The displacement is zero at the centres of the rarefactions at P and Q and at the centre of the intervening compression.

perOption.A: Shows positive displacement on both sides of the intervening compression.
perOption.B: Shows negative displacement on both sides of the intervening compression.
perOption.C: Correct. The displacement is positive on the left of the compression and negative on its right.
perOption.D: Places displacement maxima at P and Q, where the displacements are zero.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q15.body: The first filter transmits $I_0\cos^2 30^\circ$ and polarises the transmitted wave along its axis. The second axis is $60^\circ$ from that direction, so $I=(I_0\cos^2 30^\circ)(\cos^2 60^\circ)=0.19I_0$.

perOption.A: Applies the second filter to the original vertical polarisation.
perOption.B: Uses $60^\circ$ for both filters instead of using $30^\circ$ for the first.
perOption.C: Correct. The two intensity factors are $\cos^2 30^\circ$ and $\cos^2 60^\circ$.
perOption.D: Uses $30^\circ$ for both filters instead of using $60^\circ$ for the second.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q16.body:
The in-phase amplitudes initially add to $A+A=2A$, giving $I=k(2A)^2$. Doubling P’s amplitude changes the total to $2A+A=3A$, giving $I'=k(3A)^2$.

Dividing gives $I'/I=(3A)^2/(2A)^2=9/4$, so $I'\approx2.3I$.

perOption.A: Inverts the squared amplitude ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the amplitude ratio directly as the intensity ratio.
perOption.C: Correct. Squaring the amplitude ratio gives $9/4$.
perOption.D: Uses the new amplitude in units of a single wave’s amplitude as the intensity multiplier.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q17.body: The fringe spacing is $x=\lambda D/a=\left(\frac{3.00\times10^8}{1.5\times10^{12}}\right)\left(\frac{4.0}{80\times10^{-3}}\right)=10\ \mathrm{mm}$. The third minimum is two and a half fringe spacings from the central maximum, so the sensor moves $2.5x=25\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: The distance is less than the $5.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ needed to reach even the first minimum.
perOption.B: Stops after one fringe spacing, at the first maximum beyond the centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The third minimum is at $2.5$ fringe spacings.
perOption.D: Counts each maximum-to-minimum interval as a full fringe spacing instead of half a spacing.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q18.body:
Nine dots give a central maximum and four orders on each side. From $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ at the limiting angle of $90^\circ$, the fourth order requires $d\ge4(5.50\times10^{-7})=2.20\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$.

The fifth order reaches that limit at $d=5(5.50\times10^{-7})=2.75\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$, so $d$ must be below this value. The spacing $2.25\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$ lies in the required range.

perOption.A: Correct. It allows orders up to the fourth on both sides.
perOption.B: This spacing already allows a fifth order on each side.
perOption.C: This spacing allows orders above the fourth, including the seventh.
perOption.D: This spacing allows orders above the fourth, including the eighth.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q19.body:
The minimum separation $s$ at distance $r$ satisfies $s/r\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the aperture diameter. Using the key’s assumed wavelength of $550\ \mathrm{nm}$ gives $\frac{s}{20(3.00\times10^8)(365)(24)(60)(60)}=\frac{550\times10^{-9}}{3.0}$.

Hence $s=3.47\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$, which rounds to $3.5\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: This separation subtends an angle far below the diffraction limit at the assumed wavelength.
perOption.B: This separation also subtends an angle too small for the aperture to resolve at the assumed wavelength.
perOption.C: Correct. It matches the diffraction limit using $550\ \mathrm{nm}$.
perOption.D: This is ten times the minimum separation from the diffraction calculation.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The question supplies no wavelength. C is the intended approximate answer for visible light, and the key assumes 550 nm without stating why.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q20.body:
The current is $I=nAve$, where $n$ is the electron number density. For $N$ electrons in the wire, $n=N/(AL)$, so the cross-sectional area cancels.

Thus $v=IL/(Ne)=\frac{5.0(2.0)}{(1.5\times10^{24})(1.6\times10^{-19})}=4.17\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The drift speed rounds to $4.2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.B: This speed would require a larger current for the given number of electrons per metre.
perOption.C: This speed is more than two orders of magnitude too large for the specified charge flow.
perOption.D: This speed is far too large because the given electron population needs only a small drift to carry $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The options give speed only. The electron drift direction is opposite to conventional current.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q21.body: In the school’s model, the diode’s resistance becomes negligible once the threshold voltage is reached. The fixed resistor has a constant voltage-to-current ratio, so its own $I$–$V$ graph is a straight line through the origin. The key selects D, showing a sharp turn-on followed by a straight line.

perOption.A: Starts the linear region at zero current at the threshold, which the key represents with a vertical turn-on.
perOption.B: Shows a nonzero current at zero applied voltage.
perOption.C: Shows a nonzero current at zero applied voltage.
perOption.D: Correct. It shows the sharp turn-on and linear region used by the key.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The key prints D and keyAnswer is D, but A is the physically consistent piecewise-linear model. Above threshold the diode retains an approximately constant voltage drop, so $I=(V-V_{\mathrm{th}})/R$ rises continuously from zero. D’s vertical segment at fixed total voltage is incompatible with the series resistor.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q22.body: The current travels a length $l=V^{1/3}$ through a cross-sectional area $A=V^{2/3}$. Substituting into $R=\rho l/A$ gives $R=\rho V^{1/3}/V^{2/3}=\rho/V^{1/3}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by the side length while omitting the face area.
perOption.B: Multiplies by the face area instead of using the length-to-area ratio.
perOption.C: Correct. The side length cancels one factor of the face area.
perOption.D: Divides by the face area while omitting the side length.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q23.body: The $10$ and $6.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors share the same potential difference, so they are in parallel. The $30$ and $18\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors also form a parallel pair. The two equivalents are in series, so $R_{\mathrm{eff}}=[(1/10+1/6.0)^{-1}+(1/30+1/18)^{-1}]\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=15\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The two parallel equivalents add to 15 kΩ.
perOption.B: Adds only the two resistances on the right-hand side.
perOption.C: Adds only the two resistances on the left-hand side.
perOption.D: Adds all four resistances as though they were in series.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q24.body: The two external branches have the same potential difference, so $0.48(15)=0.45R+0.45(2.0)$, giving $R=14\ \Omega$. The voltage across the $15\ \Omega$ resistor is also the e.m.f. minus the voltage lost across $r$. Thus $0.48(15)=10-(0.45+0.48)r$, giving $r=3.0\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both the branch voltage and internal voltage drop are accounted for.
perOption.B: Uses the full e.m.f. across the external branch, giving too large a value for R.
perOption.C: Uses only the 0.48 A branch current to calculate the drop across r.
perOption.D: Uses only the 0.48 A branch current for r and the full e.m.f. across the branch for R.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q25.body: Particle Y is undeflected, so its electric and magnetic forces must act in opposite directions. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a downward magnetic force for a positive particle moving right, with the direction reversed for a negative particle. In either case the electric field must point upwards, from plate M to the lower-potential plate L.

perOption.A: Force balance requires Y’s speed to equal $E/B$.
perOption.B: Correct. The upward electric field points toward the lower-potential plate L.
perOption.C: The deflections depend on the particles’ speeds as well as their charge signs.
perOption.D: The paths also depend on the speeds and charges, so they do not establish a mass ordering.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q26.body: Increasing $I_S$ increases the magnetic force on XY into the page, so its moment about KL increases. Moving the weighted slider toward WZ increases the perpendicular distance from its line of action to KL. The larger moment of the weight balances the increased magnetic moment.

perOption.A: Increasing $I_W$ further increases the magnetic moment.
perOption.B: Reversing the frame current reverses the magnetic moment so it acts in the same sense as the weight’s moment.
perOption.C: Correct. The slider has a larger moment arm about KL.
perOption.D: Increasing the number of solenoid turns strengthens the field and further increases the magnetic moment.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q27.body: By Faraday’s law, $|\mathcal{E}|=NA|\Delta B|/\Delta t=50(0.40)(0.08\times0.05)/0.20=0.40\ \mathrm V$. By Lenz’s law, the induced current produces flux into the page to oppose the decrease in flux into the page. The right-hand grip rule gives a clockwise current.

perOption.A: Correct. The induced e.m.f. is 0.40 V and the current is clockwise.
perOption.B: An anticlockwise current would produce flux out of the page.
perOption.C: Doubles the e.m.f. given by the stated change in flux linkage.
perOption.D: Doubles the e.m.f. and gives a current that would produce flux out of the page.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q28.body: For output 1, the sine wave has $V_{\mathrm{rms},1}=\sqrt{(V_o^2/2)T/T}=V_o/\sqrt{2}$. Output 2 is at $V_o$ for half the period and zero for the other half, so $V_{\mathrm{rms},2}=\sqrt{V_o^2(T/2)/T}=V_o/\sqrt{2}$. Their ratio is $1$.

perOption.A: Reports the mean-square fraction of the peak for a single waveform instead of the ratio of r.m.s. voltages.
perOption.B: Treats the pulsed output’s peak voltage as its r.m.s. voltage.
perOption.C: Correct. Both outputs have the same r.m.s. voltage.
perOption.D: Treats the half-period at zero as halving the pulse’s r.m.s. voltage relative to the sine wave.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q29.body: A hydrogen spectral line comes from a transition between electronic energy levels. The largest bound-level energy gap is limited by the ionisation energy, which is too small to produce an X-ray photon.

perOption.A: Attributes the spectral limit to neutrons instead of electronic energy-level spacings.
perOption.B: Heating changes which levels are populated without increasing the gaps between them.
perOption.C: Invokes a cut-off frequency without identifying the limit set by the atomic energy levels.
perOption.D: Correct. The ionisation energy bounds the photon energies of hydrogen’s spectral lines.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q30.body: Most alpha particles pass undeflected, indicating that the atom is largely empty space. The rare large deflections indicate a small, massive nucleus in which most of the atom’s mass is concentrated.

perOption.A: The scattering pattern does not measure the separate charges of protons and electrons.
perOption.B: The experiment does not compare the individual masses of protons and electrons.
perOption.C: Correct. The scattering is consistent with most of the mass being concentrated in a small nucleus.
perOption.D: The scattering establishes a nucleus without identifying protons and neutrons as its constituents.

ejc-2025-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The key mentions only undeflected particles, which establish that the atom is mostly empty. The explanation adds the rare large deflections needed to support the mass inference.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Rearrange to $R=vL\rho/\mu$. The units of $vL\rho$ are $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})(\mathrm m)(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$. The units of $\mu$, $\mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-2}}$, simplify to the same base units, so $R$ is dimensionless.

perOption.A: Leaves a spurious factor of time squared per length squared.
perOption.B: Leaves a spurious inverse fourth power of length after expanding the newton.
perOption.C: Leaves inverse powers of length and time even though both cancel.
perOption.D: Correct. The numerator and denominator have identical units.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Let $K=b-c=21\pm4$, adding the absolute uncertainties in $b$ and $c$. Since $a=K/d^2$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta a/a=\Delta K/K+2\Delta d/d=4/21+2(1/100)=0.210476$. This gives a percentage uncertainty of $21\%$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses only the percentage uncertainty in b.
perOption.B: Counts the fractional uncertainty in d once, giving about 20%.
perOption.C: Correct. The absolute uncertainties are added before propagating the fractional uncertainties.
perOption.D: Adds the percentage uncertainties of b and c directly before allowing for the squared denominator.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.issues: The key’s alternative max–min calculation on page 2 drops the factor of one-half in the displayed substitution, although its final number includes that factor. The explanation follows the error-propagation method on page 1.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The gradient of the displacement–time graph gives the vehicle’s velocity. In C the gradient changes rapidly, giving the greatest acceleration magnitude. In A, B and D the gradients are approximately constant.

perOption.A: The rising segment has an approximately constant positive gradient.
perOption.B: The plateau has an approximately constant zero gradient.
perOption.C: Correct. The gradient changes most rapidly in this interval.
perOption.D: The falling segment has an approximately constant negative gradient.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Energy stores include gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical potential, internal, kinetic, nuclear and electromagnetic stores. Energy can be transferred mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation. All four entries in D are energy stores.

perOption.A: Includes sound, which transfers energy through mechanical waves.
perOption.B: Includes light and electrical transfer.
perOption.C: Includes work done, which is energy transferred mechanically.
perOption.D: Correct. All four entries describe energy stores.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Electric field lines must meet each metal plate perpendicularly. The gap is narrowest at the bottom and widest at the top. By $E=-\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}r$, the field is strongest where the gap is narrowest, so D shows the closest spacing at the bottom.

perOption.A: The horizontal field lines meet the plates obliquely and are evenly spaced.
perOption.B: The horizontal lines meet the plates obliquely.
perOption.C: Even spacing depicts a uniform field despite the changing gap.
perOption.D: Correct. The curved lines meet the plates perpendicularly and crowd toward the narrow gap.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The batch marks this item as text, but all four answer choices are diagrams in the question PNG. The extracted text omits those diagrams.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The series connection gives both conductors the same current and hence the same number of charge carriers passing per unit time. In $I=nAvq$, $n$ and $q$ are the same for both, so $A_Xv_X=A_Yv_Y$. Since X has the larger cross-sectional area, $v_X<v_Y$.

perOption.A: Assigns Y a greater carrier flow rate even though the series currents are equal.
perOption.B: Assumes equal drift speeds despite the smaller cross-sectional area of Y.
perOption.C: Assigns Y a greater carrier flow rate and overlooks the increase in drift speed.
perOption.D: Correct. Y has the same carrier flow rate and a higher drift speed.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The peak-to-peak voltage is $18\ \mathrm{V}$, so the peak voltage is $V_0=9.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The voltage across the resistor is half-wave rectified, giving $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=V_0/2=4.5\ \mathrm{V}$. Hence $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=V_{\mathrm{rms}}/R=4.5/80=0.056\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the r.m.s. factor for a full sinusoid.
perOption.C: Uses the peak current or treats the peak-to-peak voltage as the peak when applying the half-wave factor.
perOption.D: Treats the peak-to-peak voltage as the peak and uses the full-sinusoid r.m.s. factor.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: Wire X has resistance $R_X=\rho L/A$. Since $R_Y=R_X$, $\rho_Y(2L)/A_Y=\rho L/A$. Thus $\rho_Y/A_Y=\rho/(2A)$, which is the ratio in B.

perOption.A: Gives $\rho_Y/A_Y=\rho/A$, twice the required ratio.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives $\rho_Y/A_Y=2\rho/A$, four times the required ratio.
perOption.D: Gives $\rho_Y/A_Y=2\rho/A$, four times the required ratio.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The series resistor and thermistor carry the same current. Their potential differences must add to $12\ \mathrm{V}$. At $0.36\ \mathrm{mA}$, the graph gives $5.4\ \mathrm{V}$ across the resistor and $6.6\ \mathrm{V}$ across the thermistor, so the total is $12\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Assigns $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ to the resistor, but the thermistor needs more than the remaining $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ at this current.
perOption.C: Uses the crossing of the curves, where the two potential differences add to more than the supply voltage.
perOption.D: Applies the full battery voltage to the fixed resistor alone.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The magnetic field circles clockwise around P. Only its vertical component contributes to the force on Q, and that component points up at Y and down at Z. With current in Q flowing to the right, Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a force out of the page at Y and into the page at Z.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses both force directions, as would reversing the field around P.
perOption.C: Treats the forces as attraction and repulsion in the plane of the page.
perOption.D: Treats the perpendicular wires as parallel currents attracting each other.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: By Faraday’s law, the induced e.m.f. has magnitude $N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$. With $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ and $\theta=55^\circ$ measured from the coil normal, this becomes $NA\cos\theta|\Delta B/\Delta t|$. Substitution gives $720(0.060)\cos55^\circ\left|\frac{(40-70)\times10^{-3}}{5.0}\right|=0.15\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses $\cos35^\circ$ by treating the angle to the plane as the angle to its normal.
perOption.C: Omits the angular projection of the magnetic field.
perOption.D: Calculates the magnitude of the change in flux linkage and omits division by the elapsed time.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.issues: The key’s first line omits the magnitude bars on the flux-linkage derivative. The subsequent steps use the magnitude correctly.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: A photon has energy $E=hf=hc/\lambda$ and momentum $p=h/\lambda$. Since X has the longer wavelength, it has both the smaller energy and the smaller momentum.

perOption.A: Treats both photon energy and momentum as increasing with wavelength.
perOption.B: Reverses the energy comparison even though energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
perOption.C: Reverses the momentum comparison even though momentum is inversely proportional to wavelength.
perOption.D: Correct.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The key uses the Heisenberg relation $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, giving $\Delta p\gtrsim h/\Delta x$. Taking $\Delta x$ to scale with the well width, reducing it by a factor of four raises the lower bound on $\Delta p$ by a factor of four. This is the lower-bound reasoning behind B.

perOption.A: Treats the uncertainty relation as an upper bound.
perOption.B: Correct. This is the intended lower-bound interpretation.
perOption.C: Predicts a decrease even though tighter confinement raises the lower bound on momentum uncertainty.
perOption.D: Predicts a decrease and interprets the factor of four as a minimum decrease.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: B is the intended answer, but the uncertainty relation only constrains the lower bound, not the ratio of actual uncertainties before and after. No option is uniquely justified without specifying how the electron state changes. At fixed quantum number, the actual uncertainty quadruples, satisfying both A and B.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Most $\alpha$-particles pass through the gold foil undeflected. The key uses this observation to infer that the nucleus is much smaller than the atom.

perOption.A: Confuses the identity of the incident particles with a finding from their scattering.
perOption.B: Treats the known positive charge of the incident particles as a result of the experiment.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Comparing the nuclear and electron charges requires additional information about the electrons.

ejc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Let $B$ be the background count rate, so the initial sample count rate is $200-B$. After four half-lives, the total is $0.25(200)=50$, giving a sample count rate of $50-B$. The sample count rate falls by a factor of $16$, so $\frac{50-B}{200-B}=(\frac12)^4=\frac1{16}$. Thus $800-16B=200-B$, giving $B=40\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Assumes there is no background, which would give a final total of only $12.5\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.
perOption.B: Divides the initial total by 16 and mistakes the result for the background.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the final total as pure background even though the sample is still contributing counts.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q1.body: A frequency of $550\ \mathrm{GHz}$ is $5.50\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Its wavelength is $\lambda=(3.0\times10^8)/(5.50\times10^{11})\approx10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$. Green light has a wavelength of order $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: A diameter of $80\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ is reasonable for human hair.
perOption.B: A volume of $200\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ is reasonable for an apple of typical size.
perOption.C: A sheet of A4 paper has a mass of roughly $5\ \mathrm{g}$, giving a weight near $50\ \mathrm{mN}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The wavelength implied by this estimate is far too long.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q2.body: For accurate measurements, the mean should lie close to the true value $x_0$. Poor precision means the measured values have a large spread, as shown by the broad curve in B.

perOption.B: Correct.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q3.body: The gradient of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration, so the initial gradient must be half the original. The area under the graph gives the distance between the stations and must be the same for both trains. B preserves that area with the same maximum speed and final deceleration.

perOption.C: The initial gradient is steeper than the original.
perOption.D: The initial gradient is steeper than the original.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The plotted endpoints in the original graph and B differ slightly from the intended grid positions. B matches the intended gradients and equal areas to the precision of the sketches.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q4.body: With equal masses, the system has zero acceleration. By Newton’s first law, the objects can continue moving at constant velocity, so B is the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: The taut string constrains the two speed magnitudes to be equal.
perOption.B: Correct. Equal masses can move at constant nonzero speeds.
perOption.C: A can be heavier and still be moving up while slowing down.
perOption.D: A can be lighter and moving up while speeding up.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q5.body: Let $u_b$ and $v_b$ be the ball’s initial and final speeds, and $v_p$ the pin’s final speed. Momentum conservation, using the mass ratio $5:1$, gives $5u_b=5v_b+v_p$. The equality of relative speeds for an elastic collision gives $u_b-0=v_p-v_b=3.33-v_b$. Solving gives $u_b=1.998\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, or $2.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Reports the ball’s final speed in place of its initial speed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the pin’s final speed as the ball’s initial speed.
perOption.D: Overstates the initial speed by a factor of two, as would omitting the factor of two from the relative-speed and momentum equations.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q6.body: Take moments about the pivot. Both forces turn the ruler in the same sense, so the torque is $2(5.0)(0.50\sin40^\circ)=3.2\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Counts only one moment.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the cosine of $40^\circ$ for the perpendicular lever arm.
perOption.D: Uses the full ruler length as the perpendicular separation.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q7.body: Let $\theta$ be the angle between the cord and the sheet. At the shortest length, $T=20\ \mathrm{N}$ and $2T\sin\theta=10\ \mathrm{N}$, giving $\sin\theta=0.25$ and $\theta=14.5^\circ$. The cord length is $2(10/\cos\theta)=20.7\ \mathrm{cm}$, which rounds to $21\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A 23 cm cord exceeds the minimum and carries less than the limiting tension.
perOption.C: A 40 cm cord exceeds the minimum set by the tension limit.
perOption.D: An 80 cm cord greatly exceeds the minimum set by the tension limit.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q8.body: $Fv$ and $Fst$ have the wrong units for energy. Since the object accelerates, $vt$ overestimates the distance travelled. The work $Fs$ equals the kinetic energy gained from rest.

perOption.A: $Fv$ has units of power.
perOption.B: Uses the final speed throughout the interval to calculate distance.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: $Fst$ has units of energy multiplied by time.

perOption.A: Calculates the tangential speed $\omega r$ instead.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Doubling the angular speed would quadruple the acceleration to about $3.1\times10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
perOption.D: Treats rpm as radians per second and leaves the radius in centimetres.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The key gives 7897 as an intermediate value, while its expression evaluates to about 7896. Both round to option B.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q10.body: For a uniform spherical Earth of mass $M$ and radius $R$, the gravitational potential at either surface site is $\phi=-GM/R$. The Earth–rocket system starts with the same gravitational potential energy at both sites, so the escape speed is the same.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Both sites are at the same radius and have equal potential.
perOption.C: Both sites are at the same radius and have equal potential.
perOption.D: The kinetic energy per unit mass needed to escape equals $-\phi$.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q11.body: Gravitational potential energy is negative, and the orbital radius is the planet’s radius plus the altitude, $R+H$. Adding the kinetic energy gives $E=\frac12mv^2-\frac{GMm}{R+H}$.

perOption.A: Uses the planet’s radius as the orbital radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a positive gravitational potential energy and the planet’s radius as the orbital radius.
perOption.D: Uses a positive gravitational potential energy.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q12.body: The same gas at the same temperature has equal mean microscopic kinetic energy and equal root-mean-square speed in the two containers. With equal amounts of gas, the larger volume of B gives it both lower pressure and lower density.

perOption.A: Equal temperatures give equal mean microscopic kinetic energies.
perOption.B: At fixed temperature and particle number, larger volume means lower pressure.
perOption.C: Equal temperatures and molecular masses give equal root-mean-square speeds.
perOption.D: Correct. The same mass occupies less volume in A.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q13.body: The clockwise loop gives net work done on the gas equal to minus the enclosed area, $W=-\pi(1)(1)\ \mathrm{J}=-3.14\ \mathrm{J}$. The gas returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$. By the first law, $\Delta U=Q+W$, so $3.14\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat enters the gas.

perOption.A: Confuses zero change in internal energy with zero heat transfer.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the sign of heat transfer for a clockwise cycle.
perOption.D: The enclosed area gives about 3 J and the clockwise direction requires heat input.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q14.body: The driving force sets the frequency of the forced oscillation. Figure (b) gives a period of $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$, so $f=1/2.0=0.50\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Uses the 3.0 s time marking as a full period.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reads the period of 2.0 s as the frequency.
perOption.D: Uses the resonance peak in Figure (a) as the driving frequency.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q15.body: After Q, the intensity is $I\cos^2 30^\circ$. The angle between Q and R is $60^\circ-30^\circ$, so after R the intensity is $I\cos^2 30^\circ\cos^2(60^\circ-30^\circ)=0.56I$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses $60^\circ$ between Q and R, measuring R’s angle from P.
perOption.B: Uses unsquared cosine factors with angles of $30^\circ$ at Q and $60^\circ$ at R.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Includes the intensity reduction at Q only.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q16.body: The source power spreads over a sphere, so $I=P_{\mathrm{source}}/(4\pi x^2)$ and $I\propto1/x^2$. At $0.5x$ the intensity is $4I$. Received power equals intensity times detector area, so the second detector receives $(4I)(2A)=8P$.

perOption.A: Ignores both the distance and area changes.
perOption.B: Accounts for only the doubling of detector area.
perOption.C: Accounts for only the quadrupling of intensity.
perOption.D: Correct.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q17.body: By Rayleigh’s criterion, the minimum resolvable angle is $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/a$. Reducing $\lambda$ or increasing $a$ lowers this limit, and reducing $D$ increases the actual angular separation of the sources at the slit. Increasing $L$ changes neither angle, so the resolution is unchanged.

perOption.A: A shorter wavelength reduces the minimum resolvable angle.
perOption.B: Moving the sources closer to the slit increases their angular separation there.
perOption.C: A wider slit reduces the minimum resolvable angle.
perOption.D: Correct.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The working spans pages 2–3. Page 3 calls reducing D option C, but it is option B on the question.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q18.body: Vertical threads produce the horizontal diffraction pattern, and horizontal threads produce the vertical pattern. For a fixed order and wavelength, $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives a smaller angle for a larger pitch $d$. The vertical spots are closer to the straight-through image, so the vertical pitch between horizontal threads is greater than the horizontal pitch between vertical threads.

perOption.A: Equal pitches would give equal spot separations in the two directions.
perOption.B: Reverses the pitches implied by the closer vertical spots.
perOption.C: Correct. The closer vertical spots indicate a greater vertical pitch.
perOption.D: The relative spot separations suffice to compare the pitches.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q18.issues: Option C treats vertical and horizontal as directions of measurement. The stem can also be read as naming the orientation of the threads being measured, in which case B describes the same geometry.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q19.body: The charge separation $r$ decreases when $+q$ moves from Y to X. The electric potential energy $U=-q^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$ becomes more negative, so it decreases.

perOption.A: The force magnitude $q^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2)$ increases as the charges get closer.
perOption.B: The two fields at O change from parallel to perpendicular, reducing the magnitude of their vector sum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The opposite scalar potentials at O still sum to zero.

hci-2022-prelim-p1-q20.body: Along PQ, $E=-\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}x$. Arrangement 1 has a uniform field, so its potential has a constant negative gradient. In arrangement 2 the field weakens toward Q, so the negative gradient becomes gentler, starting from the same gradient at P.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Curve 2 gets steeper, which would mean the field strengthens toward Q.
perOption.C: A straight line for arrangement 2 would give a constant field.
perOption.D: A straight, steeper line for arrangement 2 gives a stronger constant field and a different initial gradient.

hci-2024-other-p1-q2.body: The signed area under the acceleration–time graph gives the change in velocity. From rest to A, the negative area makes the object speed up in the negative direction. After A, positive acceleration slows it while it continues away from the start, until it momentarily stops at B. It then speeds up back toward the start until C, slows down after C, and reaches the start at D.

perOption.A: At A the acceleration is zero, but the object still has negative velocity.
perOption.B: Correct. B is the intended turning point.
perOption.C: At C the object is already moving back toward the start.
