hci-2024-other-p1-q2.issues: The unscaled sketch only suggests the area balance needed for zero velocity at B. The exact return to the start at D is also an assumption in the key.

hci-2024-other-p1-q3.body: The ball and floor have the same initial downward velocity, so the initial relative velocity is zero. Their relative acceleration is $9.81-5.8=4.01\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Thus $2.0=\tfrac12(4.01)t^2$, giving $t=1.00\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Adds the two downward accelerations instead of subtracting them.
perOption.B: Uses the ball’s free-fall acceleration alone, treating the floor as stationary.
perOption.C: Uses the elevator’s acceleration alone as the closing acceleration.
perOption.D: Correct.

hci-2024-other-p1-q4.body: The pool floor exerts a forward frictional force $f$ on the man’s feet, while the water exerts a backward drag force $f_D$. Newton’s second law along the horizontal gives $f-f_D=ma$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses weight and upthrust, which act vertically.
perOption.C: Reverses the horizontal force signs and includes vertical forces.
perOption.D: Includes vertical upthrust in the horizontal force balance.

hci-2024-other-p1-q5.body: The impulse is the triangular area under the graph, $\tfrac12(150)(40\times10^{-3})=3\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. It points opposite to the initial momentum, so the magnitudes satisfy $\Delta p=p_f+p_i$. Thus $(0.060)(30)+p_i=3$, giving $p_i=1.2\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This is the outgoing momentum.
perOption.C: Adds the outgoing momentum to the impulse when finding the incoming magnitude.
perOption.D: Reads the peak time in milliseconds as if it were a momentum.

hci-2024-other-p1-q6.body: At the launch threshold, upward thrust equals the rocket’s weight. Since thrust is $v\,\mathrm{d}m/\mathrm{d}t$, the required exhaust mass flow rate is $\mathrm{d}m/\mathrm{d}t=Mg/v=(500)(9.81)/1000=4.9\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides the rocket’s mass by the exhaust speed and omits the factor of gravitational acceleration.
perOption.B: Reverses the mass-to-speed ratio and omits the factor of gravitational acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a flow rate that produces much more thrust than is needed to balance the weight.

hci-2024-other-p1-q7.body: The weights of the wood and rubber act at their midpoints, $1.10l$ and $1.90l$ from the pivot, respectively. With common cross-sectional area $A$, balancing moments gives $A(5.00l)\rho_{\mathrm{wood}}g(1.10l)=A(l)\rho_{\mathrm{rubber}}g(1.90l)$. Cancelling common factors gives $\rho_{\mathrm{rubber}}/\rho_{\mathrm{wood}}=5.50/1.90=2.89$.

perOption.A: This ratio fails to balance the moments when the midpoint distances are used.
perOption.B: Uses the length ratio alone, effectively giving the two weights equal moment arms.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the density of wood divided by the density of rubber.

hci-2024-other-p1-q8.body: For rotational equilibrium, the hinge force’s line of action passes through the intersection of the cable tension and the shelf’s weight. This intersection lies below and to the right of the hinge. For translational equilibrium, the forces must sum to zero, so the hinge force points down and right to oppose the cable tension’s leftward component.

perOption.A: Its leftward component adds to the cable tension’s leftward component, so the forces cannot sum to zero.
perOption.B: A vertical force leaves the cable tension’s horizontal component unbalanced.
perOption.C: Its horizontal line of action misses the intersection of the tension and weight lines.
perOption.D: Correct.

hci-2024-other-p1-q9.body: The block has zero kinetic energy at release and at maximum compression. Equating the gain in elastic potential energy to the loss of gravitational potential energy gives $\tfrac12(85)x^2=(0.20)(9.81)(0.15+x)$. This becomes $42.5x^2-1.962x-0.2943=0$, with positive root $x=0.109\ \mathrm{m}$, or $11\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Equates spring force to weight, giving the static equilibrium compression.
perOption.B: Ignores the initial drop when equating gravitational energy lost to elastic energy gained.
perOption.C: Counts the initial 15 cm drop but omits the additional descent while the spring compresses.
perOption.D: Correct.

hci-2024-other-p1-q10.body: At maximum speed the engine force balances the drag $kv$. The power is therefore $P=(kv)v=kv^2$. With one engine, $32/64=(v_{\mathrm{one}}/14)^2$, giving $v_{\mathrm{one}}=9.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Applies the square of the power ratio to speed instead of taking its square root.
perOption.B: Halves the speed as if speed were directly proportional to power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes quadratic drag, which would make power proportional to the cube of speed.

hci-2024-other-p1-q11.body: The cage force $R$ and the person’s weight $W$ are the only forces acting. Their resultant points horizontally toward the centre of the circle, to the right. The upward component of $R$ balances the weight, and its rightward component provides the centripetal force.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A purely rightward cage force leaves the weight unbalanced.
perOption.C: Its downward component adds to the weight.
perOption.D: The horizontal component would point away from the centre.

hci-2024-other-p1-q12.body: The gravitational force is $F_g=-\mathrm{d}E_p/\mathrm{d}x$. The field strength is approximately constant over small heights above Earth’s surface, so the energy graph has a constant gradient. Its magnitude is $(E_3-E_1)/(x_3-x_1)$.

perOption.A: Uses the height above Earth’s surface in place of the distance from Earth’s centre.
perOption.B: Takes the ratio of energy to position instead of the gradient of the energy graph.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Multiplies energy by distance instead of taking the gradient.

hci-2024-other-p1-q13.body: Static friction from P is the restoring force on Q, with magnitude $m_Q\omega^2|x|$. Its largest required value occurs at displacement magnitude $A$, so at the threshold $5.0=0.20[(2\pi)(1.5)]^2 A$. This gives $A=0.28\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the combined mass of P and Q for the force exerted on Q alone.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of P in the force equation for Q.
perOption.C: Would require only about $1.0 mathrm{N}$ of friction at the extreme, so it is below the limiting amplitude.
perOption.D: Correct.

hci-2024-other-p1-q14.body: The $x$-component of uniform circular motion is simple harmonic motion, so $a_x\propto -x$. The graph is a straight line through the origin with a negative slope. The same relationship holds for the motion along the $y$-axis.

perOption.A: The ellipse assigns two possible accelerations to a single displacement.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows a sinusoidal dependence on position and gives acceleration the same sign as displacement.
perOption.D: Shows an inverse dependence and an unbounded acceleration near zero displacement.

hci-2024-other-p1-q15.body: Shift the wave profile slightly to the right to see that P moves upward. P is at its equilibrium position, so its speed is maximum and its acceleration is zero. The profile has a constant amplitude, so P and the other particles each oscillate with amplitude $A$.

perOption.A: The rightward shift of the profile shows that P is moving in the positive direction.
perOption.B: P’s speed is maximum as it passes through equilibrium.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: P’s acceleration is zero at equilibrium.

hci-2024-other-p1-q16.body: For small angles the Rayleigh limit is $\theta_{\min}=\lambda/b$. The two images are easier to resolve when the angle $\theta$ subtended by the sources at the slit is larger relative to $\theta_{\min}$. Reducing $D$ increases $\theta$ while leaving $\theta_{\min}$ unchanged.

perOption.A: Increasing the wavelength raises the minimum resolvable angle while the source angle stays fixed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Narrowing the slit raises the minimum resolvable angle while the source angle stays fixed.
perOption.D: Increasing the screen distance changes neither the source angle nor the minimum resolvable angle.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q2.body: Take upward displacement as negative, with zero at the ground. The sandbag initially continues upward, so the graph starts at $-10\ \mathrm{m}$ with a negative slope. Its downward acceleration brings the slope to zero at the highest point, after which the sandbag moves downward.

perOption.A: Shows the sandbag falling immediately as if released from rest.
perOption.B: Correct. The sandbag rises briefly before falling.
perOption.C: Starts with zero slope, implying zero release velocity.
perOption.D: The straight line implies constant velocity.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q3.body: The trolleys have equal mass and A is faster, so their total momentum is non-zero and directed to the right. Newton’s third law gives equal and opposite forces during contact. After separation, if B were stationary or moving left, A would have to be moving left to separate from B, contradicting conservation of rightward momentum. A collision is elastic if total kinetic energy is conserved, so the claim about contact time is false.

perOption.A: This statement is true because both trolleys at rest would have zero total momentum.
perOption.B: This statement follows from Newton’s third law.
perOption.C: This statement is true because the trolleys must separate while conserving rightward momentum.
perOption.D: Correct. Short contact time does not establish elasticity.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q4.body: With the rule horizontal, the two springs have the same extension $x$. Taking moments about the left end gives $k_2x(1.00)=(0.250)(0.200)g+(0.500)(0.0500)g=0.075g$. Taking moments about the right end gives $k_1x(1.00)=(0.750)(0.200)g+(0.500)(0.0500)g=0.175g$. Dividing the equations gives $k_2/k_1=0.075/0.175=3/7\approx0.43$.

perOption.A: Omits the weight of the metre rule.
perOption.B: Correct. The spring constant ratio is $3/7$.
perOption.C: Inverts the correct ratio.
perOption.D: Omits the weight of the metre rule and inverts the ratio.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q5.body: By the principle of flotation, the upthrust equals the weight of the floating cube. The cube has volume $L^3$, so its weight is $mg=\rho_0Vg=\rho_0L^3g$.

perOption.A: Uses the cube’s density in the pressure expression $\rho gh$, which gives units of pressure.
perOption.B: Gives the water’s gauge pressure at depth $h$ without multiplying by the face area.
perOption.C: Correct. The upthrust equals the cube’s weight.
perOption.D: Uses the entire cube volume as the displaced water volume.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q6.body: Neglect the shelf’s weight, so the system’s weight acts through the centre of the book. In equilibrium the three lines of action meet where the extended line of the rope intersects the vertical through the book. The wall force points down and to the right along the line from the wall attachment to that intersection, closing the force triangle.

perOption.A: Lies along the required line but points left, adding to the rope’s leftward pull.
perOption.B: Points above the shelf, missing the intersection of the tension and weight lines.
perOption.C: Assumes a purely horizontal reaction, whose line misses the intersection of the other two forces.
perOption.D: Correct. The wall force points down and to the right.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q6.issues: Worked solution starts on page 1 and continues on page 2.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q7.body: Taking $x$ positive from O towards P, $F=-\frac{dU}{dx}=-\frac{d(kx^2)}{dx}=-2kx$. For positive $k$, the negative sign gives a force from P towards O.

perOption.A: Omits the minus sign in the force–potential energy relation.
perOption.B: Omits both the minus sign and the factor of two from differentiating.
perOption.C: Gets the direction right but misses the factor of two from differentiating.
perOption.D: Correct. The force has magnitude $2kx$ towards O.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The stem does not explicitly state that $k>0$, which is required for the keyed direction and magnitude.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q8.body: The upward component of the normal force balances the weight, so $N\sin\theta=mg$. The inward component provides the centripetal force, so $N\cos\theta=m(0.8g)$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta=1.25$, so $\theta=51.3^\circ$.

perOption.A: Uses $\cos^{-1}(0.8)$, treating $0.8$ as a component-to-normal-force ratio.
perOption.B: Swaps the sine and cosine components and obtains the complementary angle.
perOption.C: Correct. The angle is approximately $51^\circ$.
perOption.D: Uses $\sin^{-1}(0.8)$, treating $0.8$ as a component-to-normal-force ratio.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q9.body: Earth’s rotation reduces the free-fall acceleration measured relative to its surface below the gravitational field strength away from the poles. At the poles the rotational correction vanishes, so the two are equal.

perOption.A: Assumes equality everywhere, ignoring the rotational correction.
perOption.B: Reverses the latitude trend, since free-fall acceleration is smaller at the Equator.
perOption.C: Assumes free-fall acceleration is independent of latitude.
perOption.D: Correct. The two quantities are equal at the poles.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The key uses free-fall acceleration relative to the rotating Earth and gravitational field strength due to gravitation alone.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q10.body: Orbit 2 has a larger radius $r$, so the gravitational potential energy $-GMm/r$ becomes less negative and therefore increases. The orbital speed drops as the gravitational pull weakens. Equivalently, the kinetic energy $GMm/(2r)$ decreases as $r$ increases.

perOption.A: Predicts a higher orbital speed at larger radius.
perOption.B: Predicts a higher orbital speed and treats a less negative potential energy as a decrease.
perOption.C: Treats a less negative potential energy as a decrease.
perOption.D: Correct. Kinetic energy decreases and gravitational potential energy increases.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q11.body: Kinetic theory gives $p=\frac13\rho\langle c^2\rangle$. The gases occupy equal volumes and contain equal numbers of moles, so oxygen is $32/2=16$ times as dense as hydrogen. At equal pressure, the hydrogen molecules’ root-mean-square speed is $\sqrt{16}=4$ times that of the oxygen molecules.

perOption.A: Squares the density ratio instead of taking its square root.
perOption.B: Uses the inverse linear density ratio for speed instead of for mean-square speed.
perOption.C: Correct. The rms speed ratio is 4.
perOption.D: Assumes equal pressures imply equal rms speeds even with different gas densities.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q12.body: By the first law of thermodynamics, internal energy can decrease through mechanical work. For example, an expanding gas can decrease its internal energy by doing work on its surroundings without transferring energy by cooling.

perOption.A: Correct. A gas can lose internal energy by doing work.
perOption.B: During a change of state, microscopic potential energy can change while temperature stays constant, as in melting or freezing.
perOption.C: Temperature depends on average microscopic kinetic energy, while internal energy includes microscopic potential energy and depends on the amount of substance.
perOption.D: This kinetic-only expression applies to an ideal gas, whose microscopic potential energy is taken as zero.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q13.body: Newton’s second law gives $F_\mathrm{gas}-mg=ma$ when the downward force is the piston’s weight alone. Hence $F_\mathrm{gas}=m(g+a)=0.75(9.81+3.5)=9.983\ \mathrm{N}$. The work done by the gas is $F_\mathrm{gas}s=9.983(0.12)=1.20\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Calculates the work of the net force $ma$, omitting the force needed to lift the piston’s weight.
perOption.B: Correct. The gas does $1.20\ \mathrm{J}$ of work in the key’s model.
perOption.C: Overestimates the work by using more than the required upward force of about $10$ N over the stated distance.
perOption.D: Overestimates the work by treating the gas force or piston travel as far larger than the stated data imply.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key neglects any external pressure and friction on the piston and treats the given average acceleration as representative over the displacement.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q14.body: The velocity graph gives a period of $12\ \mathrm{s}$ and a peak speed of $3.0\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$. Using $v_0=\omega x_0$, we have $3.0=(2\pi/12)x_0$ in centimetre units, giving $x_0=5.730\ \mathrm{cm}$. Then $a_0=\omega^2x_0=(2\pi/12)^2(5.730)=1.571\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-2}}$. The maximum restoring force is $3.0(1.571\times10^{-2})=4.7\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses the peak speed in place of the displacement amplitude in $\omega^2x_0$.
perOption.B: Correct. The maximum restoring force is $0.047\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: Uses a period of $10\ \mathrm{s}$ from $15/1.5$ instead of the $12\ \mathrm{s}$ between peaks.
perOption.D: Drops the angular-frequency dependence when finding acceleration and simply multiplies mass by the peak speed, $3.0(0.03)$.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The printed working gives $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$ for peak acceleration. The correct unit is $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-2}}$.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q15.body: For a right-moving pulse, the part that reaches P last is the leftmost part of the spatial profile, and the part that reaches P first is the rightmost. This reverses the order of all the points on the time graph, including the slopes of the two triangular sections.

perOption.A: Copies the time trace without reversing the order of the pulse features.
perOption.B: Swaps the two sections but keeps the slope direction within each section.
perOption.C: Correct. The spatial profile reverses the full time trace.
perOption.D: Reverses each section’s slope but keeps the positive section before the negative section.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q16.body: The first sheet halves the intensity of the unpolarised light, so the second must halve it again. Malus’ law gives $(I_0/2)\cos^2\theta=I_0/4$, so $\cos^2\theta=1/2$ and $\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt{2})=45^\circ$. Rotating either sheet by $45^\circ$ from the crossed arrangement leaves the axes $45^\circ$ apart.

perOption.A: Correct. Either rotation gives the required $45^\circ$ between the axes.
perOption.B: Leaves an angle of $30^\circ$ between the axes, giving an output of $3I_0/8$.
perOption.C: Leaves the last sheet crossed with the middle sheet, so the output is zero.
perOption.D: Leaves a single sheet that transmits half the incident intensity.

hci-2025-prelim-p1-q16.issues: Worked solution starts on page 3 and continues on page 4.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Using $V=P/I$, one volt is one watt per ampere. Since $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}$, the volt has base units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,A^{-1}\,s^{-3}}$.

perOption.A: Leaves the derived unit ohm unexpanded.
perOption.B: Uses the derived units coulomb and ohm.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Leaves the coulomb unexpanded as an ampere-second.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: The maximum speed occurs at a peak or trough of the velocity–time graph, where $a=dv/dt=0$. Direction changes when velocity changes sign, and displacement increases wherever velocity is positive.

perOption.A: At $t=T$ the velocity is zero and the displacement has returned to zero, although the interior zero crossing does coincide with maximum displacement.
perOption.B: Direction changes when $v$ changes sign, while $a=0$ at the velocity extrema.
perOption.C: Displacement increases whenever $v>0$, even if the acceleration is negative.
perOption.D: Correct. The greatest speed occurs at a horizontal tangent.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.issues: The key rejects A using the endpoint at t = T. The interior zero crossing does give the greatest displacement, so A is also defensible if read as identifying when the maximum occurs.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: Let $L$ be the lift. On descent, Newton’s second law gives $Mg-L=2M$, so $L=M(g-2)$. On ascent, for the remaining mass $M_1$, $L-M_1g=4M_1$, so $L=M_1(g+4)$. Equating the lifts gives $M_1=0.57M$, so the mass removed is $0.43M$.

perOption.A: Counts only the initial downward acceleration in the required change of acceleration.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the mass remaining after removal.
perOption.D: Overstates the mass reduction by doubling the required fraction.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Balancing moments about A gives $F_B(5.0)=200(2.5)+880(0.80)$, so $F_B=240.8\ \mathrm{N}$. Vertical force balance gives $F_A=880+200-240.8=839.2\ \mathrm{N}$. Hence $F_A/F_B=839.2/240.8\approx3.48\approx3.5$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio to $F_B/F_A$.
perOption.B: Divides $F_A$ by the total weight of $1080\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Divides the total weight by $F_B$ without first subtracting $F_B$ to find $F_A$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: By Hooke’s law, $15=k(0.090-0.060)$, so $k=500\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. The maximum extension is $0.100\ \mathrm{m}$, giving a maximum load $ke_{\max}=500(0.100)=50\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Treats the loaded length of 90 mm as the extension when finding the spring constant.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the 60 mm unstretched length to the 100 mm extension before applying Hooke’s law.
perOption.D: Adds the initial 15 N load to a force already calculated using the full 160 mm spring length.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Assuming Hooke’s law, the force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin, so its triangular area gives stored energy $\tfrac12 Fe$. At equilibrium $F=mg$ and $e=y-x$, so the stored energy is $\tfrac12 mg(y-x)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the rectangular area under the final force and omits the factor of one-half.
perOption.C: Squares the extension even though the expression already uses the final force.
perOption.D: Squares the extension and omits the triangular-area factor.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The work done against friction becomes heat, $30(3.0)=90\ \mathrm{J}$. The pulling force does work $80(3.0)=\Delta E_k+40(3.0\sin30^\circ)+90$. Solving gives $\Delta E_k=90\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Overstates the frictional work and assumes the object gains zero kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the full slope distance as the vertical rise, overstating the gravitational energy gain.
perOption.D: Treats all the pulling work as kinetic energy and overstates the heat from friction.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: All points on the rigid disc complete one revolution in the same time, so Y has period $3.2\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $v=r\omega$ and Y is half as far from the centre as X, $v_Y=0.5v_X=0.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Scales the speed with the square of the radius and halves the shared period.
perOption.B: Scales the speed with the square of the radius.
perOption.C: Halves the period along with the speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$ and $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$. The speed therefore increases as the orbital radius decreases. The period $T=2\pi r/v=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}$ decreases because the orbit is shorter and the satellite travels faster.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Both orbital speed and gravitational force increase at the smaller radius.
perOption.C: Kinetic energy increases and gravitational potential energy decreases.
perOption.D: Both total mechanical energy and orbital period decrease.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: At Earth’s surface, $W=GMm/R^2$ and $\phi=-GM/R$. At height $3R$, the distance from Earth’s centre is $4R$. Thus $W'=GMm/(4R)^2=W/16$ and $\phi'=-GM/(4R)=\phi/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the height above the surface as the distance for the potential.
perOption.C: Scales weight with inverse distance instead of inverse distance squared.
perOption.D: Uses inverse-distance scaling for weight and uses the height above the surface for the potential.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12 m c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32 kT$, so at the same temperature $m\propto1/c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$. For neon, $m/(5m)=c_{\mathrm{Ne}}^2/1800^2$, giving $c_{\mathrm{Ne}}=804.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx800\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides the speed by five instead of dividing by the square root of five.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes r.m.s. speed increase with the square root of mass.
perOption.D: Makes r.m.s. speed directly proportional to mass.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: The energy removed to cool and freeze the water is $mc\Delta T+mL_f=0.750(4200)(18)+0.750(330000)=304200\ \mathrm{J}$. Dividing by the cooling power gives $t=304200/135=2253.3\ \mathrm{s}$, or about $38\ \mathrm{min}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the energy removed while cooling the liquid to its freezing point.
perOption.B: Counts only the latent heat removed during freezing.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overcounts the energy to be removed, for example by including the latent heat of fusion twice.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: From $pV=nRT$, at fixed cylinder volume $p\propto nT$. Thus $9.5/10=n_1(273.15+7)/[n_2(273.15+27)]$, giving $n_2=0.98249n_1$. Mass is proportional to amount of gas, so $m_2=0.98249(19)=18.667\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $19-18.667\approx0.33\ \mathrm{kg}$ escapes.

perOption.A: Underestimates the loss by leaving too much gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the loss by leaving too little gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.D: Uses a temperature ratio based on Celsius readings instead of absolute temperatures.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key says V and n are constant. The cylinder volume is fixed, but n decreases as air escapes.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: In SHM the maximum acceleration has magnitude $\omega^2 A$. Thus $3=(\omega_Y/\omega_X)^2(0.5)$, so $(\omega_Y/\omega_X)^2=6$. Using $E=\tfrac12 m\omega^2 A^2$, the energy ratio is $2(6)(0.5)^2=3.0$.

perOption.A: Omits the doubling of the mass.
perOption.B: Uses only the mass ratio and ignores the changes in angular frequency and amplitude.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the amplitude ratio to the first power in the energy expression.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Starting at the extreme position gives $x=A\cos(2\pi t/T)$. At the halfway point, $0.5A=A\cos[(2\pi/2.0)t]$. The first solution is $t=0.33\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Uses a sine equation with zero initial displacement, as if the pendulum started at equilibrium.
perOption.B: Assumes the pendulum covers half the distance to equilibrium in half the time.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses half a period, when the pendulum reaches the opposite extreme.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The first polariser reduces the incident intensity $I$ to $I/2$. The final intensity is $0.125I$, so Malus’s law gives $(I/2)\cos^2\theta=0.125I$. Hence $\theta=60^\circ$.

perOption.A: Using $30^\circ$ as the angle between the axes gives a transmitted fraction of $0.375$.
perOption.B: Using $40^\circ$ gives a transmitted fraction of about $0.293$, which is too high.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Using $75^\circ$ gives a transmitted fraction of about $0.033$, which is too low.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: For the open tube’s fundamental, $\lambda/2=L$, so $f=v/(2L)$. With one end closed, the fundamental satisfies $\lambda_1/4=L$, so $f_1=v/(4L)=0.5f$.

perOption.A: Treats the quarter-wave condition as a fourfold frequency increase relative to the open tube.
perOption.B: Treats frequency as increasing when the fundamental wavelength doubles.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a quarter of the original frequency, overlooking that the open tube already contains only half a wavelength.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Using the key’s Rayleigh estimate with visible light at about $500\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\sin\theta=\lambda/b=(500\times10^{-9})/(5\times10^{-3})$, so $\theta\approx0.0001\ \mathrm{rad}$. The minimum separation is approximately $3.0(0.0001)=0.0003\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of one hundred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of one thousand.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The question omits wavelength. The key assumes 500 nm and omits the 1.22 factor for a circular aperture. Including the factor still leaves A as the closest choice.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The fixed charge’s potential doubles in magnitude at half the distance, giving $-2.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ at the midpoint. The given potential and distance imply a fixed charge of about $-e$, so the alpha particle’s charge of $+2e$ contributes $+4.8\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ there. Adding the signed potentials gives $+2.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the magnitude of the fixed charge’s potential at X without calculating the net midpoint potential.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes only the alpha particle’s contribution.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of the two contributions despite their opposite signs.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key calls the fixed charge an electron. The printed question leaves its identity unspecified, but its magnitude and sign follow from the given potential and distance.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: When the variable resistance is $r$, the voltage divider gives $V=Er/(r+r)=0.5E$ and $v=0.5E$. At $3r$, it gives $V=E(3r)/(3r+r)=0.75E$ and $v=0.25E$. Since $v+V=E$, the graph is the descending line segment joining these points.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows both voltages falling together, although their sum must stay at $E$.
perOption.C: Reverses the coordinates of the endpoint at $3r$, making $V$ decrease as the load resistance rises.
perOption.D: Shows both voltages increasing together, although their sum must stay at $E$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: Closing switches can add parallel current paths and reduce the effective resistance. With all three switches open, the left section is a single resistor $R$ in series with the right section, where three resistors remain in parallel. The total resistance is $R+R/3\approx 1.33R$, the largest of the listed combinations.

perOption.A: Closing all three switches gives $R_{XY}=0.85R$.
perOption.B: Closing $S_1$ and $S_3$ gives $R_{XY}=0.92R$.
perOption.C: Closing $S_3$ adds a right-hand parallel path, giving $R_{XY}=1.25R$.
perOption.D: Correct. All three open give the largest resistance.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The key says the all-open circuit contains only series resistors, but three right-hand resistors remain in parallel. Its resistance values and answer letter are correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The capacitor stores $\tfrac12 CV^2$. If a constant fraction $k$ becomes gravitational potential energy, then $mgh=k(\tfrac12 CV^2)$ and $h=\frac{kC}{2mg}V^2$. Thus a graph of $h$ against $V^2$ is a straight line.

perOption.A: Correct. The height is proportional to the squared voltage.
perOption.B: This treats $h$ as linear in $V$, though it is quadratic.
perOption.C: If the horizontal variable is $\sqrt V$, the height varies as its fourth power.
perOption.D: If the horizontal variable is $1/\sqrt V$, the height varies as its inverse fourth power.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The key drops the factor of one-half when rearranging for h. Its proportionality and answer letter are correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The normal reaction falls to half the weight, so the upward magnetic force must supply the other half for equilibrium. Thus $0.5mg=BIL\sin60^\circ$, giving $B=\frac{0.5(50\times10^{-3})(9.81)}{10(0.20)(0.866)}=0.142\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The upward magnetic force balances half the weight.
perOption.B: Using $\cos60^\circ$ in the force expression gives about $0.25\ \mathrm{T}$.
perOption.C: Using the full weight as the magnetic force gives about $0.28\ \mathrm{T}$.
perOption.D: Using the full weight together with $\cos60^\circ$ gives about $0.49\ \mathrm{T}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Acceleration from rest gives $\tfrac12 mv^2=eV$, so $e/m=v^2/(2V)$. In the velocity selector, the electric and magnetic forces balance, giving $Bev=eE$ and $v=E/B$. Substituting this speed gives $\frac{e}{m}=\frac{E^2}{2VB^2}$.

perOption.A: This substitutes $v$ where the energy equation requires $v^2$.
perOption.B: This inverts the speed ratio $E/B$ before squaring it.
perOption.C: This multiplies by $2V$ when isolating $e/m$, which requires division by $2V$.
perOption.D: Correct. It combines the energy equation with the force balance.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The left vertical arm moves across the field, making P positive relative to the bottom of that arm. The horizontal arm moves along its length, so it develops no e.m.f. along the wire. The right arm develops the same e.m.f. as the left arm, making Q positive by the same amount. P and Q therefore stay at the same potential throughout the motion in the uniform field.

perOption.A: This assigns a nonzero terminal e.m.f. at the ends of the motion even though the arm e.m.f.s cancel.
perOption.B: Changing speed changes both arm e.m.f.s equally, so there are no terminal pulses.
perOption.C: Correct. The terminal e.m.f. stays zero.
perOption.D: This follows the speed as if only one vertical arm contributed to the terminal e.m.f.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: A transformer couples the primary and secondary coils through a shared magnetic field, usually guided by a soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux linkage in the secondary, inducing an e.m.f. by Faraday’s law.

perOption.A: The coils couple magnetically, and steady direct current produces a constant flux after switch-on.
perOption.B: Magnetic coupling is required, but steady direct current cannot sustain a changing flux.
perOption.C: Alternating current supplies the changing flux, but the coupling between the coils is magnetic.
perOption.D: Correct. Alternating current produces the changing flux needed for mutual induction.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The slit confines each electron’s vertical position to approximately the slit width $\Delta y$. Narrowing the slit raises the lower bound on the vertical momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$ under Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. The larger spread of vertical momenta makes the beam fan out more in the vertical direction after the slit.

perOption.A: Narrowing the slit increases the spread in $p_y$, causing more vertical spreading.
perOption.B: The slit confines the $y$ coordinate, so the relevant uncertainty is in $p_y$.
perOption.C: Correct. The beam spreads out more vertically.
perOption.D: The uncertainty principle applies to electrons as well as photons.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key prints $\Delta y\Delta p_y\ge h$. For standard deviations, the bound is $\Delta y\Delta p_y\ge\hbar/2$, and slit width is an estimate of position spread. The qualitative conclusion is correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The concentric rings arise from electron diffraction by the carbon film. Decreasing the electron speed reduces its momentum and increases its de Broglie wavelength, $\lambda=h/p$. The longer wavelength gives greater diffraction angles, so the rings grow in diameter.

perOption.A: This attributes the rings to electrostatic repulsion and predicts smaller rings for a longer wavelength.
perOption.B: The predicted increase in diameter is right, but electron diffraction produces the rings.
perOption.C: The longer wavelength at lower speed gives larger diffraction angles and larger rings.
perOption.D: Correct. Diffraction produces larger rings at lower speed.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Subtracting the background of 300 counts per minute gives net counts of 744, 738, 196 and 1 per minute for no absorber, paper, aluminium and lead respectively. Paper makes little difference, so the readings give no evidence of alpha radiation. The aluminium reduces the count by 542 per minute, consistent with beta absorption. With 1 mm of lead the count returns to approximately background, so the residual count through aluminium is consistent with more penetrating beta particles.

perOption.A: Correct. The absorption pattern suggests beta only.
perOption.B: The negligible change with paper gives no evidence of alpha radiation.
perOption.C: The count with lead is approximately background, so the measurements give no evidence of a detectable gamma component.
perOption.D: Paper and lead give no evidence of detectable alpha or gamma components.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.issues: The solution continues on page 9. Page 8 says 0.1 mm of lead in its prose, while the table and question specify 1 mm. The readings suggest beta only, but the near-background count cannot prove that other emissions are absent.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The present ratio is $N_{\mathrm{Sr}}/N_{\mathrm{Rb}}=0.062$. Since $N_{\mathrm{Sr}}=N_0-N_{\mathrm{Rb}}$, the surviving rubidium fraction is $N_{\mathrm{Rb}}/N_0=1/1.062\approx0.9416$. Using $N_{\mathrm{Rb}}/N_0=e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln2/t_{1/2}$ gives $t=-\frac{\ln(0.9416)}{\ln2}(4.88\times10^{10})\approx4.24\times10^9$ years.

perOption.A: This age is too short to produce the observed strontium-to-rubidium ratio.
perOption.B: Correct. The surviving fraction gives an age of about 4.24 billion years.
perOption.C: Treating 0.062 as the fraction of the initial rubidium that decayed gives an age close to this value.
perOption.D: This age is almost one half-life, which would give a daughter-to-parent ratio near one.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: The quantity $\tan\alpha$ is unitless, so both $Q$ and $P/\sqrt M$ are unitless. Therefore $P$ has the same units as $\sqrt M$, namely $\mathrm{kg}^{1/2}$.

perOption.A: The inverse square-root unit fails to cancel $\sqrt M$, and $Q$ must be unitless.
perOption.B: The units of $P$ must match the denominator $\sqrt M$.
perOption.C: This gives the units of the angle to $Q$, which is added to a unitless quantity.
perOption.D: Correct. The units of $P$ cancel those of the denominator.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Taking downward as positive, Newton’s second law gives $ma=W-R$, where $R$ is air resistance. At release the speed and air resistance are zero, so $a=g$. As the speed rises, air resistance increases and acceleration falls. When air resistance balances the weight, the acceleration is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity.

perOption.A: A positive final acceleration would mean the object was still speeding up at terminal velocity.
perOption.B: At release, the absence of drag gives an initial acceleration of $g$.
perOption.C: The graph starts at zero, though gravity gives an acceleration of $g$ immediately on release.
perOption.D: Correct. Acceleration falls from $g$ towards zero.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: An elastic collision has the same total kinetic energy before and after impact. During contact, some kinetic energy can temporarily become elastic potential energy as the spheres deform. The claim that kinetic energy is conserved throughout the collision is therefore the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: This statement is true because the conserved total momentum is $2Mv-Mv=Mv$, so the spheres cannot both be at rest.
perOption.B: Correct. Kinetic energy can temporarily become elastic potential energy.
perOption.C: This statement is true because conservation of momentum requires equal and opposite momentum changes.
perOption.D: This statement is true by Newton’s third law.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Along the runway at $15^\circ$, Newton’s second law gives $mg\sin15^\circ-f=ma$. At $20^\circ$, it gives $mg\sin20^\circ-f=2ma$. Doubling the first equation and subtracting the second eliminates $a$, giving $f=mg(2\sin15^\circ-\sin20^\circ)=0.86\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: This friction is too small to make the second net force twice the first.
perOption.B: This is the increase in the downhill component of weight, which equals $ma$ for the first incline.
perOption.C: Correct. This friction satisfies both force equations.
perOption.D: This is the trolley’s full weight and would exceed the downhill component on both inclines.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Removing the quarter reduces the weight and shifts the centre of gravity to the right. The submerged volume is initially unchanged, so the upthrust stays the same and exceeds the new weight. The upthrust acts to the left of the new centre of gravity, producing a clockwise moment about it.

perOption.A: The unchanged upthrust exceeds the new weight and produces a clockwise moment about the new centre of gravity.
perOption.B: Correct. The resultant force is upward and the moment is clockwise.
perOption.C: The clockwise moment is right, but the reduced weight leaves a net upward force.
perOption.D: The upthrust acts to the left of the new centre of gravity, making the moment clockwise.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Constant velocity means the net force along the slope is zero. The engine force and the downhill component of weight together balance the resistive force, so $F=2000-1500(9.81)\sin6.0^\circ=462\ \mathrm N$. The engine power is $P=Fv=462(30)\approx14\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Gravity supplies part of the downhill force.
perOption.B: This assigns the full resistive force to the engine and omits gravity’s downhill contribution.
perOption.C: This adds the downhill component of weight to the resistance when solving for the engine force.
perOption.D: This power implies a driving force far above the resistance, even before gravity’s downhill contribution is included.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The useful output power is $P_o=0.25P_i=0.25(10)=2.5\ \mathrm W$. The useful energy required is $E=mgh=20(0.50)=10\ \mathrm J$. Using $P_o=E/t$ gives $t=10/2.5=4.0\ \mathrm s$.

perOption.A: This time would require 250 W of useful power, far above the 2.5 W available.
perOption.B: This is the result of multiplying the ideal lifting time by the efficiency, which understates the time.
perOption.C: Correct. The motor delivers 10 J of useful work in 4.0 s.
perOption.D: This treats the load’s 20 N weight as a 20 kg mass and multiplies by gravitational acceleration again.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: At the top of the circle, both tension and weight point down towards the centre. Their sum is the required centripetal force, so $T+mg=mv^2/r$. Hence $T=mv^2/r-mg$.

perOption.A: This reverses the subtraction needed to isolate the tension.
perOption.B: This attributes the entire centripetal force to tension and omits weight.
perOption.C: Correct. Weight supplies part of the required inward force.
perOption.D: This uses the sign appropriate to the bottom of the circle, where weight points away from the centre.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: At Earth’s surface the satellite’s weight is $W=GMm/R^2$. Its orbit is at a distance $R+5R=6R$ from Earth’s centre. There its weight is $GMm/(6R)^2=W/36$.

perOption.A: Correct. The centre-to-satellite distance is six Earth radii.
perOption.B: This uses the altitude as the distance from Earth’s centre.
perOption.C: This uses the altitude as the orbital radius and assumes an inverse-linear dependence.
perOption.D: Orbital free fall gives zero apparent weight, while gravity still supplies the centripetal force.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: In a uniform gravitational field, the potential energy lost over displacement $x$ along the field is $E=mgx$, giving $g=E/(mx)$. The field points towards lower gravitational potential, so the acceleration is from P to Q, to the right.

perOption.A: The quantity $E/x$ gives the gravitational force and must be divided by the mass.
perOption.B: The expression $E/x$ gives a force, and the leftward arrow points towards higher potential.
perOption.C: Correct. The acceleration points from P to Q.
perOption.D: The magnitude is right, but gravity points towards lower potential at Q.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The average translational kinetic energy of one helium atom is $\frac32 kT$, with $T$ in kelvin. Substituting gives $\frac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(27+273.15)=6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Substitutes $27$ directly instead of converting the temperature to kelvin.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The calculation must use the Boltzmann constant to obtain the energy per atom.
perOption.D: Uses the energy of the full $2.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ of helium.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: At steady state the pressures in the two flasks are equal. The ideal gas law gives $\frac{n_PRT_P}{V_P}=\frac{n_QRT_Q}{V_Q}$. Since both flasks contain the same gas, $\frac{M_P}{M_Q}=\frac{n_P}{n_Q}=\frac{T_Q}{T_P}\frac{V_P}{V_Q}=3\times3=9$.

perOption.A: Reverses the requested mass ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the inverse volume ratio and misses the temperature difference.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two factors of three.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Internal energy is the sum of the microscopic kinetic and potential energies of the molecules in a system. Work done on the system can increase that sum even when no energy is transferred by heating.

perOption.A: During a change of state, internal energy can rise while the temperature stays constant.
perOption.B: Correct. Work can increase internal energy by itself.
perOption.C: Samples with different amounts of gas can have the same total internal energy at different temperatures.
perOption.D: Heat transferred into the system plus work done on it gives the change in internal energy.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: For resonance, the frequency of hitting the bumps equals the suspension’s natural frequency. The time between bumps is $T=1/2.0=0.50\ \mathrm{s}$. Using $d=vT$ gives $5.0=v(0.50)$, so $v=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This speed gives one bump every $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$, so the driving frequency is too low.
perOption.B: Multiplies by the period instead of dividing the spacing by it.
perOption.C: This speed gives one bump per second, only half the natural frequency.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Increasing the damping decreases the oscillation frequency and therefore increases the period. With the damping held fixed, the amplitude decreases over time while the period stays constant.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Increasing the damping increases the period because the frequency falls.
perOption.C: Damping dissipates energy, so the amplitude decreases over time.
perOption.D: At fixed damping the period stays constant as the amplitude decays.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The key says damping does not change the period or frequency when discussing C and D. This applies to the passage of time at fixed damping. Changing the damping changes the period and frequency.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: By Malus’ law, the intensity after rotating Q through $\theta$ is $I\cos^2\theta$. A 30% reduction gives $0.70I=I\cos^2\theta$, with an acute solution of $33^\circ$. Since $\cos^2\theta$ repeats every $180^\circ$, $180^\circ+33^\circ=213^\circ$ is a possible rotation.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Its equivalent angle of $46^\circ$ transmits about 48% of $I$.
perOption.C: Its equivalent angle of $57^\circ$ transmits about 30% of $I$, a reduction of about 70%.
perOption.D: Its equivalent angle of $73^\circ$ transmits only about 9% of $I$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Sound intensity $I$ is proportional to the square of the amplitude $A$. With $y$ as one vertical grid unit, the original amplitude is $4y$, so $\frac{I_{\mathrm{new}}}{I_{\mathrm{old}}}=0.50=\left(\frac{A_{\mathrm{new}}}{4y}\right)^2$. This gives $A_{\mathrm{new}}=2.8y$, with the original period unchanged.

perOption.A: Keeps the original amplitude and halves the period.
perOption.B: Keeps the original amplitude and shortens the period.
perOption.C: Halves the amplitude, which would reduce the intensity to one-quarter.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Using the limiting angle $\theta \approx \lambda/b$, the minimum angular separation is $\frac{500\times10^{-9}}{25\times10^{-3}}=2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$. At $9.0\ \mathrm{m}$, the small-angle relation gives a minimum separation of $(9.0)(2.0\times10^{-5})=0.18\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Halves the calculated separation, which already represents the full gap between the points.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a separation much larger than the diffraction limit at the given distance.
perOption.D: Overestimates the limiting angle for a $25\ \mathrm{mm}$ aperture.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The key uses the syllabus approximation θ ≈ λ/b. The circular-aperture Rayleigh factor 1.22 would give about 0.22 mm, which is absent from the options.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Each corner contributes the same field magnitude at the centre. The vectors cancel completely in A and B, while D leaves two aligned contributions. In C the vertical components cancel and all four horizontal components add, giving $4\cos45^\circ=2\sqrt2$ times the field from one corner, the largest resultant.

perOption.A: The fields from diagonally opposite charges cancel in pairs.
perOption.B: The equal-sign charges on each diagonal produce opposing fields that cancel.
perOption.C: Correct. All four horizontal components reinforce each other.
perOption.D: One diagonal pair cancels, leaving only two aligned fields.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: For proton number density $n$ and beam cross-sectional area $A$, the current is $I=evAn$. A beam segment of length $\ell$ containing $N$ protons has $An=A\frac{N}{A\ell}=\frac{N}{\ell}$. Thus the number per unit length is $An=\frac{I}{ev}$.

perOption.A: Gives the number of protons passing per unit time.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Multiplies the proton rate by $v$ instead of dividing by it.
perOption.D: Gives charge per unit length and omits division by the charge $e$ per proton.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The diodes in A and B are reverse-biased. When the thermistor is cold, its resistance is high and the potential difference across it is high. The heater branch should therefore be connected across the thermistor with the diode forward-biased.

perOption.A: Its reverse-biased diode blocks current through the heater.
perOption.B: Its reverse-biased diode blocks current through the heater.
perOption.C: The heater branch is across the fixed resistor, whose potential difference falls as the thermistor cools.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The current is $I=Q/t=6.0/(2.0\times60)=0.050\ \mathrm A$. The power dissipated in $R$ satisfies $P=VI$, so $48/(2.0\times60)=V(0.050)$ and $V=8.0\ \mathrm V$. Using $\mathcal E=IR+Ir$ gives $9.0=8.0+0.050r$, so $r=20\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Divides the $1.0\ \mathrm V$ lost voltage by the charge $6.0\ \mathrm C$ instead of by the current.
perOption.B: Treats the current in coulombs per minute as amperes when dividing the lost voltage by current.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the voltage across the external resistor and finds its resistance.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The question expands e.m.f. as electromagnetic force. The term is electromotive force.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so $B|q|v=mv^2/r$. Cancelling $v$ and using $v=2\pi r/T$ gives $B|q|=2\pi m/T$. Therefore $T=2\pi m/(B|q|)$, independent of the particle’s velocity.

perOption.A: The period is directly proportional to the mass.
perOption.B: The period is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the charge.
perOption.C: The period is inversely proportional to the magnetic flux density.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The electric force gives a vertical acceleration of $a=F_E/m=|q|E/m=(1.6\times10^{-19})(20000)/(9.11\times10^{-31})=3.51\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The initial vertical velocity is zero, so $s=ut+\frac12 at^2=\frac12(3.51\times10^{15})(4.0\times10^{-9})^2=0.0281\ \mathrm m$.

perOption.A: The vertical displacement must be calculated using the electron’s acceleration $|q|E/m$ and the squared transit time.
perOption.B: The field acting for $4.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm s$ produces a much larger displacement when the electron’s mass is included in the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds the horizontal travel $vt$ to the vertical displacement.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Over one period $T$, the current spends half the time at $I_0$ and half at $-I_0$, so $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{[I_0^2(T/2)+I_0^2(T/2)]/T}=I_0$. The original average power is $P=I_0^2R$. Doubling the peak doubles the rms current, giving a new average power of $(2I_0)^2R=4P$.

perOption.A: Assumes the rms current is unchanged when the peak doubles.
perOption.B: Uses a square-root factor instead of squaring the doubled current.
perOption.C: Treats average power as proportional to current instead of current squared.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The de Broglie relation $\lambda=h/(mv)$ gives $v=h/(m\lambda)$. At a fixed wavelength, speed is inversely proportional to mass. The helium-4 nucleus has the largest mass, so it has the smallest speed.

perOption.A: A proton is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The electron has the smallest mass and requires the greatest speed.
perOption.D: A neutron is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: Each photon has momentum of magnitude $p=h/\lambda$. Total reflection reverses that momentum, so the change in momentum has magnitude $p-(-p)=2h/\lambda$. At $n$ photons per second, the force on the mirror is the rate of momentum transfer, $2nh/\lambda$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by $\lambda$ instead of dividing and omits the factor of two from reflection.
perOption.B: Counts only the incident momentum, as for absorption.
perOption.C: Accounts for the reversal but multiplies by wavelength instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: The total linear momentum is zero before the stationary nucleus emits the $\gamma$ photon. By conservation of linear momentum, the recoiling nucleus must have momentum equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the photon’s momentum.

perOption.A: Nuclear stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon rather than total binding energy.
perOption.B: A reaction with greater product rest mass can occur if enough energy is supplied to the reactants.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: In the usual nuclear-decay model, chemical reactions leave the half-life of the radionuclide unchanged.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactant. Multiplying each binding energy per nucleon by its nucleon number gives $(8.2\times146)+(8.6\times87)-(7.6\times235)=159.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Combines the tabulated per-nucleon values without weighting by nucleon number.
perOption.B: Undercounts the net binding-energy gain of the two fragments combined.
perOption.C: Undercounts the net binding-energy gain of the two fragments combined.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The two named fragments account for 233 of the 235 nucleons. Two free neutrons are implicit and contribute zero binding energy.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Rearranging gives $g=2h/t^2$. The maximum fractional uncertainties add as $\frac{\Delta g}{g}=\frac{\Delta h}{h}+2\frac{\Delta t}{t}$. The maximum percentage uncertainty in $h$ is therefore $2.0\%-2(0.0008/0.4000)\times100\%=1.6\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Subtracts the time uncertainty only once, forgetting the squared time in the denominator.
perOption.C: Adds the time uncertainty once instead of subtracting it twice.
perOption.D: Adds the doubled percentage uncertainty in time to the 2% budget.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Estimate the football’s diameter as $20\ \mathrm{cm}=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$, giving a radius of $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. The volume scales as $r^3$, and $\frac{4}{3}\pi(0.10)^3\approx 4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, closest to $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.

perOption.A: Implies a sphere only about a centimetre across.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the surface area $4\pi r^2$, which is measured in $\mathrm{m^2}$.
perOption.D: Implies a sphere over ten metres across.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: At the threshold of slipping, the maximum friction $0.25mg$ balances the downslope component $mg\sin\theta$. Thus $\sin\theta=0.25$ and $\theta\approx14^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses an angle at which the downslope component is already half the weight.
perOption.C: Uses the $60^\circ$ angle at which the downslope component is about $0.87mg$.
perOption.D: Uses the perpendicular component $mg\cos\theta$ in the friction balance.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The key and option A give 14°, while arcsin(0.25) is about 14.48°.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: In the regular hexagon, $\angle OBA=60^\circ$. Balancing moments about $O$ gives $P(OD)=200(OB)\sin60^\circ$, so with $OD=OB$, $P\approx170\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ for the moment factor.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the $200\ \mathrm{N}$ force as perpendicular to $OB$.
perOption.D: Divides by $\sin60^\circ$, applying the moment factor to the wrong force.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Let $a=g\sin30^\circ$ be the common downslope acceleration. At collision, A is $4t-\frac12at^2$ up from the bottom and B is $\frac12at^2$ down from the top. These displacements sum to $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$, so the acceleration terms cancel and $t=5.00/4.00=1.25\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Double-counts the effect of gravity on the closing motion by treating A as speeding up the slope.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a time at which $4.00t=6.00\ \mathrm{m}$, greater than the initial separation.
perOption.D: Uses a time long enough for B to have already reached the bottom.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The opening sentence reverses the positions of A and B relative to the diagram and launch description. The question’s speed unit is malformed. The key’s first method calls A’s net displacement a distance even though A turns before collision, and one line of its second method prints 1.25 m instead of 1.25 s.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: For a constant interval $T$, bead $n$ must fall for $nT$, so its starting height is $s=\frac12g(nT)^2$. The heights above the floor are therefore proportional to $0,1,4,9,16,\ldots$, as in D.

perOption.A: Spaces the beads more closely toward the ceiling, where the gaps need to be larger.
perOption.B: Uses equal height gaps, which give shorter time gaps at greater heights.
perOption.C: Increases the gaps but misses the square-number heights, starting with heights in the ratio $1:3$ instead of $1:4$.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The worked solution begins on page 1 and continues on page 2.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: Using $P=Fv$ for the useful output power gives $0.40(800)=13F$, so the driving force is $24.6\ \mathrm{N}$. At constant velocity the driving and resistive forces balance, giving a resistive force of about $25\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the $60\%$ of power lost by the engine.
perOption.C: Uses all $800\ \mathrm{W}$ as useful output power.
perOption.D: Divides the input power by the efficiency before using $P=Fv$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: Friction supplies the centripetal force $mr\omega^2$. Before slipping, Q needs more friction because both objects share the same angular velocity and Q is farther from the axis. Q reaches the maximum available static friction first.

perOption.A: Q needs more friction than P before slipping.
perOption.B: P needs less friction because it is closer to the axis.
perOption.C: Q and P have the same angular velocity while they rotate with the turntable.
perOption.D: Correct. Q reaches the friction limit first.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The stem describes increasing angular velocity and also calls the initial motion uniform. During spin-up friction has a tangential component as well, but the larger-radius object still reaches the friction limit first.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: If $F_T$ is the tension and $T$ is the period, the horizontal component satisfies $F_T\sin\theta=mr(2\pi/T)^2$. Vertically, $F_T\cos\theta=mg$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta=4\pi^2r/(gT^2)$, so $T=\sqrt{4\pi^2r/(g\tan\theta)}$.

perOption.A: Drops the $\tan\theta$ factor from the force ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the horizontal projection factor and misses the vertical component in the ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Puts $r$ in the denominator, giving the wrong dimensions for a period.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The question options and key duplicate some trigonometric function names. C is correct with the intended single tangent. The key also uses T for both period and tension.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The orbital radii measured from Earth's centre are $2R$ for P and $4R$ for Q. Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $mv^2/r=GMm/r^2$ and orbital speed is proportional to $1/\sqrt r$. Hence $v_P/v_Q=\sqrt{4R/(2R)}=\sqrt2$ and $v_P=\sqrt2\,v$.

perOption.A: Uses the surface altitudes as radii and makes the inner satellite slower.
perOption.B: Inverts the orbital-radius ratio for the two speeds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the surface altitudes $R$ and $3R$ as orbital radii.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: Gravitational potential at the surface is $\phi=-GM/r$. The Moon’s radius is $0.25$ times Earth’s radius, the same ratio as for the diameters. Thus $\phi_M=(0.012/0.25)(-63)\approx-3.0\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by the radius ratio although potential varies inversely with radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-square dependence appropriate to gravitational field strength.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio of the Moon’s potential to Earth’s potential.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: For simple harmonic motion, the acceleration and displacement amplitudes obey $a_0=\omega^2x_0$. The graph gives $0.30\times10^{-2}=\omega^2(6.0\times10^{-2})$, so $\omega=0.22\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\omega^2$ directly as the angular frequency.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Takes the square root of the reciprocal ratio $x_0/a_0$.
perOption.D: Uses $x_0/a_0$ and also omits the square root.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.issues: The graph omits minus signs at the negative ticks and malforms the acceleration unit. The slope and axis positions establish the intended signs and unit.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: P starts at its positive maximum, so its displacement is $y_P=A\cos(\omega t)$. S is $0.75\lambda$ to the right of P, so it lags by $2\pi(0.75)=3\pi/2$.

perOption.A: Uses the correct initial motion for S but gives half the phase lag.
perOption.B: Makes P start at zero displacement and gives half the phase lag.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Makes S start at $-A$ although it starts at zero.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The angular-frequency symbol is missing from the stem and the option formulas. C uses the intended cosine argument and gives the lag of S relative to P.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The cross-sectional area grows by a factor of $(16/2.0)^2=64$. The same wave power crosses both areas, so the intensity falls to $I/64$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, the amplitude falls to $A/\sqrt{64}=A/8$.

perOption.A: Scales intensity by the width ratio and gives an amplitude inconsistent with that intensity.
perOption.B: Gets the intensity right but takes the wrong square root for the amplitude ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses $16$ as the width ratio instead of dividing by the initial width of $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: The pipe closed at one end has fundamental wavelength $4L$, so the sound speed is $v=4fL$. At frequency $f/2$ the wavelength is $v/(f/2)=8L$. The fundamental of an open pipe fits half a wavelength, so its length is $4L$.

perOption.A: Uses an open pipe whose fundamental is $2f$, already above $f/2$.
perOption.B: Uses a quarter wavelength, which fits the fundamental of a pipe closed at one end.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Fits one and a half half-wavelengths, whereas an open pipe requires a whole number of half-wavelengths.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The worked solution starts on page 2 and continues on page 3.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: Use the longest wavelength, $600\ \mathrm{nm}$, because it diffracts through the largest angle in each order. With grating spacing $d=0.001/500\ \mathrm{m}$, $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives $\sin\theta=0.30n\leq1$. Orders 1 through 3 are complete on each side, giving six spectra.

perOption.A: Counts the complete spectra on only one side.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes the excluded central maximum.
perOption.D: Includes fourth orders, which lack the longest wavelengths.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Initially, the ideal gas law gives a total of $9pV/(283R)$ moles at common pressure $p$. At steady state, conservation of moles gives $p'V/(353R)+8p'V/(283R)=9pV/(283R)$, so $p'=1.022530p$. The fraction remaining in A is $1.022530(283/353)=0.819762$, so about $0.18n$ moles leave A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the transfer by leaving less gas in A than the final common pressure requires.
perOption.C: Reports the amount remaining in A as the amount transferred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the transfer by leaving only $0.14n$ in A.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The last line of the key calls 0.18n a fraction. It is the transferred amount in moles.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: For specific latent heat $L$, the two power balances are $P_1=m_1L+h$ and $P_2=m_2L+h$. Subtracting cancels the common heat loss, leaving $P_1-P_2=(m_1-m_2)L$. Thus $L=(P_1-P_2)/(m_1-m_2)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats all of the first heater input as power used for boiling.
perOption.C: Averages two estimates that each include a contribution from heat loss.
perOption.D: Adds the balances, retaining a heat-loss term of $2h$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The two charges each contribute $kq/r$ to the potential at R, so $V_R=2k(-30\times10^{-6})/0.20\approx-2.7\times10^6\ \mathrm{V}$. The work required from infinity is $\Delta U=(-e)V_R\approx4.3\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$, where $e$ is the magnitude of the electron charge.

perOption.A: Has the wrong sign and power of ten for the work required to bring in the electron.
perOption.B: Uses the negative electric potential directly as the work.
perOption.C: Uses the magnitude of the electric potential as work without multiplying by the electron charge magnitude.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The question PNG corrupts or omits the micro prefix on the two source charges. The key’s intermediate potential confirms the intended microcoulombs, but the key labels the potential in C and omits the electron’s negative sign in the work expression. The literal diagram labels in coulombs would give no listed answer.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: For square side $r$, the fields at Z from W and X initially have magnitudes $kQ/r^2$ and $kQ/(2r^2)$, with $45^\circ$ between them. The cosine rule gives an initial resultant of about $1.399kQ/r^2$. At Y, the moved charge produces a field at Z of magnitude $kQ/r^2$ perpendicular to W’s field, so the resultant rises to about $1.414kQ/r^2$.

perOption.A: The moved charge is closer to Z, so the potential there increases.
perOption.B: The charges are farther apart, so their potential energy decreases.
perOption.C: The charges are farther apart, so their repulsive force decreases.
perOption.D: Correct. The resultant field at Z increases.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key’s proof spans pages 3–4 and describes the field from Y at Z as rightward. It points left. The perpendicular geometry and numerical result are unaffected.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The turns ratio gives the secondary r.m.s. voltage $V_S=(1600/200)(25)=200\ \mathrm{V}$. Ohm’s law gives the secondary r.m.s. current $200/150=1.333\ \mathrm{A}$. The mean resistor power is $V_S^2/R=200^2/150=266.7\ \mathrm{W}$, which rounds to $270\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the turns ratio and predicts a step-down.
perOption.B: Uses the primary voltage directly across the secondary resistor.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the peak voltage to calculate mean power, doubling the result.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The charge added is $Q=It=(2.5\times10^{-6})(200)=5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the voltage increase gives $C=Q/\Delta V=(5.0\times10^{-4})/5.0=100\ \mathrm{\mu F}$.

perOption.A: Gives too little capacitance to store the calculated charge at the stated voltage increase.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses millifarads and also gives the wrong numerical value in microfarads.
perOption.D: Uses millifarads for a value calculated in microfarads.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: Each parallel group has capacitance $C+C+C=3C$. The two groups are in series, giving $C_{\mathrm{total}}=(1/(3C)+1/(3C))^{-1}=3C/2$.

perOption.A: Treats all six capacitors as being in series.
perOption.B: Reverses the series and parallel connections by treating the circuit as two parallel branches of three series capacitors.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats all six capacitors as being in parallel.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Both ions pass through the velocity selector undeflected, so they have the same speed. In the uniform magnetic field, $Bqv=mv^2/r$, giving $r=mv/(Bq)$. Since $B$ and $v$ are the same for both ions, $r_Q=(3.7)(1.5/2)=2.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Divides by both the mass factor and the charge factor.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Inverts the mass-to-charge ratio when scaling the radius.
perOption.D: Multiplies by the charge factor even though radius is inversely proportional to charge.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: From the force on the current-carrying wire, $B=F/(IL)$. The induced e.m.f. peaks at the maximum wire speed, $v_{\max}=\omega x_0=2\pi f x_0$. Thus $E_0=BLv_{\max}=(10\times10^{-3})(2\pi\times90)(1.8\times10^{-3})/5.0=0.00204\ \mathrm{V}$, or $2.0\ \mathrm{mV}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses frequency in place of angular frequency and misses the factor of $2\pi$.
perOption.B: Correct.

perOption.D: Reads the numerical result in volts instead of millivolts.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: The flux linkage is $NBA\cos(\omega t)$. Taking its negative time derivative gives $E=2\pi NBAf\sin(2\pi ft)$. Doubling $f$ doubles the peak e.m.f. to $2(2\pi NBAf)$ and halves the period.

perOption.A: Doubles the peak e.m.f. but keeps the original period.
perOption.B: Halves the period but incorrectly reduces the peak e.m.f.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The threshold frequency depends on the minimum energy required to release an electron from europium, which is independent of light intensity. At the same frequency, higher intensity means more photons reach the metal per unit time, so more electrons are emitted per unit time.

perOption.A: Incorrectly lowers the threshold and overlooks the increase in photon arrival rate.
perOption.B: Incorrectly lowers the threshold frequency when only intensity changes.
perOption.C: Overlooks the increase in electron emission rate as more photons arrive each second.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: When electrons escape, the electroscope becomes positively charged and the gold leaf rises. Using $E=hc/\lambda$, a red photon has energy $1.9125\ \mathrm{eV}$, below both work functions. A blue photon has energy $2.7625\ \mathrm{eV}$, above potassium’s work function but below aluminium’s, so the leaf rises only for potassium under blue light.

perOption.A: Assumes blue photons can also overcome aluminium’s $4.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ work function.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the predictions for potassium and assumes both photon energies exceed aluminium’s work function.
perOption.D: Reverses the predictions for potassium and incorrectly treats red photons as energetic enough for aluminium.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: The positively charged gold nucleus repels both alpha particles. Of the two particles with equal energies, the one passing closer to the nucleus is deflected through the larger angle.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows the farther particle continuing straight even though the nucleus also repels it.

perOption.D: Shows both particles bending towards the positively charged nucleus.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The number of parent nuclei halves from its initial value in about 3 years. To estimate the half-life of $D_1$, use the part of the curve where very little P remains, so production of new $D_1$ is negligible. The number of $D_1$ nuclei at year 29 is about halved by year 44, giving 15 years.

perOption.A: Uses a 20-year interval for the daughter, whose late-time count halves in about 15 years.
