perOption.A: Correct. Y is speed ($\propto\sqrt{x}$) and Z is electric potential energy (linearly decreasing).
perOption.B: The force in a uniform field is constant, so it would be a horizontal line, not a decreasing line.
perOption.C: Kinetic energy is linear in $x$, not curved like $\sqrt{x}$.
perOption.D: Kinetic energy is linear in $x$ and the electric force is constant, so neither graph matches.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q20.body:
By the potential divider method, the two sources in parallel have effective internal resistance $r/2$, so the p.d. across the internal resistance is

$E\,\dfrac{r/2}{R + r/2} = E\,\dfrac{r}{2R + r}$.

Fraction of power lost $= \dfrac{P_r}{P_\text{total}} = \dfrac{IV_r}{IE} = \dfrac{V_r}{E} = \dfrac{r}{2R+r}$.

perOption.A: Not obtained from the ratio of the internal p.d. to the e.m.f.
perOption.B: Greater than 1, which is impossible for a fraction of power.
perOption.C: Correct. $\dfrac{r}{2R+r}$.
perOption.D: This is the fraction of power delivered to the lamp, not lost in the internal resistance.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q21.body:
$D_1$ is reverse biased, so the p.d. across it is $E$ (in magnitude) and the p.d. across $R_1$ is $0\ \mathrm{V}$.

The current flows through $D_2$, $R_2$ and $R_3$, so $R_2$ has a non-zero p.d. while $D_2$ is forward biased with a small p.d.

Order: $D_1 > R_2 > R_1$.

perOption.A: Puts $R_1$ above $R_2$, but no current flows in the $D_1$ branch so $R_1$ has $0\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $D_1$ takes the full e.m.f., $R_2$ takes some, $R_1$ has $0\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.C: Puts $R_1$ first, wrongly assuming current flows through the reverse-biased branch.
perOption.D: Puts $R_2$ first and $D_1$ last, ignoring that the reverse-biased diode takes the whole e.m.f.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q21.issues: School working is a single line; the explanation adds a short clause about the other branch. perOption for A, C, D inferred.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q22.body:
For the steady current, $P = I^2R$.

For half-wave rectified a.c. the rms current is $I_0/2$, and the resistance is now $\tfrac12 R$:

$P = \left(\dfrac{I_0}{2}\right)^2\left(\dfrac12 R\right) = I^2R$

So $I_0 = \sqrt{8}\,I = 2.8\,I$.

perOption.A: Ignores the halving of resistance and the half-wave factor.
perOption.B: Uses $I_0=\sqrt2 I$, the full-wave result, and ignores the diode and halved resistance.
perOption.C: Ignores the factor from the halved resistance.
perOption.D: Correct. $I_0=\sqrt{8}\,I = 2.8\,I$.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q22.issues: School's working is terse; it uses rms current $I_0/2$ for half-wave and the halved resistance.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q23.body:
By the right-hand grip rule, the magnetic flux density at O due to P and Q points in direction C.

The flux density due to R and S points in direction A.

Adding the equal-magnitude perpendicular contributions, the resultant flux density at O is in direction B.

perOption.A: Only the contribution from R and S; P and Q are ignored.
perOption.B: Correct. Resultant of C (from P and Q) and A (from R and S).
perOption.C: Only the contribution from P and Q; R and S are ignored.
perOption.D: The opposite direction to the resultant; direction sign error from the right-hand grip rule.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q23.issues: School gives no comments on distractors; perOption for A, C, D inferred.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q24.body:
By the right-hand grip rule, opposite currents give fields at the midpoint that point in the same direction, perpendicular to the plane of the wires, so the resultant flux density is perpendicular to the plane.

The velocity $v$ is also perpendicular to this plane, so it is parallel to the resultant flux density.

The magnetic force $F = Bqv\sin\theta = 0$ since $\theta = 0^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct. $v$ is parallel to the resultant $B$ so $F=0$.
perOption.B: Uses the field of a single wire at distance $d/2$ with $F=Bqv$.
perOption.C: Assumes the field is perpendicular to $v$ and uses a single wire at distance $d$.
perOption.D: Adds both wires' fields as if the velocity were perpendicular to $B$.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q24.issues: Key's working is a single sentence; expanded with the grip-rule reasoning (fields from opposite currents add and are perpendicular to the plane, so parallel to v). perOption for B, C, D inferred.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q25.body:
Turning the coil over once reverses the flux through it, so the change in flux linkage is $2NBA\sin60^\circ$.

$\varepsilon = \dfrac{(2)(50)(30\times10^{-4})(4.0\times10^{-4})\sin60^\circ}{0.60}$

$= 1.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{V}$

perOption.A: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ and no factor of 2: $NBA\cos60^\circ/t = 5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.B: Omits the factor of 2 for turning the coil over.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ with the factor of 2, taking the angle from the normal.
perOption.D: Correct. $2NBA\sin60^\circ/t$.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q25.issues: School gives no comments on distractors; perOption for A, B, C inferred from the numbers (A: cos60 without 2; B: sin60 without 2; C: cos60 with 2).

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q26.body:
The inner loop experiences a decreasing flux linkage, so by Lenz's law the induced current flows in the same direction as that in the outer loop (clockwise) to oppose the decrease.

The current in the outer loop decreases at a constant rate, so the rate of decrease of $B$ and hence of flux linkage is constant. The induced e.m.f. in the inner loop is therefore constant, and so is the induced current.

perOption.A: Correct. Constant and clockwise.
perOption.B: Direction is right, but the rate of change of flux is constant so the current is not variable.
perOption.C: Direction is opposite to what Lenz's law requires for a decreasing flux.
perOption.D: Both direction and constancy are wrong.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q27.body:
When the electron velocity decreases, the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/p$ increases.

The pattern is caused by diffraction, and the diffraction angle satisfies $\sin\theta \propto \lambda$, so $\sin\theta$ increases and the circles have larger diameter.

perOption.A: Wrong cause (refraction) and wrong change.
perOption.B: Wrong cause: electrons passing through a carbon film diffract.
perOption.C: Correct cause but the wrong change: smaller $v$ means larger $\lambda$, so larger circles.
perOption.D: Correct. Diffraction; diameters increase.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q28.body:
Einstein's photoelectric equation with the stopping potential: $hf = \Phi + eV_s$.

$3.5\times10^{-19} = \Phi + (1.6\times10^{-19})(0.25)$, so $\Phi = 3.1\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts 0.25 eV twice (or adds wrongly); not the work function.
perOption.B: Correct. The stopping energy is $0.25\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.4\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.
perOption.C: Ignores the stopping potential and takes the photon energy as the work function.
perOption.D: Adds $eV_s$ to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

tjc-2022-prelim-p1-q29.body:
Total binding energy before: $7.59\times235 = 1783.65\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Total binding energy after: $(8.26\times121)+(8.52\times113) = 1962\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Change in binding energy $= +179\ \mathrm{MeV}$, released as energy since the products are more stable. (The neutrons have no binding energy.)

perOption.A: Counts only part of the nucleons, or omits a product; gives 73.9 MeV.
perOption.B: Wrong magnitude and the wrong sense (absorbed).
perOption.C: Correct. Binding energy increases, so energy is released.
perOption.D: Right magnitude but the wrong sense; higher binding energy means energy is released.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q1.body:
$v = s/t = (385-115)/(3.50-1.50) = 270/2.00 = 135\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

Add fractional uncertainties: $\dfrac{\Delta v}{v} = \dfrac{\Delta s}{s}+\dfrac{\Delta t}{t} = \dfrac{1+1}{270}+\dfrac{0.02+0.02}{2.00}$.

$\Delta v = 3.7 \approx 4\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the uncertainty in time only and mishandles the ratio.
perOption.B: Combines the uncertainties incorrectly and gets a far too small value.
perOption.C: Uses a single reading uncertainty and ignores that differences add uncertainties.
perOption.D: Correct. Uncertainties in a difference add, then fractional uncertainties add for the quotient.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q2.body:
The second displacement is resultant minus first. Resolving gives a right-angled triangle with sides 150 cm and 140 cm.

Magnitude $=\sqrt{150^2+140^2} = 205\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Direction $= 90 - 30 - \tan^{-1}(140/150) = 17^\circ$ below the $x$-axis, i.e. $343^\circ$ anticlockwise from $+x$.

perOption.A: Adds magnitudes (150+140) and ignores the angles.
perOption.B: Adds magnitudes (150+140) and ignores the angles.
perOption.C: Correct magnitude but the angle is taken above the x-axis instead of below.
perOption.D: Correct. $17^\circ$ below the $x$-axis is $343^\circ$ anticlockwise.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q3.body:
At the start: $1.2\times10^5 = 2(1.0\times10^5)a$, so $a = 0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At $t=20\ \mathrm{s}$, $v = 0.60\times20 = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The back carriage then moves at constant $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: in 20 s it travels $240\ \mathrm{m}$.

The front carriage now has $a = 1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: $s = 12(20)+\tfrac12(1.2)(20)^2 = 480\ \mathrm{m}$.

Separation $= 480-240 = 240\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Not obtained from the correct motion of either carriage.
perOption.B: Correct. Front 480 m minus back 240 m.
perOption.C: Not obtained from the correct motion of either carriage.
perOption.D: This is the distance travelled by the front carriage alone, not the separation.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Ball A: $h=\tfrac12 gt^2$ gives $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$, so $x_A = 2v\sqrt{2h/g}$.

Ball B: $2h=\tfrac12 gt^2$ gives $t=\sqrt2\sqrt{2h/g}$, so $x_B = v\sqrt2\sqrt{2h/g}$.

$\dfrac{x_A}{x_B} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt2} = \sqrt2 = 1.41$.

perOption.A: Uses the speed ratio only and ignores the longer fall time of B (2.83 = $2\sqrt2$).
perOption.B: Correct. Time ratio is $1/\sqrt2$, speed ratio is 2.
perOption.C: Assumes the two effects cancel exactly.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio or mishandles the time dependence (0.353).

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Whole system: $F-6f = 6Ma$, so $a = \dfrac{F-6f}{6M}$ (friction is proportional to mass: $f$, $2f$, $3f$).

For block $3M$: $F_1 - 3f = 3Ma$, so $F_1 = 3M\left(\dfrac{F-6f}{6M}\right)+3f = \dfrac F2$.

perOption.A: Correct. The friction terms cancel.
perOption.B: Adds $3f$ to $F/2$ again; friction on $3M$ is already included.
perOption.C: Splits $F$ equally between the three blocks.
perOption.D: Splits $F$ equally between the three blocks and adds friction wrongly.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q6.body:
Conservation of momentum in the collision: $(5.0)(200) = (5.0+95)u$, so $u = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Conservation of energy afterwards: $\tfrac12(100)(10^2) = (100)(9.81)H$, so $H = 5.1\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Mass units cancel.
perOption.B: Uses $g=10$ with $u$ wrongly, or ignores the combined mass.
perOption.C: Uses the pellet's speed or mass inconsistently.
perOption.D: Applies energy conservation to the pellet's initial speed (about 2000 m).

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q7.body: The rack is in equilibrium under three forces (weight, the push from the bottle's neck at the top, and the table's contact force at the bottom). For three non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point. Only diagram C satisfies this.

perOption.A: The lines of action do not meet at a point.
perOption.B: Forces are all vertical, so the torque cannot balance with the top force.
perOption.C: Correct. The three lines of action are concurrent.
perOption.D: The lines of action do not meet at a point.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q8.body:
For each mass, tension + upthrust = weight, so tension = weight $-$ upthrust.

The rod is horizontal and pivoted at its centre, so the tensions are equal.

Upthrust $=V\rho g$ is greater for P because liquid X is denser, so P's weight must be greater to give the same tension as Q.

perOption.A: Same volume but different liquid densities give different upthrusts.
perOption.B: P is in the denser liquid so its upthrust is larger, not smaller.
perOption.C: Reverses the conclusion: P needs the larger weight.
perOption.D: Correct. Larger upthrust on P means P must be heavier.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Vertical: $T\cos30^\circ = mg$ (1). Horizontal: $T\sin30^\circ = mr\omega^2$ (2).

(2)/(1): $\tan30^\circ = r\omega^2/g$, with $r = 3.0+5.0\sin30^\circ = 5.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

$\omega = 1.01\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, so $T = 2\pi/\omega = 6.2\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Not from the correct radius or angular speed.
perOption.B: Uses $r=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ or similar wrong radius.
perOption.C: Uses $r=5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ or a wrong radius (omits the 3.0 m offset).
perOption.D: Correct. Radius of the circle is $3.0+5.0\sin30^\circ$.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Tangentially: $F - mg\sin\theta = 0$. Radially: $T - mg\cos\theta = mr\omega^2$.

So $T = mr\omega^2 + mg\cos\theta$, which varies with $\cos\theta$.

Tension is largest at the lowest point ($\theta=0$) and smallest at the highest point ($\theta=\pi$), matching graph C.

perOption.A: Constant tension would need no weight component.
perOption.B: Has two cycles per revolution; $\cos\theta$ has one.
perOption.C: Correct. Maximum at $\theta=0$, minimum at $\theta=\pi$.
perOption.D: Minimum at $\theta=0$, which is reversed.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q11.body:
At P: $\Phi_P = -\dfrac{GM}{r/3}-\dfrac{GM_B}{2r/3} = -\dfrac Gr(3M+1.5M_B)$.

At Q: $\Phi_Q = -\dfrac{GM}{2r/3}-\dfrac{GM_B}{r/3} = -\dfrac Gr(1.5M+3M_B)$.

$\Phi_Q = 1.25\Phi_P$ gives $1.5M+3M_B = 1.25(3M+1.5M_B)$, so $M_B = 2M$.

perOption.A: Algebra slip in the potential contributions.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong distances for one planet.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong distances for one planet.
perOption.D: Correct. Add the potentials from both planets at each point.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q12.body:
Gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=mr\omega^2$, so $\omega^2\propto 1/r^3$. When $r$ decreases, both the gravitational force and $\omega$ increase, so A and B are wrong.

$KE=+\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $GPE=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. As $r$ decreases, KE increases while GPE decreases, so only D is correct.

perOption.A: Angular velocity increases since $\omega^2\propto1/r^3$.
perOption.B: Force $\propto 1/r^2$ increases as $r$ decreases.
perOption.C: KE $=GMm/2r$ increases as $r$ decreases.
perOption.D: Correct. GPE becomes more negative.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q13.body:
Let $h$ be the rate of heat loss. Then $10 = \dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}+h$ (1) and $18 = \dfrac{3mc\Delta\theta}{t}+h$ (2).

Subtracting: $8 = 2\dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}$, so $\dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}=4\ \mathrm{W}$, giving $h = 6.0\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Does not satisfy both equations.
perOption.B: Correct. $10-4 = 6.0\ \mathrm{W}$.
perOption.C: Does not satisfy both equations.
perOption.D: Does not satisfy both equations.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q14.body:
At constant pressure, $V \propto T$. When the gas is cooled, $T$ decreases so $V$ decreases. The gas is compressed, so work is done on the gas and $w$ is positive.

When $T$ decreases, $\Delta U$ is negative. From $\Delta U = q + w$: negative $= q + (\text{positive})$, so $q$ must be negative.

perOption.A: Takes $w$ as negative, as if the gas expanded; cooling at constant pressure compresses it.
perOption.B: Correct. $\Delta U<0$, $q<0$ (heat lost), $w>0$ (compression).
perOption.C: Gives $\Delta U$ positive, but cooling lowers the internal energy of an ideal gas.
perOption.D: Gives all three positive, which contradicts cooling (heat must leave the gas).

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q15.body:
Given $x_0 = 0.030\ \mathrm{m}$. From the graph, the kinetic energy repeats every 1.0 s, which is half the period of the motion, so $T = 2.0\ \mathrm{s}$.

$v_{max} = x_0\omega = 0.030 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{2.0} = 0.094\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Gives a value about 6 times too large, from a wrong angular frequency.
perOption.B: Gives about 3 times too large, from a wrong angular frequency.
perOption.C: Uses the KE period of 1.0 s as the period of the motion, doubling $\omega$.
perOption.D: Correct. $T = 2.0$ s, $v_{max} = x_0\omega = 0.094\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q16.body:
At X, the two neighbouring particles are moving towards the particle at X, so X is a compression.

At Y, the two neighbouring particles are moving away from the particle at Y, so Y is a rarefaction.

perOption.A: Treats Y as a compression too; at Y the neighbours move apart.
perOption.B: Correct. Neighbours converge at X (compression) and diverge at Y (rarefaction).
perOption.C: Swaps the two: X is where neighbours converge, not diverge.
perOption.D: Treats X as a rarefaction; neighbours move towards X.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q17.body:
By Rayleigh's criterion, the minimum angle of resolution is $\theta \approx \lambda/b$, where the pupil size acts as the slit width $b$.

If $b$ increases, $\theta$ decreases, so the dots are easier to resolve. Darkening the room enlarges the pupil.

perOption.A: Correct. Larger pupil $b$ gives smaller $\lambda/b$, so closer dots can be resolved.
perOption.B: Red light has a longer wavelength, increasing $\lambda/b$ and making resolution worse.
perOption.C: Brightness does not change the minimum resolvable angle.
perOption.D: Moving the dots closer decreases their angular separation, making them harder to resolve.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q19.body:
The electric field inside the conductor is zero, since there is no net field or potential difference within a conductor.

The external regions still have a uniform electric field pointing from the positive to the negative plate, so $E$ is constant outside the conductor and zero over the width $d$.

perOption.A: Field varies linearly with x, which would need charge between the plates, and is non-zero inside the conductor.
perOption.B: Shows field going to zero and then negative; the field never reverses direction.
perOption.C: Reverses the field direction beyond the conductor; the field points from + to - throughout.
perOption.D: Correct. Uniform field outside, zero inside the conductor.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q20.body:
$R = \rho L/A$ and $R = V/I$, so $V/I = \rho L/A$ and $L = VA/(I\rho)$.

$L = \dfrac{240\,[\pi(3.0\times10^{-4})^2]}{2.0 \times 1.4\times10^{-6}} = 24\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too small; check the area $A=\pi r^2$ and the factor of $I\rho$ in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct. $L = VA/(I\rho) = 24$ m.
perOption.C: Not from the school's working; likely an arithmetic slip in the area.
perOption.D: About four times the answer, from using the diameter as the radius in $A = \pi r^2$.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q21.body:
Let each resistor be $R$. In A, the ammeter branch has one resistor across $V$: $I_A = V/R$.

In B, a resistor $R$ is in series with a parallel pair $R/2$, so the total is $3R/2$, the total current is $2V/3R$, and the ammeter takes half: $I_A = V/3R$.

In C, $I_A = V/R$. In D, the ammeter is in the branch with two resistors: $I_A = V/2R$. B is the smallest.

perOption.A: $I_A = V/R$, the largest possible with a single resistor across the supply.
perOption.B: Correct. $I_A = V/3R$, the minimum.
perOption.C: The ammeter branch is one resistor across the supply, $V/R$.
perOption.D: Two resistors in series in the ammeter branch give $V/2R$, which is greater than $V/3R$.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q22.body:
$V = E - Ir$. When $I = 0$, $V = E = 2.5\ \mathrm{V}$.

From the graph, $0.9 = 2.5 - 0.80\,r$, so $r = 2.0\ \Omega$. Equivalently, the gradient of the graph is $-r$.

perOption.B: Not obtained from the graph intercept and gradient.
perOption.C: Not obtained from the graph intercept and gradient.
perOption.D: Likely $0.9/0.80 = 1.1\ \Omega$, which is the external resistance R at that point, not r.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q24.body:
The electron passes undeflected, so the electric force equals the magnetic force: $qE = Bqv$.

The charge $q$ cancels, so the condition $v = E/B$ does not depend on the mass or charge. The alpha particle also has the same $v$, and its electric and magnetic forces (both reversed in direction relative to the electron) still balance, so it is undeflected.

perOption.A: Correct. $v = E/B$ is independent of charge and mass.
perOption.B: Assumes the magnetic force exceeds the electric force for the positive alpha particle.
perOption.C: Assumes the electric force exceeds the magnetic force for the alpha particle.
perOption.D: Forces from these fields act in the plane of the page; none points into the page.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q25.body:
This is like Faraday's homopolar generator. The induced current is $I = \varepsilon/R = B\pi r^2 f/R$, which is constant when $r$ and $f$ are kept constant.

The direction of the current alternates between clockwise and anticlockwise depending on which radius is cutting the flux (use Fleming's right-hand rule), giving a square wave.

perOption.A: Shows a rectified, varying magnitude; the emf magnitude is constant.
perOption.B: Triangular waveform would need a changing rate of flux cutting.
perOption.C: Correct. Constant magnitude, alternating direction.
perOption.D: Sinusoidal would arise for a coil rotating in a field with constantly changing flux, not here.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q26.body:
$\lambda = h/mv$, so $\lambda \propto 1/m$ at the same speed $v$. The electron mass is much smaller than the proton mass, so $\lambda_e > \lambda_p$.

For single-slit diffraction, $b\sin\theta = \lambda$, so $\sin\theta \propto \lambda$. The diffraction angle (pattern width) for electrons is much larger than for protons.

perOption.A: Wrong wavelength comparison: smaller mass gives longer wavelength.
perOption.B: Wrong on both: electrons have the longer wavelength and wider pattern.
perOption.C: Correct. $\lambda_e > \lambda_p$ and wider electron pattern.
perOption.D: Right wavelength comparison but a longer wavelength gives a wider, not narrower, pattern.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q27.body:
Electrons per second: $dN_e/dt = I/e = 2.0\times10^{-6}/1.6\times10^{-19}$.

Photons per second: $dN_p/dt = P/E = 0.31\times10^{-3}/(3.11\times1.6\times10^{-19})$.

Ratio $= 0.020$.

perOption.A: Likely inverts or mishandles the powers of ten.
perOption.B: Correct. $2.0\times10^{-2}$.
perOption.C: Assumes every photon releases an electron.
perOption.D: Reports a count rate rather than a ratio.

perOption.A: Wrong power of ten; not from $\Delta x = h/\Delta p$ with $\Delta p = 0.002p$.
perOption.B: Wrong power of ten and prefactor.
perOption.C: Correct. $\Delta x = h/\Delta p = 2.4\times10^{-7}$ m.
perOption.D: Wrong power of ten, for example from taking 0.2% as 0.0002 or similar slip.

tjc-2023-prelim-p1-q30.body:
Initial true count rate from the source $= 90 - 10 = 80\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

Number of half-lives $= 12/24 = 0.5$, so $C = 80(1/2)^{0.5} = 57\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

Add back the background: final count $= 57 + 10 = 67\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Halves 90 directly, ignoring background and using one half-life.
perOption.B: Halves the source count after subtracting background (one full half-life, 40 + 10).
perOption.C: Gets the source count rate (57) but forgets to add back the background.
perOption.D: Correct. $57 + 10 = 67\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q1.body:
Units of $\Delta P = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ and units of $\rho = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

Units of $\Delta P/\rho = \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Since $v$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $k$ has no unit, $(\mathrm{m^2 s^{-2}})^n = \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, hence $n = 0.5$.

perOption.A: Correct. $(\mathrm{m^2 s^{-2}})^{0.5} = \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.B: Gives $\mathrm{m^2 s^{-2}}$, the units of $v^2$.
perOption.C: Gives $\mathrm{m^3 s^{-3}}$, which is not a speed.
perOption.D: Gives $\mathrm{m^4 s^{-4}}$, which is not a speed.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q3.body:
The pilot must aim partly into the wind so that the westerly wind cancels the aircraft's westward velocity component. The airspeed (350 km/h) is the hypotenuse of the velocity triangle, and the wind (100 km/h) is the perpendicular side.

$v_{\text{ground}} = \sqrt{350^2 - 100^2} = 335\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ (north).

perOption.A: Subtracts 100 from 350 instead of using Pythagoras.
perOption.B: Correct. Velocity triangle with 350 as hypotenuse.
perOption.C: Uses $\sqrt{350^2+100^2}$, treating the wind as adding to the northward speed.
perOption.D: Adds 350 and 100 as if the wind were a tailwind.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q4.body: Both balls are launched horizontally from the same height, so each has zero initial vertical velocity and the same vertical acceleration $g$. Their vertical motion is identical and independent of the horizontal motion, so the time to fall is the same: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$. They land together; Y simply travels farther horizontally.

perOption.A: Landing nearer does not mean landing earlier; fall time depends only on height.
perOption.B: Horizontal speed does not affect the time of fall.
perOption.C: Correct. Same height and same $g$ give the same fall time.
perOption.D: Air resistance is neglected in the intended reasoning, and the final speeds would differ anyway (Y is faster horizontally).

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q4.issues: The school key gives only the letter for Q4 (no working); explanation is generated.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Change in momentum equals the area under the $F$-$t$ graph.

Area from 0 to 10 s $= \tfrac12(8+4)(12) + \left[-\tfrac12(2)(12)\right] = 60\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

$60 = mv - 0$, so with $m = 0.300$ kg, $v = 200\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Impulse 60 N s divided by 0.300 kg.
perOption.B: Not supported by the net area of 60 N s.
perOption.C: Not supported by the net area of 60 N s.
perOption.D: Ignores the negative area (adds 12 N s instead of subtracting), or similar area error.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q6.body:
Force on water = rate of change of momentum $= \dfrac{\rho V}{\Delta t}\Delta v = \rho \pi r^2 v (0 - v) = -\rho\pi r^2 v^2$.

$= -1000\pi(2.0\times10^{-2})^2(0.50)^2 = -0.314\ \mathrm{N}$.

By Newton's third law, the force by the water on the wall is $0.314$ N.

perOption.A: Correct. $F=\rho\pi r^2 v^2$.
perOption.B: Treats the water as rebounding (momentum change $2mv$), which the question rules out.
perOption.C: Uses diameter instead of radius, which gives four times the correct force.
perOption.D: Uses $\rho\pi r^2 v$ and omits a factor of $v$, or similar slip.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q6.issues: Distractor explanations for B, C, D are my inference of the likely errors (school gave none).

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q7.body:
The cuboids have equal volume and are fully immersed, so the upthrust $U$ is the same on each.

$T + U = mg = \rho_{\text{material}} V g$, so $T = \rho_{\text{material}}Vg - U$.

Cuboid W has the largest density, so the tension in its string is the greatest.

perOption.A: Y is denser than water, so its weight exceeds the upthrust (the string supplies the difference).
perOption.B: Upthrust is the same for all three because volume displaced is equal.
perOption.C: Tensions differ because the weights differ.
perOption.D: Correct. $T=\rho Vg-U$ is largest for the densest cuboid.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q8.body:
For a wire obeying Hooke's law, the graph of tension against extension is a straight line. The extra energy stored is the area of the trapezium between $x_1$ and $x_2$:

$\tfrac12(T_2 + T_1)(x_2 - x_1)$.

perOption.A: Correct. Area of the trapezium under the $T$-$x$ graph.
perOption.B: Uses $T_2-T_1$, which gives the energy of a triangle starting from $T_1$ (wrong shape).
perOption.C: Uses $x_2+x_1$ instead of the change in length.
perOption.D: Uses both differences wrongly; neither factor is the trapezium's width and mean height.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q9.body:
P and Q are on the same turntable, so they have the same angular velocity $\omega$.

Linear speed $v = r\omega$ is greater for P since $r_1 > r_2$.

Centripetal force $F = mr\omega^2$ is also greater for P since $r_1 > r_2$.

perOption.A: Speeds differ because $v=r\omega$; and the force is greater for P, not Q.
perOption.B: Same angular speed does not mean same linear speed.
perOption.C: Force is greater for P (larger radius), not Q.
perOption.D: Correct. Both $v$ and $F$ increase with $r$ at fixed $\omega$.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q10.body:
At P (just in contact, $N\approx0$): $mg = mv^2/r$, so $v^2 = rg$.

P and Q are at the same height, so the kinetic energy (and speed) at Q equals that at P.

At Q: $mg - N = mv^2/(2r)$, so $N = mg - m(rg)/(2r) = mg/2$.

By Newton's third law the cart exerts $mg/2$ on the track.

perOption.A: The cart still needs less than $mg$ of centripetal force at Q, so $N$ is not zero.
perOption.B: Correct. $N = mg - mv^2/2r = mg/2$.
perOption.C: Ignores the centripetal force needed at Q.
perOption.D: Adds instead of subtracts; at the top of a hill, $mg$ exceeds $N$.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q11.body:
By conservation of energy, $KE_i + GPE_i = KE_f + GPE_f$.

The object starts 6R above the surface, i.e. $7R$ from the centre:

$0 - \dfrac{GMm}{7R} = \tfrac12 mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{12GM}{7R}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $GM/R$ (surface escape-style value), ignoring the starting distance.
perOption.B: Not from the energy equation; mishandles the $1/7R$ and $1/R$ terms.
perOption.C: Correct. $v^2 = 2GM(1/R - 1/7R)=12GM/7R$.
perOption.D: Not from the energy equation; wrongly combines the distances.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q11.issues: keyAnswer is A (parser answer-conflict) but the key's answer table prints C for Q11. The worked solution box is labelled D, yet its result $\sqrt{12GM/7R}$ is option C on the printed paper. Treating C as correct; box label D looks like a typo.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q12.body: The antenna has the same speed as the spacecraft and so is still bound in the same orbit. The gravitational force still acts on it and provides the centripetal force, so it continues in the same circular motion.

perOption.A: Gravity still acts, so it cannot leave in a straight line.
perOption.B: It has orbital speed, not zero, so it does not fall on a parabola into the planet.
perOption.C: Correct. Same speed and radius means the same orbit.
perOption.D: It would fall straight down only if its horizontal velocity were zero.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.body:
$pV = \tfrac13 Nm\langle c^2\rangle$. $V$ and $m$ are unchanged, so $\dfrac{N\langle c^2\rangle}{p}$ is constant.

$\dfrac{N(3.0\times10^5)}{p} = \dfrac{\tfrac34 N\langle c^2\rangle}{p/2}$

$\langle c^2\rangle = 2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Misapplies the ratio of $N$ and $p$ (e.g. $\langle c^2\rangle\propto p/N$ with wrong fractions).
perOption.B: Correct. $\langle c^2\rangle = 3.0\times10^5\times\frac{1/2}{3/4}$.
perOption.C: Inverts the ratio, giving $3.0\times10^5\times 1.5$.
perOption.D: Treats $\langle c^2\rangle$ as proportional to $p$ with a different factor and ignores the lost molecules, e.g. multiplying by 3.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.issues: Distractor explanations for A, C, D are inferred.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.body:
$ma = mg - R$. The object loses contact when $R = 0$, so $ma = mg$.

For SHM, $a = \omega^2 x_0 = (2\pi f)^2 x_0 = g$.

$x_0 = \dfrac{g}{(2\pi f)^2} = \dfrac{9.81}{(2\pi\times3.0)^2} = 0.028\ \mathrm{m} = 2.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $x_0 = g/(2\pi f)^2$.
perOption.B: Uses $f = 2.0$ Hz (the value in the school working typo) instead of 3.0 Hz.
perOption.C: Not from $g/\omega^2$; likely a slip with $f$ or $\omega$.
perOption.D: Double the value in B; likely a factor-of-2 slip.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The school's working shows an intermediate '(2\u03c0(2.0))' typo; the final line correctly uses f = 3.0 Hz. Distractor explanations are generic.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.body:
$I \propto A^2$, so $I = kA^2$.

The waves start in antiphase and have a path difference of a whole number of wavelengths, so they arrive in antiphase: resultant amplitude $= A - 0.6A = 0.4A$.

$I_R = k(0.4A)^2 = 0.16kA^2 = 0.16I$.

perOption.A: Correct. Destructive interference with amplitude $0.4A$.
perOption.B: Uses $0.4A$ but forgets to square it.
perOption.C: Treats the waves as in phase and adds intensities ($1+0.6$) without squaring.
perOption.D: Adds the amplitudes (constructive) and forgets to square: $1.6\ldots$ then adds.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.issues: Distractor explanations for C and D are inferred and loosely worded.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Using $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$: for diagram 1, $2 = 8\cos^2\theta$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$.

For diagram 2 the polariser is rotated another $90^\circ$, so the angle is $90^\circ + 60^\circ = 150^\circ$:

$I = 8\cos^2(90^\circ + 60^\circ) = 6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Would need the polariser to be crossed with the polarisation direction ($90^\circ$), but the angle is $150^\circ$.
perOption.B: Same as diagram 1; ignores the extra $90^\circ$ rotation.
perOption.C: Correct. $8\cos^2150^\circ = 6$.
perOption.D: Would need the polariser aligned with the light ($\theta=0$).

perOption.A: Correct. $\theta$ from the geometry, then $d\sin\theta=2\lambda$.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin\theta = 20/75$ instead of $\tan\theta$.
perOption.C: Uses $n=1$ instead of $n=2$ (gives double: 858 nm).
perOption.D: Uses $\sin\theta = 20/75$ and $n=1$.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.issues: Distractor explanations for B and D are inferred.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q19.body:
The field points from high to low potential, so it points towards Y (right).

The electron is negatively charged, so the electric force on it points towards X, i.e. away from Y.

Change in electric potential energy from X to Y: $\Delta E_p = (-eV_Y) - (-eV_X) = -70\ \mathrm{eV} + 100\ \mathrm{eV} = +30\ \mathrm{eV}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Force towards X and the electron gains 30 eV.
perOption.B: Force direction is wrong (that would be for a positive charge) and the sign of the energy change is wrong.
perOption.C: Force direction is wrong (that would be for a positive charge); the +30 eV is right.
perOption.D: Force direction is right, but the sign of the energy change is wrong: the electron moves to a lower potential, so its potential energy increases.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q20.body:
$R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} \propto \dfrac{L}{A}$.

The cuboid has length $5d$ between X and Y and cross-sectional area $2d \times d = 2d^2$ (2 rows of cubes).

$\dfrac{R'}{4.0} = \dfrac{5d}{d} \times \dfrac{d^2}{2d^2}$, so $R' = 10\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio: $4.0\times 2/5 = 1.6\ \Omega$.
perOption.B: Only divides by the 2 rows and ignores the five-fold increase in length.
perOption.C: Correct. Length is 5 times, area is 2 times, so $R = 4.0 \times 5/2$.
perOption.D: Adds all ten cubes in series, ignoring the doubled cross-sectional area.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q21.body:
In the driver circuit, the p.d. across XY should be minimised for the largest balance length, so the NTC thermistor's resistance should be maximised (potential divider rule). Hence the temperature should be low.

The terminal p.d. of the test cell circuit should be maximised, so the resistance of the LDR should be maximised (less current drawn, less lost to internal resistance). Hence the environment should be dark.

perOption.A: High temperature lowers the NTC resistance and bright light lowers the LDR resistance; both work against a long balance length.
perOption.B: Dark is right for the LDR, but high temperature lowers the NTC resistance and raises the p.d. across XY.
perOption.C: Low temperature is right for the NTC, but bright light lowers the LDR resistance and so the terminal p.d.
perOption.D: Correct. Low temperature and dark.

perOption.A: 12 is the r.m.s. secondary voltage, not a power.
perOption.B: This is the mean power $V_{rms}^2/R = 24$ W, not the peak power.
perOption.C: Correct. Peak power is twice the mean power of 24 W.
perOption.D: Doubles the correct peak power.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q23.body:
Take moments about the pivot (the top side). The magnetic force $F_B$ acts horizontally on the lowest side, at perpendicular distance $L\cos 30^\circ$ from the pivot; the weight acts at the centre, at perpendicular distance $\dfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ$.

$F_B \times L\cos 30^\circ = 0.12 \times \dfrac{L}{2}\sin 30^\circ$

$50B(0.40)(60\times10^{-3})\cos 30^\circ = 0.12 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 30^\circ$

$B = 0.029\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Moments about the pivot with $F_B = NBIL$.
perOption.B: Twice the answer: omits the factor of one half for the weight acting at the centre.
perOption.C: Three times the answer; likely a wrong trigonometric ratio in the moments.
perOption.D: Ignores the moment arms and the number of turns.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q24.body:
The force causing the deflection acts upwards, so the magnetic force is upwards.

Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the current is opposite in direction to the motion of the particle, so it must be negatively charged.

If the magnetic force is upwards, the electric force must be downwards. For a negative charge this means the electric field must be upwards (+y).

perOption.A: Positive charge is wrong: the magnetic force would then be downwards, not upwards.
perOption.B: Positive charge is wrong, and the field direction does not match either.
perOption.C: Correct. Negative charge; the field points +y so the force on the negative charge is -y.
perOption.D: Negative charge is right, but a -y field would give a +y electric force on a negative charge, adding to the magnetic force.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q25.body:
Maximum flux linkage occurs when the B field lines are perpendicular to the coil, i.e. the normal is parallel to the field. This needs a rotation of $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ anticlockwise.

When flux linkage is maximum, the induced e.m.f. is minimum (zero), and vice-versa. So the e.m.f. is maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field, a further $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ away from that position, i.e. a rotation of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ clockwise from the initial position.

perOption.A: Rotation angles and directions are both reversed between the two cases.
perOption.B: The directions are right for neither case: the flux-linkage rotation should be $\pi/3$, not $\pi/6$.
perOption.C: Angles are swapped between the two cases and the directions are wrong.
perOption.D: Correct. $\pi/3$ anticlockwise for maximum flux linkage, $\pi/6$ clockwise for maximum e.m.f.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q25.issues: The school's solution is brief and only justifies the maximum flux linkage case (and the flux/e.m.f. phase relation); the pi/6 clockwise step for maximum e.m.f. was filled in by the explainer.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q26.body:
A step-up transformer has $N_s > N_p$.

For an ideal transformer the magnetic flux $\phi$ through each turn is the same in both coils, so flux linkage is $N_s\phi > N_p\phi$, giving a ratio $>1$.

$\dfrac{I_s}{I_p} = \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s} < 1$.

perOption.A: Flux linkage ratio is $N_s/N_p > 1$, not less than 1.
perOption.B: Correct. Flux linkage ratio $>1$, current ratio $<1$.
perOption.C: The current ratio is less than 1, since power is conserved and the secondary voltage is larger.
perOption.D: Both ratios are reversed.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.body:
The school's key prints only the letter D for this question.

The continuous X-ray spectrum has a sharp cut-off at $\lambda_{min}$. This occurs when an electron gives up all its kinetic energy $eV$ in a single collision, producing one photon of the maximum energy: $eV = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{min}}$.

perOption.A: The threshold wavelength belongs to photoelectric emission, not X-ray production.
perOption.B: The cut-off depends on the accelerating voltage, not on the ionisation energy of the target.
perOption.C: It is a photon wavelength, not the electron's de Broglie wavelength.
perOption.D: Correct. All the electron's energy goes into one photon.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.issues: Key prints only the letter D with no working; explanation generated.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.body:
$E = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2mE}$.

The mass of an alpha particle is $4u$, so $p = \sqrt{8uE}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{8uE}} = \dfrac{h}{2\sqrt{2uE}}$.

perOption.A: Uses mass $u$ instead of $4u$, or drops a factor of 2 inside the root.
perOption.B: Inverted: wavelength is $h/p$, not $p/h$.
perOption.C: Correct. $h/\sqrt{8uE}$.
perOption.D: Inverted: wavelength is $h/p$, not $p/h$.

tjc-2024-prelim-p1-q29.body:
Paper does not reduce the count rate, so there is no $\alpha$ (which would not pass through paper).

$\beta$ is stopped by a few mm of aluminium, which is why the rate falls from 1000 to 250.

Only $\gamma$ can pass through thick steel, which is why a count remains (50 s$^{-1}$).

perOption.A: Alpha is absorbed by paper, but the rate is unchanged by paper.
perOption.B: No alpha: paper makes no difference. Aluminium reduces the count, so beta is present.
perOption.C: No alpha; and the count remaining behind thick steel shows gamma is present.
perOption.D: Correct. Beta (absorbed by aluminium) and gamma (penetrates steel).

perOption.A: Half the correct value.
perOption.B: Correct. Hour converted to 3600 s.
perOption.C: Twice the correct value.
perOption.D: Divides by 60 instead of 3600 s.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q1.body:
Units of $Q$: $\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{A\,s}$.

Units of $V$: $\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}} / \mathrm{A\,s}$.

Hence units of $C = Q/V$ are $\mathrm{A^2\,s^4\,m^{-2}\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $\mathrm{A^2\,s^4\,m^{-2}\,kg^{-1}}$.
perOption.B: Missing the ampere, and the power of s is wrong.
perOption.C: Missing the powers of seconds.
perOption.D: The coulomb is not an SI base unit.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q2.body:
Average of $h$ (in $10^{-34}$ J s): A 6.63, B 6.63, C 6.65, D 6.62.

A, B and D are accurate (close to the accepted 6.63).

Range of variation: A 0.04, B 0.02, C 0.07, D 0.02. B and D are precise.

So the student who is accurate but imprecise is A.

perOption.A: Correct. Accurate mean 6.63, but a larger spread (range 0.04) than B and D.
perOption.B: Accurate and precise (range 0.02).
perOption.C: Mean 6.65 is less accurate, and the range is largest at 0.07: neither accurate nor precise.
perOption.D: Accurate and precise (range 0.02).

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q3.body:
$v = k\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma}{\lambda\rho}}$, so the power of $1/2$ applies to the sum of the fractional uncertainties.

$\dfrac{\Delta v}{v} \times 100\% = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{0.05}{4.30} + \dfrac{20}{1450} + 0.05\right) \times 100\% = 3.8\% \approx 4\%$.

perOption.A: Too small: underestimates the sum of the terms.
perOption.B: Too small: underestimates the sum of the terms.
perOption.C: Correct. 3.8%, which rounds to 4%.
perOption.D: Does not apply the power $1/2$ (adds the fractional uncertainties without halving: 7.5%).

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Both balls start from rest, so each falls $s = \tfrac12 g t^2$ in the same time $\Delta t$.

Both fall by the same distance, so the gap between them stays equal to the gap at release.

perOption.A: Correct. Equal fall distances in equal times keep the gap constant.
perOption.B: Wrongly assumes the lower ball falls more slowly or the upper catches up.
perOption.C: Wrongly assumes the lower ball accelerates less or the upper one faster; both have acceleration $g$.
perOption.D: Confuses this with a case where the lower ball has an initial velocity; both start from rest.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Force equals rate of change of momentum of the paint: $F = N\rho A v^2$.

$F = (27)(900)(0.4\times10^{-6})(3.0)^2 = 0.087\ \mathrm{N} = 87\ \mathrm{mN}$.

perOption.A: Does not match the calculation; likely a slip in the number of holes or a missing factor.
perOption.B: Does not match the calculation; probably an arithmetic or unit slip.
perOption.C: Does not match the calculation; probably an arithmetic or unit slip.
perOption.D: Correct. $F = \rho A v^2$ per hole, times 27 holes.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Power = $Fv + P_{\text{friction}}$, where $F$ is the component of the passengers' weight along the escalator.

$P = (62\times20\times9.81\times\tfrac{30}{60}\times0.75) + 2.5\times10^3 = 7.1\times10^3\ \mathrm{W} = 7.1\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Does not include the full passenger load contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. Passenger load power plus 2.5 kW friction.
perOption.C: Does not match the working; likely an error in the sine of the incline or the mass.
perOption.D: Likely uses the wrong component of weight (e.g. no $\sin\theta$ factor handled correctly).

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Work done by the external force = mass $\times$ change in potential.

$W = (1)(\phi_{final} - \phi_{initial}) = -\dfrac{3GM}{2R} - \left(-\dfrac{GM}{R}\right) = -\dfrac{GM}{2R}$.

perOption.A: Adds the two potentials instead of taking the difference.
perOption.B: Correct. Final minus initial potential.
perOption.C: Sign error: initial minus final.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes and gets the sign wrong.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Net force towards the centre is $mr\omega^2$, with $\omega = 2\pi/3.7$.

Top: $F_{top} + mg = mr\omega^2$, so $F_{top} = 77[4(2\pi/3.7)^2 - 9.81] = 133\ \mathrm{N}$ downwards.

Bottom: $F_{bottom} = mg + mr\omega^2 = 77[4(2\pi/3.7)^2 + 9.81] = 1640\ \mathrm{N}$ upwards.

perOption.A: Swaps the magnitudes between top and bottom and misjudges the directions.
perOption.B: Gives the right magnitudes at the wrong positions with wrong directions.
perOption.C: Correct. At the top the wheel pushes down (weight helps); at the bottom it pushes up.
perOption.D: Right magnitudes but directions reversed.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.body:
The satellite moves in a circle about the Sun, so the resultant force towards the Sun equals $ma_c = m R\omega^2$.

The Sun pulls it towards the Sun with $\dfrac{GM_S m}{R^2}$, while the Earth pulls it away from the Sun (it lies between them) with $\dfrac{GM_E m}{r^2}$.

So $\dfrac{GM_S m}{R^2} - \dfrac{GM_E m}{r^2} = m(R\omega^2)$.

perOption.A: Ignores the Earth's pull on the satellite.
perOption.B: Uses only the Earth's pull; the orbit is about the Sun.
perOption.C: Subtracts in the wrong order, giving a resultant towards the Earth.
perOption.D: Correct. Resultant towards the Sun = centripetal force.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.issues: The school's worked solution is a single line; the opposing Earth pull explanation is a short connecting clause.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q12.body:
$E_p = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ and gravitational force = centripetal force gives $E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so $E_p = -2E_k$.

New orbit: $E_p' = E_p + E$, so $-2E_k' = -2E_k + E$.

Hence $E_k' = E_k - \dfrac{E}{2}$: kinetic energy decreases by $E/2$.

perOption.A: Assumes kinetic energy rises as the satellite goes higher.
perOption.B: Assumes KE changes by the full amount that GPE changes (energy exchange without the factor of 2).
perOption.C: Gets the magnitude but not the direction; speed decreases in a higher orbit.
perOption.D: Correct. $E_p = -2E_k$, so $\Delta E_k = -\tfrac12\Delta E_p$.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.body:
With $x = x_0\sin\omega t$ (the graph of $a$ starts at zero and goes negative, matching this), at $t = 5T/8$:

$\dfrac{x}{x_0} = \sin\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\times\dfrac{5T}{8}\right) = \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4} = -0.71$.

perOption.A: Correct. $\sin(5\pi/4) = -0.71$.
perOption.B: Sign error; $5\pi/4$ lies in the third quadrant.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos$ or $\sin(2\pi/3)$-type angle giving 0.87 in magnitude.
perOption.D: Wrong function and wrong sign.

perOption.A: Forgets the $9.0$ from $f^2$ or squares incorrectly.
perOption.B: Uses the factor of frequency and amplitude without squaring.
perOption.C: Correct. $0.5\times9\times0.16 = 0.72$.
perOption.D: Does not square the amplitude factor: $0.5\times9\times0.4 = 1.8$.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Intensity $I = \dfrac{P}{2\pi r d} \propto \dfrac1r$, and $I \propto A^2$, so $A \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt r}$.

$\dfrac{A'}{2.0} = \sqrt{\dfrac{150}{1200}}$, so $A' = 0.71\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Uses $A \propto 1/r^3$ or similar over-steep dependence.
perOption.B: Uses $A \propto 1/r$ giving $0.25$ would be C; this uses an inverse-square-type error.
perOption.C: Uses $A \propto 1/r$ (point-source spherical spreading).
perOption.D: Correct. Circular spreading gives $A \propto 1/\sqrt r$.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Unpolarised light passing a polariser has its intensity halved, so $I_P = \tfrac12 I$. This eliminates A and B.

The amplitude stays at $A$ along the first axis. The angle between the two axes is $75^\circ$ (or $105^\circ$), so resolving the field gives $A' = A\cos75^\circ = A\sin15^\circ$.

perOption.A: Intensity $I/\sqrt2$ is wrong; unpolarised light is halved.
perOption.B: Wrong intensity, and an extra factor of $\tfrac12$ in amplitude.
perOption.C: Correct. $I/2$ and $A\sin15^\circ$.
perOption.D: Right intensity but an extra $1/\sqrt2$ factor in the amplitude.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q17.issues: School treats amplitude after the first polariser as $A$ (strictly $A/\sqrt2$ if intensity halves), but the options are consistent with the key letter C.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q18.body:
First minimum: $b\sin\theta = \lambda$.

From the graph the first minimum is at $\sin\theta = 0.05$, so $\lambda = (0.010\times10^{-3})(0.05) = 5.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 500\ \mathrm{nm}$.

perOption.A: Correct. First minimum at $\sin\theta = 0.05$.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin\theta = 0.075$, which is not a minimum on the graph.
perOption.C: Unit slip by a factor of 1000.
perOption.D: Unit slip and wrong sine value.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Electric potential energy $U = qV$. The electron has negative charge, X is at a positive potential and Y at a negative potential, so $U_Y > U_X$.

Force $F = qE$. The equipotentials are closer together at Y, so $E_Y > E_X$ and $F_Y > F_X$.

perOption.A: Wrong sign for $U$ and wrong comparison of field strength.
perOption.B: Wrong sign for $U$ (treats the electron like a positive charge).
perOption.C: Right $U$ comparison but misjudges field strength; lines are closer at Y.
perOption.D: Correct. $U_Y > U_X$ and $F_Y > F_X$.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Break in the negative wire of the cable: the voltmeter reads 24 V whether connected to X or Y.

(For comparison, a break in the positive wire gives 0 V at both X and Y, and a break within the motor gives 24 V at X and 0 V at Y.)

perOption.A: This pair of readings would be neither fault; a positive-wire break gives 0 V at both.
perOption.B: A reading of 12 V does not arise from any single break.
perOption.C: A break within the motor would give 0 V at Y, not 24 V.
perOption.D: Correct. Both terminals are at 24 V relative to the supply negative.

tjc-2025-prelim-p1-q21.body:
Potential divider with the 5 k$\Omega$ resistor.

Dark: $V = \dfrac{5\times10^3}{5\times10^3 + 5\times10^6}\times6 = 0.0060\ \mathrm{V}$.

Bright: $V = \dfrac{5\times10^3}{5\times10^3 + 1\times10^3}\times6 = 5.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

So the p.d. switches between about 0 V and 5 V.

perOption.A: Correct. Swings between about 0 V and 5 V.
perOption.B: Shows a non-zero baseline of about 1 V; the dark p.d. is only 0.006 V.
perOption.C: Shows a swing between about 0 and 4 V, not 5 V.
perOption.D: Shows the p.d. near 6 V and dipping, which reverses the dark and bright cases.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Thermal energy $Q$ has SI base units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$. From $k=(Q/t)L/[A(T_1-T_2)]$, the units of $k$ are $(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})/(\mathrm{m^2\,K})=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses degrees Celsius for the temperature difference in a base-unit expression.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses degrees Celsius and fails to carry the inverse-square seconds from the energy unit through the calculation.
perOption.D: Drops the inverse-square seconds from the energy unit.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Estimate the handset volume as $0.10\times0.25\times0.010\ \mathrm{m^3}$, of order $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. An atom with diameter about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$ has volume of order $10^{-30}\ \mathrm{m^3}$. The ratio gives about $10^{-4}/10^{-30}=10^{26}$ atoms.

perOption.A: Underestimates how many atoms fit by using an atomic volume much too large.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Would require atomic dimensions much smaller than the typical $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.D: Would require an atomic volume of order $10^{-41}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, far smaller than the estimate.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: For P the resultant force is zero, but the forces have a non-zero torque about the centre. For Q the torque about the centre vanishes, but there is a net upward force. For R the torque also vanishes, but the two upward components total only $2(50)\cos30^\circ$, leaving a net downward force.

perOption.A: Misses P’s net torque and Q’s upward resultant force.
perOption.B: Misses P’s net torque and assumes the inclined forces on R balance the downward force.
perOption.C: Assumes Q and R are in equilibrium because their torques vanish, overlooking their vertical resultants.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The key says R has an upward resultant. Its resultant is downward because 2 × 50 cos 30° < 100 N. D remains correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Let $N$ be the reaction of the sloping plane and $F$ that of the vertical plane. Vertical equilibrium gives $N\sin60^\circ=mg$, and horizontal equilibrium gives $N\cos60^\circ=F$. Dividing gives $F=mg\cot60^\circ=1.5(9.81)\cot60^\circ=8.5\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Omits the wall reaction needed to balance the horizontal component of the sloping plane’s reaction.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the sphere’s weight as the wall reaction.
perOption.D: Calculates the full reaction of the sloping plane.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: The magnitude of the momentum–time gradient is $(2.7-1.5)/0.40=3.0\ \mathrm{N}$, giving the magnitude of the resultant force. Momentum decreases, so the resultant acts opposite to the motion. Thus $5.0-F=3.0$ and $F=2.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Takes the magnitude of the resultant as the applied force.
perOption.C: Assumes the applied and resistive forces balance despite the falling momentum.
perOption.D: Adds the resultant magnitude to the resistive force, giving a resultant in the direction of motion.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The letter appears on page 1 and the worked solution continues on page 2.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Let $h$ be the total rise and $v$ the speed at the start of the final second. Over that second, $0=v^2-2g(0.25h)$ and $0=\sqrt{0.50gh}-g(1)$, giving $h=19.62\ \mathrm{m}$. For the whole ascent, $0=u^2-2(9.81)(19.62)$ gives the launch speed $u=19.62\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The ascent time $T$ then follows from $0=19.62-9.81T$, so $T=2.00\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Adds 25% of a second to the final second, confusing a distance fraction with a time increment.
perOption.B: This time makes the final second cover about 44% of the rise, from the constant-acceleration distance relation.
perOption.C: This time makes the final second cover about 36% of the rise, from the constant-acceleration distance relation.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The balls start with equal total mechanical energy and there are no resistive forces, so their final total mechanical energies are equal. They undergo the same net energy conversion between X and Y, and ball 2 takes less time, so it has the higher average rate of conversion.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Assigns extra energy to ball 2 and credits the slower ball with the higher average rate.
perOption.C: Confuses ball 2’s higher rate of energy conversion with a higher final total energy.
perOption.D: Assigns the higher rate to the ball that takes longer to undergo the same net energy conversion.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: Let $T$ be the tension in the string. The blocks move at constant speed, so force balance gives $T=Mg\sin\theta=mg$. The rate at which the tension transfers energy to P is $Tv=Mgv\sin\theta=mgv$, so expressions 1 and 2 both apply.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Misses that the tension also equals the component of P’s weight along the slope.
perOption.C: Includes the sum of the weights and misses that Q’s weight equals the tension.
perOption.D: Misses that the tension equals the weight of Q.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: The horizontal velocity is constant, with $u_x=18/1.5=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At the highest point the vertical component is zero, so $E_{\mathrm k}=\tfrac12 m u_x^2=\tfrac12(0.40)(12)^2=28.8\ \mathrm{J}$, or $29\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Treats zero vertical velocity at the apex as zero total velocity.
perOption.B: Uses the horizontal speed without squaring it in the kinetic energy formula.
perOption.C: Uses the launch vertical speed of about $7.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in place of the horizontal speed at the apex.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The letter and horizontal-speed calculation are on page 2, with the kinetic-energy calculation on page 3.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: At P, the drag force acts opposite to the upward and forward velocity, so it has a horizontal component and a downward component. The horizontal acceleration is therefore non-zero. The downward component of drag adds to the weight, making the vertical acceleration greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ in magnitude.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal component of drag.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the acceleration components for a projectile with negligible air resistance.
perOption.D: Includes the horizontal drag but omits the downward component of drag.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The momentum component parallel to the side of the table is unchanged, so the average force is perpendicular to the side. Taking away from the side as positive, the average force is $\Delta p/\Delta t=[m(v\cos30^\circ)-m(-v\cos30^\circ)]/\Delta t=2mv\cos30^\circ/\Delta t$.

perOption.A: Uses the initial momentum magnitude in place of the change in normal momentum.
perOption.B: Uses just one normal component and misses the reversal.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the component along the side, which is the component that stays constant.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.issues: A and D are numerically identical since 2 sin 30° = 1. Both are incorrect.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: Conservation of momentum gives $u=v+w$, and conservation of kinetic energy gives $u^2=v^2+w^2$. Squaring the first equation and comparing with the second gives $2vw=0$. For an actual collision the proton takes the incoming velocity, $w=u$, and the neutron stops, $v=0$. Opposite outgoing velocities of equal magnitude would give zero total momentum, so statement C is wrong.

perOption.A: This statement correctly applies momentum conservation after cancelling the equal masses.
perOption.B: This statement correctly applies kinetic-energy conservation for an elastic collision.
perOption.C: Correct. The statement would give zero final momentum.
perOption.D: This statement correctly describes the transfer of velocity to the initially stationary proton.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Static friction supplies the centripetal force on the mass. It acts from P towards the centre O.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This is tangent to the circle opposite the velocity, so it would slow the mass.
perOption.C: This is tangent to the circle along the velocity, so it would speed the mass up.
perOption.D: This points radially outward, opposite the centripetal acceleration.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The loss in gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy, so $mgh=\frac12mv^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. At the bottom, $N-mg=mv^2/R$, so $N=mg+2mgh/R=mg(1+2h/R)$. By Newton’s third law, the block exerts a force of this magnitude downward on the track.

perOption.A: Sets the normal force equal to the weight, giving zero radial acceleration.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $v^2=gh$, missing the factor of two from kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Gives the net inward force on the block and omits the weight term.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The worked solution starts on page 3 and continues on page 4.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: At the point where the net force on the third mass is zero, the attractions from $M$ and $m$ are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Since $M>m$, that point is nearer the smaller mass $m$.

perOption.A: Places the zero near the midpoint, where the larger mass still pulls more strongly.
perOption.B: Keeps the resultant positive throughout the gap, missing the cancellation point.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Places the minimum nearer the smaller mass but leaves a nonzero force there.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The curves are schematic. For spherical masses with inverse-square external fields, the force magnitude has a cusp at an interior zero, whereas C draws a smooth minimum.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: Reducing damping reduces energy loss, increasing the amplitude near resonance. The resonance peak narrows and shifts towards the undamped natural frequency, which is higher than the damped peak frequency. Only statement 3 is correct.

perOption.A: Statement 1 reverses the effect of lower damping on the amplitude near resonance.
perOption.B: Statement 2 reverses the shift of the peak frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Includes statements 1 and 2, which reverse the changes in amplitude and peak frequency.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: The microphone intercepts the fraction $a/(4\pi r^2)$ of the emitted power. Its detected power is $P'=\frac{0.85\times10^{-4}}{4\pi(4.0)^2}(50.0)=2.1\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the intercepted fraction for the stated area and radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treating the numerical area in square centimetres as square metres makes the result $10^4$ times too large.
perOption.D: This is close to the intensity $50.0/(4\pi r^2)$, which still needs to be multiplied by the microphone area.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The first filter transmits $I/2$ from the unpolarised beam. By Malus’ law, the second transmits $(I/2)\cos^2 10^\circ$. For the third, $(I/2)\cos^2 10^\circ\cos^2\theta=I/3$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the second and third axes. Solving gives $\theta=34^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adds the initial $10^\circ$ tilt and reports an angle relative to the first filter.
perOption.C: An angle of $47^\circ$ attenuates the beam below one-third of its initial intensity.
perOption.D: Using $54^\circ$ in the last Malus factor gives too little transmitted light.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The key’s third-filter equation contains a stray intermediate equality and drops the factor I in its next term. The rewrite retains the intended Malus factors.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Use $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, with $d=1/(6\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. For $n=1$, $\sin\theta=(490\times10^{-9})/d$ gives $\theta=17^\circ$. Since $\sin\theta\leq1$, $n\leq d/\lambda=3.4$, so the highest order is 3. There are $2(3)+1=7$ maxima including the central maximum.

perOption.A: The grating equation gives a first-order angle of $17^\circ$.
perOption.B: The third order is still allowed because $3\lambda/d<1$.
perOption.C: Increasing the line density decreases the spacing and lowers the upper bound on the order.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The worked solution starts on page 4 and continues on page 5.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The heater heats both the water and the tank, so $Q=(mc+C)\Delta T=[10(4200)+5000](45-25)=9.4\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}$. Using $P=Q/t$, the time is $t=(9.4\times10^5)/(3.0\times10^3)=313\ \mathrm{s}$, which rounds to $310\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Uses too small an energy input for the combined heat capacities and the $20\ \mathrm{K}$ rise.
perOption.B: Accounts for heating the water alone and omits the tank.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses too large an energy input for the stated temperature rise and combined heat capacities.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, $pV\propto T$, so $T_f/T_i=(p_fV_f)/(p_iV_i)=2\times2=4$. Since $\frac12mv_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac32kT$, the squared speed ratio is also 4. Hence $v_f=2v_i=2u$.

perOption.A: Assumes the temperature stays constant even though $pV$ quadruples.
perOption.B: Counts only one of the two factors of two in $pV$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Scales speed directly with temperature instead of scaling its square.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Both gases have the same temperature, so their molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, $\frac32 kT$. Since this energy is also $\frac12m\langle v^2\rangle$, the lighter nitrogen molecules have a greater mean square speed and rms speed.

perOption.A: Internal energy is a system quantity and can depend on the amount of each gas.
perOption.B: The lighter nitrogen molecules have greater mean square speed at the same temperature.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Taking the square root of the mean square speed preserves the difference between the gases.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The drift current is $I=nqvA=(8.2\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})(2.3\times10^{-5})(8.0\times10^{-6})=2.41\ \mathrm{A}$. The resistance is $R=V/I=3.0/2.41=1.2\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Would require a current of about $38\ \mathrm{A}$, much larger than the drift current.
perOption.B: Would require a current of about $19\ \mathrm{A}$, much larger than the drift current.
perOption.C: Implies a current of $3.75\ \mathrm{A}$, overestimating the drift current.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.issues: The school prints no letter, but its worked value of 1.2 Ω corresponds to D. The batch keyAnswer is A and keyStatus is answer-missing.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Reducing the light intensity increases the LDR’s resistance. The total circuit resistance therefore increases and the current decreases. The potential difference across the fixed resistor decreases as well.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies the voltage change across the LDR to the voltmeter, which is across the fixed resistor.
perOption.C: Reverses the current change and overlooks that the fixed resistor’s voltage follows the current.
perOption.D: Overlooks that the increased total resistance reduces the current.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: For the original stationary droplet, $qE=mg$. The oil density stays the same, so $m\propto r^3$ and doubling the radius gives $m_2=8m$. The second droplet has charge $q/2$, so $(q/2)E_2=8mg=8qE$. Cancelling $q$ gives $E_2=16E$.

perOption.A: Accounts for halving the charge but keeps the original weight.
perOption.B: Treats the mass as proportional to radius, giving only a factor of two in weight.
perOption.C: Accounts for the eightfold weight increase but keeps the original charge.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials at every crossing. They point from higher to lower potential, here from $7\ \mathrm{V}$ through $5\ \mathrm{V}$ to $3\ \mathrm{V}$. Only C satisfies both rules.

perOption.A: The arrows point towards lower potential but cross the outer equipotentials obliquely.
perOption.B: The arrows point towards higher potential and cross the outer equipotentials obliquely.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The lines cross perpendicularly but the arrows point towards higher potential.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Each segment experiences a force of magnitude $BIL$. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives upward components for both forces and horizontal components that cancel. Each upward component is $BIL\sin30^\circ$, so the resultant is $2BIL\sin30^\circ=BIL$ towards the top of the page.

perOption.A: Reverses the force direction given by the current and inward field.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the full force magnitudes and reverses the resultant direction.
perOption.D: Adds the full magnitudes instead of their upward components.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The printed letter B agrees with the batch and the question. The key’s worked text describes a different straight-wire question, so it provides no usable working for this diagram.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: At the rim, $v=r\omega=2\pi fr$, so $f=v/(2\pi r)$. A radius sweeps an area $\pi r^2$ per revolution, giving $E=B\pi r^2f$. Substituting gives $E=Brv/2=Bdv/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the entire radius as moving at the rim speed, giving $B(d/2)v$.
perOption.C: Uses the full diameter with the rim speed in the straight-conductor expression.
perOption.D: Omits a length factor, so the expression does not have units of voltage.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The letter is on page 6 and the working is on page 7.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Using $K=p^2/(2m)$ with $K=(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})\ \mathrm{J}$ and $m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $p=2.312\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The momentum uncertainty is $\Delta p=0.01p=2.312\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta p\,\Delta x\approx h$, the minimum position uncertainty is approximately $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Requires a much smaller momentum uncertainty than the stated 1.0% of the calculated momentum.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Is about $\sqrt{10}$ too large, consistent with a factor-of-ten underestimate of the energy in the momentum calculation.
perOption.D: Implies a momentum uncertainty larger than the full proton momentum under the syllabus estimate.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.issues: The key and syllabus use the order-of-magnitude convention ΔxΔp ≳ h. The exact standard-deviation bound ħ/2 would yield about 2.28 × 10⁻¹³ m, which is absent from the options.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Multiply each binding energy per nucleon by the corresponding nucleon number, with zero binding energy for free neutrons. This gives $121(8.26)+113(8.52)-235(7.59)=178.57\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx179\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Uses a much smaller binding-energy gain than the difference between the nuclear totals.
perOption.B: Underestimates the gain by failing to account for the full change in nuclear binding energy.
perOption.C: Undercounts the binding-energy gain of the two daughter nuclei.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The printed key shows D, but the batch keyAnswer is A and keyStatus is answer-missing. The key prints 112 for silver-113, which gives 170.05 MeV. Using the printed question’s 113 gives the key’s stated 179 MeV.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q25.body:
For an ideal transformer, $V_s = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}V_p$.

Power in the secondary $= \dfrac{V_s^2}{R} = \dfrac{(N_s V_p/N_p)^2}{R} = \dfrac{N_s^2 V_p^2}{N_p^2 R}$, and since the transformer is ideal this equals the power in the primary coil.

perOption.A: Inverts the turns ratio and does not square $V_p$.
perOption.B: Does not square the turns ratio when squaring $V_s$.
perOption.C: Correct. $P = V_s^2/R$ with $V_s = (N_s/N_p)V_p$.
perOption.D: Squares the turns ratio but forgets to square $V_p$.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q26.body:
Consider one period ($1.0\ \mathrm{ms}$), in which $V = 46\ \mathrm{V}$ for $0.25\ \mathrm{ms}$ and zero otherwise.

1. Square the graph: $V^2 = 46^2 = 2116\ \mathrm{V^2}$.

2. Mean over one period: $\langle V^2 \rangle = \dfrac{\text{area}}{\text{period}} = \dfrac{(2116)(0.25\times10^{-3})}{1.0\times10^{-3}} = 529\ \mathrm{V^2}$.

3. Take the square root: $V_{rms} = \sqrt{529} = 23\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: This is roughly the mean voltage ($46 \times 0.25 \approx 12\ \mathrm{V}$), not the r.m.s. value.
perOption.B: Correct. $\sqrt{\langle V^2\rangle} = \sqrt{529} = 23\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.C: Uses $V_0/\sqrt{2}$, which applies only to sinusoidal voltages.
perOption.D: Gives the mean of $V^2$ but forgets to take the square root.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q27.body:
From $hf = \phi + E_{max}$, $E_{max} = hf - hf_0$.

The $x$-intercept is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi/h$, so a larger work function gives a larger threshold frequency: Y's line starts further right. The gradient of the graph is Planck's constant, so it does not change and the lines are parallel.

perOption.A: Shows a smaller threshold frequency, which corresponds to a smaller work function.
perOption.B: Correct. Larger $f_0$, same gradient $h$.
perOption.C: Shows a smaller threshold frequency and a steeper gradient; the gradient must stay $h$.
perOption.D: Has the larger threshold frequency but a smaller gradient; the gradient must stay $h$.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q28.body:
Uncertainty in momentum: $\Delta p = m\Delta v = (9.11\times10^{-31})(5.8\times10^{6})\left(\dfrac{0.2}{100}\right) = 1.0568\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

Using $\Delta p\,\Delta x \geq h$: $\Delta x_{min} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{1.0568\times10^{-26}} = 6.3\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Divides $h$ by $\Delta v$ only, omitting the electron mass.
perOption.B: This is $\Delta p$, not $\Delta x$.
perOption.C: Uses the full momentum $mv$ (giving the de Broglie wavelength) instead of the uncertainty $\Delta p$.
perOption.D: Correct. $\Delta x = h/\Delta p$ with $\Delta p = 0.2\%$ of $mv$.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q30.body:
The count rate drops sharply when paper is inserted, so the radiation is stopped by paper: it must be $\alpha$ radiation, which has low penetrating power.

The remaining $24\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ is the background count rate, so the initial count rate due to the source is $532 - 24 = 508\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

After two half-lives the source count rate is $\tfrac{1}{4}(508) = 127\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, so the reading is $127 + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct radiation, but forgets to add the background count back to the reading.
perOption.B: $\beta$ radiation would not be stopped by paper, and the background is not added back.
perOption.C: Correct. $\alpha$; $\tfrac{1}{4}(532-24) + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: $\beta$ radiation would pass through paper.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q1.body:
Estimate a pen as a cylinder of length $14.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and diameter $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Volume $= \pi\left(\dfrac{1.0}{2}\right)^2(14.0) \approx 11\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, closest to $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

perOption.A: Far too small; about the volume of a small bead.
perOption.B: Too small by a factor of ten; a pen is much longer than 1 cm.
perOption.C: Correct. $\pi(0.5)^2(14) \approx 11\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
perOption.D: Too large; that is about the volume of a small cup of water.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q2.body:
Change in velocity = total area under the $a$–$t$ graph.

Total area $= \tfrac{1}{2}(4.0)(2.4) + \left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(6.0)(3.6)\right) = 4.8 - 10.8 = -6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Assumes the positive and negative areas cancel; they do not.
perOption.B: Averages the two extreme accelerations instead of finding the area.
perOption.C: Correct. Net area $= 4.8 - 10.8 = -6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Treats both areas as negative ($-(4.8 + 10.8)$) instead of taking the area above the axis as positive.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q3.body:
Newton's 2nd law: the forces must act on the same body to produce a resultant force. Only $F_3$ and $F_4$ (both on the concrete) satisfy this.

Newton's 3rd law: the forces must act on different bodies. Only $F_2$ (on the Earth) and $F_4$ (on the concrete) satisfy this.

perOption.A: Correct. $F_3, F_4$ both act on the concrete; $F_2, F_4$ act on different bodies.
perOption.B: $F_1$ and $F_2$ both act on the Earth, so they cannot be a 3rd-law pair.
perOption.C: $F_1$ acts on the Earth and $F_3$ on the concrete, so they cannot combine into one body's resultant force.
perOption.D: $F_1, F_3$ act on different bodies (not a 2nd-law pair) and $F_1, F_2$ act on the same body (not a 3rd-law pair).

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q4.body:
Two pairs of the forces are antiparallel and separated by a perpendicular distance $d$, forming two couples, each of torque $Fd$.

Total torque $= Fd + Fd = 2Fd$.

The other forces act along lines through the centre, so they produce no torque.

perOption.A: Counts only one of the two couples.
perOption.B: Correct. Two couples of $Fd$ each.
perOption.C: Counts an extra couple; forces whose lines of action pass through the centre give no torque.
perOption.D: Treats all eight forces as producing torque, but four act through the centre.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q5.body:
Atmospheric pressure acts on both the top and bottom of the drum, so its effect cancels.

At equilibrium, weight of drum and content = weight of water displaced $= V\rho g = 0.80\times0.19\times1.1\times10^{3}\times9.81 = 1640\ \mathrm{N}$.

Mass of drum and content $= \dfrac{1640}{9.81} = 167\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $m = \rho V = 1.1\times10^3 \times 0.80 \times 0.19 = 167\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from the displaced volume and the seawater density.
perOption.C: This is the weight in newtons, not the mass in kilograms.
perOption.D: Does not follow from the displaced volume; the upthrust equals the weight, so the mass is $\rho V$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q6.body:
The net force from the rope on the wheel is $100 - 20 = 80\ \mathrm{N}$, and the rim moves at $0.30 \times 50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Output power of the motor $= (100-20)(0.30)(50) = 1200\ \mathrm{W}$.

Electrical power supplied $= \dfrac{1200}{0.2} = 6000\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies the output power by the efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.B: Adds the two tensions and multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Adds the tensions ($120\ \mathrm{N}$) instead of taking their difference.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q7.body:
Angular velocity $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r} = \dfrac{6.0}{0.40} = 15\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

From A to B the body turns through a right angle, so the angular displacement is $\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1.6\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies $v$ by $r$ for $\omega$ and gives the arc length ($0.63\ \mathrm{m}$) instead of the angle.
perOption.B: Multiplies $v$ by $r$ instead of dividing.
perOption.C: Gives the arc length $r\theta = 0.63\ \mathrm{m}$ instead of the angle in radians.
perOption.D: Correct. $\omega = v/r$ and $\theta = \pi/2$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q8.body:
Gravitational force $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$.

On the ground, $r = R$: $W = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$ (1). At a height $2R$ above the ground, $r = 3R$: $F = \dfrac{GMm}{(3R)^2}$ (2).

Dividing (2) by (1) gives $F = \dfrac{W}{9}$.

perOption.A: Treats the force as inversely proportional to height, not to the square of distance from the centre.
perOption.B: Uses $r = 3R$ but forgets to square it.
perOption.C: Uses the height $2R$ as the distance from the Earth's centre.
perOption.D: Correct. $r = 3R$, so $F = W/3^2$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q9.body:
For an orbiting satellite, gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = mr\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$, so $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$.

The orbit radius is independent of the satellite's mass $m$, so with the same period the radius is the same: ratio $= 1$.

perOption.A: Wrongly assumes the radius is inversely proportional to the satellite's mass.
perOption.B: Correct. $m$ cancels, so $r$ depends only on $T$.
perOption.C: Wrongly assumes the radius depends on the square root of the satellite's mass.
perOption.D: Wrongly assumes the radius is proportional to the satellite's mass.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q10.body:
From the graph, amplitude $x_0 = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and maximum speed $v_0 = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$v_0 = \omega x_0 \Rightarrow 20 = \omega \times 4.0$, so $\omega = 5.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{5.0} = 1.257\ \mathrm{s}$.

Speed goes from maximum (at equilibrium) to zero (at the extreme) in $\tfrac{1}{4}T = 0.31\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Gives $1/\omega$ instead of a quarter period.
